explanationUnits: Binary and decimal prefixes use different scales

objectives.description: Understand the difference between and use: kibi and kilo; mebi and mega; gibi and giga; tebi and tera
explanationUnits: Binary and decimal prefixes use different scales

knowledgeUnits.heading: Binary and decimal prefixes use different scales

leadVisual.title: Binary and decimal magnitude prefixes

coreExplanation: Binary prefixes use powers of 1024; decimal prefixes use powers of 1000.
Convert through bytes when changing byte units; 1 B = 8 b.
n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns, representing unsigned values 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

teachingBlocks.text: A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. Two distinguishable physical states can represent these alternatives. Bits do not identify their own meaning: an agreed representation determines whether a pattern stands for a number, a character, a colour or something else.
teachingBlocks.title: From two states to information

teachingBlocks.text: A nibble contains four bits and a byte contains eight bits. Lower-case b means bit; upper-case B means byte. A capacity counts available storage, whereas the value represented by one stored pattern depends on its encoding.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the unit and the meaning

teachingBlocks.text: Appending one independent bit doubles the possibilities. Eight bits therefore have 256 patterns, but the largest unsigned value is 255 because zero uses one pattern. These same pattern counts will determine character capacity, colour choices and sound levels.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the power of two

teachingBlocks.text: Each binary prefix level multiplies by 1024; each decimal level multiplies by 1000. The prefix attaches a multiplier to the unit: KiB counts bytes, while Kib counts bits. Keep the i and the case when copying a specification.
teachingBlocks.title: Two scales for the same quantity
Worked example: express a 4 MiB file in bytes and MB
items: 4 × 2²⁰ = 4,194,304 bytes. Multiplication expands the larger unit into individual bytes.
4,194,304 ÷ 1,000,000 = 4.194304 MB. Division groups those bytes into decimal megabytes.
4.194304 × 1,000,000 = 4,194,304 bytes. Both labels describe exactly the same file.

teachingBlocks.title: Worked example: how many complete files fit?
items: A device has 1 KiB = 1024 bytes available. Every file occupies exactly 300 bytes, with all overhead already included.
3 × 300 = 900 fits; 4 × 300 = 1200 does not. Three complete files fit.
1024 − 900 = 124 bytes remain. A fractional fourth file is not a complete saved file.

teachingBlocks.text: For a mixed-unit calculation, convert bits to bytes as well as converting the prefix. For example, 24,000 bits ÷ 8 = 3000 bytes = 3 kB. Check that the final unit answers the question; a result in bits is eight times its numerical value in bytes.
teachingBlocks.title: Check dimensions and plausibility

knowledgeUnits.heading: Positional number systems: denary and binary

leadVisual.title: Read an unsigned byte by position

coreExplanation: The base determines the legal digits and the place values.
Decode binary by adding the weights of its 1 bits; encode by selecting weights or repeated division.
Keep the requested width and reverse-check the value.

teachingBlocks.text: A positional number system assigns a place value to each position. Denary has ten digit symbols, 0 to 9, and multiplies each place by 10 as you move left. Binary has two symbols, 0 and 1, and multiplies each place by 2. Leading zeros do not change a non-negative value, but they can be required by a storage width.
teachingBlocks.title: Start with the familiar denary system
The same written digits can mean different values
rows: 407; zero preserves the empty tens position

teachingBlocks.title: Worked example: binary 00111011 to denary
items: From left to right the eight places are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 59. The 0 in the 4s position contributes nothing.

teachingBlocks.title: Reverse direction: build 59 using descending weights

teachingBlocks.text: Reading the decisions from the 128s place to the 1s place gives 00111011. The final remainder is zero, and decoding returns 59. If an unsigned result needs more than the supplied width, report that it cannot fit; deleting its leading 1 would change its value.
teachingBlocks.title: Finish and verify the conversion

teachingBlocks.text: Another method divides repeatedly by 2 and records the remainders. Each remainder is the next least-significant bit, so read them upwards at the end. For 13: 13 ÷ 2 gives quotient 6 remainder 1; 6 gives 3 remainder 0; 3 gives 1 remainder 1; 1 gives 0 remainder 1. Stop at quotient 0 and read 1101; pad to 00001101 for eight bits.
teachingBlocks.title: Understand repeated division

knowledgeUnits.heading: Hexadecimal

leadVisual.title: One value in three notations

coreExplanation: Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and A–F with powers-of-16 place values.
One hexadecimal digit maps to four bits; group binary integers from the right.
Hexadecimal is compact, reversible notation for addresses, debugging data and colour values.

teachingBlocks.text: Hexadecimal is base 16. Its single-digit values are 0 to 9 followed by A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15. Places from the right are 1, 16, 256 and 4096. A letter such as B is one digit, not the denary numeral 11 occupying two places.
teachingBlocks.title: Sixteen digit values

teachingBlocks.text: Four binary bits have 2⁴ = 16 patterns, exactly enough for one hexadecimal digit. This is why nibble grouping works directly. It changes the notation people read, not the underlying stored bits. Memory addresses and debugging values become shorter; RGB colour components can also be shown as pairs of hexadecimal digits.
teachingBlocks.title: Why the four-bit shortcut works
Worked conversion in all directions: the value 59
rows: 59 ÷ 16 gives quotient 3 and remainder 11; 11 maps to B.

teachingBlocks.title: Worked example: convert denary 300 to hexadecimal
items: 300 ÷ 16 gives quotient 18, remainder 12 (C). This is the units digit.
18 ÷ 16 gives quotient 1, remainder 2. Then 1 ÷ 16 gives quotient 0, remainder 1; stop.

teachingBlocks.text: For a binary integer, group from the right. Binary 101101 becomes 0010 1101 after padding the incomplete left group, giving 2D. Padding on the right would multiply the value instead. A byte always needs two hexadecimal digits when its full width is required: 00000101 becomes 05.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve position and width

teachingBlocks.text: For example, a debugging display can show the same byte as 00111011 or 3B. A programmer can recover either nibble immediately. The computer does not need to store an extra hexadecimal copy simply because the display uses hexadecimal.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain an application through its benefit

knowledgeUnits.heading: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)

leadVisual.title: 407 as three BCD digit groups

coreExplanation: BCD assigns four bits to each decimal digit; only codes 0000–1001 are valid.
Preserve every required digit, including zero, and decode groups independently.
Direct decimal-digit handling can justify BCD despite its storage cost.

teachingBlocks.text: Binary Coded Decimal encodes each denary digit separately in four bits. Those groups are digit codes, not powers-of-16 places in one integer. Only 0000 through 1001 are valid digit codes; 1010 through 1111 do not represent decimal digits in this BCD model.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep decimal digits separate
Worked example: encode and decode 407
items: The digits are 4, 0 and 7; the zero must retain its position.
0100 1010 0111 is invalid BCD because 1010 is not a decimal digit. Do not silently read it as A.

teachingBlocks.title: Compare the representations of 59
rows: Hexadecimal notation for the unsigned byte

teachingBlocks.text: A clock or calculator can handle each displayed decimal digit directly from its BCD group. This is useful when the digits themselves are important. The cost is space: two BCD digits need eight bits, although unsigned 59 needs only six bits. There is no rule that all digital clocks must use BCD internally.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect purpose to a trade-off

teachingBlocks.text: A display can retain a leading zero: 007 is 0000 0000 0111 when three digit positions are required. Its numerical value is still 7. Decimal fractions and signed BCD formats require additional conventions; this lesson uses non-negative integer digits only.
teachingBlocks.title: State the encoding boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: One's complement

leadVisual.title: Eight-bit one’s-complement landmarks

coreExplanation: Encode a negative one’s-complement integer by inverting every bit of its positive magnitude at the stated width.
Decode a negative pattern by inversion and restore its minus sign.
Eight-bit one’s complement has range −127 to +127 and two zero patterns.

teachingBlocks.text: A fixed width contains a limited set of bit patterns. A signed representation assigns some patterns to negative values. In one’s complement, non-negative values use ordinary binary with a leading 0. Negating a value inverts every bit at that same width, including leading zeros.
teachingBlocks.title: Define the interpretation before changing bits
Worked round trip for −23 in eight bits
rows: The leading 1 identifies a negative pattern.

teachingBlocks.text: With n bits, the largest positive pattern has a leading 0 followed by n − 1 ones: 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1. Its inverse is the most negative value. Eight-bit one’s complement therefore covers −127 to +127. The two remaining zero patterns are 00000000 (+0) and 11111111 (−0), so 256 patterns represent only 255 distinct integer values.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the range and the two zeros

teachingBlocks.text: An input of −128 does not fit eight-bit one’s complement. Increasing the width changes the available range and the stored pattern. An unsigned interpretation is a different rule: 11101000 is unsigned 232, not unsigned −23.
teachingBlocks.title: Check width and representation

teachingBlocks.text: Bit inversion makes sign reversal simple. Arithmetic still needs the rules of this representation; the two’s-complement rule for discarding the final carry cannot be transferred blindly. Lesson 003 includes a short end-around-carry comparison.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect representation to later arithmetic

knowledgeUnits.heading: Two's complement

leadVisual.title: Read −23 with the correct weights

coreExplanation: Two’s-complement weights begin with −2ⁿ⁻¹; the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1.
Encode negative values by inversion then addition of one; decode using weights or the inverse process.
The minimum negative value has no positive counterpart at the same signed width.

teachingBlocks.text: In two’s complement the most-significant bit has negative weight. An eight-bit pattern has weights −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. This gives one continuous integer range: −128 through +127. A leading 0 is non-negative; a leading 1 is negative.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a negative place value
Worked example: encode −23 at eight bits
items: Add one at the same width

teachingBlocks.text: Adding one may carry through trailing ones. To encode −18: +18 is 00010010; inversion gives 11101101. At the right, 1 + 1 writes 0 and carries 1; the next column 0 + 1 writes 1. The result is 11101110. Lesson 003 develops the full column method.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete the add-one operation
Reverse direction: decode 11101110
items: The leading 1 makes this a negative two’s-complement value.
Invert to 00010001, then add 1 to obtain 00010010 = 18. Restore the minus sign: −18.

teachingBlocks.text: For n bits the smallest value is −2ⁿ⁻¹: only the negative-weight bit is set. The largest is 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1: that bit is 0 and all remaining bits are 1. There is one zero, all bits 0. Inverting zero and adding one produces a carry beyond the width and leaves the same zero pattern.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the asymmetric range

teachingBlocks.text: At eight bits, 10000000 means −128 directly from its negative weight. Invert-and-add-one returns 10000000 again: its unsigned magnitude is 128, but +128 is not an eight-bit signed value. Do not treat this as successful signed negation; use the negative weight to decode the minimum. Positive 128 and negative 129 are both outside the signed range.
teachingBlocks.title: Handle the smallest negative value

teachingBlocks.text: For a positive magnitude m, inversion makes the unsigned value 255 − m and adding one makes 256 − m. Adding this pattern to m produces 256, leaving zero when only eight bits are retained. This explains how a fixed-width adder can handle subtraction and why the carry alone does not decide signed overflow.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why the representation supports addition

knowledgeUnits.heading: Conversion between number systems and representations

leadVisual.title: Three different operations

coreExplanation: Conversion preserves the integer value; negation changes its sign; reinterpretation keeps the bits but changes their meaning.
Name the representation and width, convert, then decode to check.
Report values outside the destination range instead of dropping significant bits.

teachingBlocks.text: Separate three tasks: changing notation while preserving a value; reinterpreting unchanged bits under a different rule; and calculating the opposite value. They are different operations. Before starting, state the source rule, destination rule, integer value and required width.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the task before the method
A separate task: represent the value −45

teachingBlocks.text: To preserve −23 while converting between signed representations, decode the source to −23 first, then encode −23 under the destination rule: one’s complement 11101000 becomes two’s complement 11101001. Keeping the bits unchanged would not preserve the value.
teachingBlocks.title: Use an intermediate value when rules differ

teachingBlocks.text: A destination may be unable to represent the value. A negative integer cannot be stored in the unsigned or non-negative BCD models used here; +200 fits eight unsigned bits but not eight-bit two’s complement. State the limitation instead of silently truncating or reinterpreting the result.
teachingBlocks.title: Reject impossible conversions

objectives.description: Perform unsigned binary addition and subtraction at a stated width.
Perform binary addition and subtraction with positive and negative fixed-width integers.
Explain how overflow occurs in fixed-width binary arithmetic.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unsigned binary addition and subtraction

leadVisual.title: Column rules

coreExplanation: Align equal widths and process columns from right to left, including each carry or borrow.
A borrowed unit has value two in the next column to the right.
Compare the true result with the unsigned range; a negative result does not fit.

teachingBlocks.text: Fix the width and representation first. Eight unsigned bits cover 0–255. Align the units columns, then work from right to left. A column total of 0 or 1 is written directly; 2 is binary 10, so write 0 and carry 1; 3 is binary 11, so write 1 and carry 1.
teachingBlocks.title: Make every carry visible

teachingBlocks.text: Read the written bits from position 7 back to position 0: 01000100. This is 64 + 4 = 68, agreeing with 45 + 23. A carry between columns is ordinary working; it does not by itself mean overflow.
teachingBlocks.title: Reassemble and check

teachingBlocks.text: For subtraction, 0 − 1 requires a borrow. One unit from the column immediately to the left is worth two units in the current column. A borrow may pass through several zero columns before reaching a 1.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain a borrow by place value
Worked subtraction: 01000000 (64) − 00000111 (7)
rows: After borrowing to the units column

teachingBlocks.text: The 64s column gives up its 1. Each intervening column receives 2, passes 1 to its right, and retains 1. The adjusted row is working notation, not a stored binary number: 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 2 still equals 64. Subtract each lower bit: the result 00111001 is 57. Check 57 + 7 = 64.
teachingBlocks.title: Track the borrow through zeros

teachingBlocks.text: Unsigned 5 − 7 has true result −2, outside 0–255. A fixed-width subtraction may retain 11111110, unsigned 254, but that is not the required result. State that the true result cannot be represented. Do not silently interpret it as signed −2.
teachingBlocks.title: Check subtraction as well as addition

knowledgeUnits.heading: Signed binary addition and subtraction

leadVisual.title: Two’s-complement subtraction

coreExplanation: Encode negative operands before adding, and decode retained bits under the same signed rule.
Two’s-complement subtraction adds the negation of the second operand.
Discarding a carry out does not establish whether the signed result is valid.

teachingBlocks.text: Use the same column adder, but encode and interpret every operand under one signed rule at the same width. The main examples here use eight-bit two’s complement. Add all eight columns, retain the lowest eight bits, then check the true signed result against −128 to +127.
teachingBlocks.title: Reuse the adder with a signed interpretation
Worked addition with different sign combinations
Worked subtraction: +7 − (+12)
items: Invert 11111011 → 00000100; add one → 00000101. The value is −5, which equals 7 − 12 and fits the range.

teachingBlocks.text: Negating the minimum eight-bit value −128 cannot produce a representable +128. For example, 0 − (−128) has true result +128 and overflows. Returning the same pattern 10000000 after invert-and-add-one is a width limit, not a valid positive result. Check the original mathematical subtraction even when the bit operations complete.
teachingBlocks.title: Handle the negation boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Overflow in fixed-width arithmetic

leadVisual.title: Eight-bit ranges

coreExplanation: State the signed or unsigned range before deciding overflow.
Unsigned carry out and signed overflow are different conditions.
Same-sign two’s-complement addends with an opposite-sign result indicate overflow; verify using the true value.

teachingBlocks.text: Overflow means that the exact mathematical result lies outside the range of the stated width and representation. Always report three things separately: the true value, the retained bit pattern, and the meaning of that retained pattern.
teachingBlocks.title: Define overflow before using a shortcut
The same adder can require different decisions

teachingBlocks.text: For unsigned addition, a carry beyond the width indicates that the sum exceeds the maximum. For two’s-complement addition, two positive operands producing a negative result, or two negative operands producing a non-negative result, indicates overflow. Opposite-sign operands cannot overflow on addition because their magnitudes partly cancel.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the rule for the stated representation

teachingBlocks.text: For subtraction, calculate the true difference and compare it with the range. For example, +127 − (−1) = +128 and −128 − (+1) = −129 both overflow. The addition sign shortcut applies to an addition of valid encoded operands; checking the true difference also catches the unrepresentable negation of −128.
teachingBlocks.title: Transfer the range test to subtraction

teachingBlocks.text: Increasing the width can make a result representable, but taking the low eight bits does not repair a result already outside the eight-bit range. A processor status flag reports an event; Lesson 021 connects these representation rules to processor registers and status information.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the result to later processor work

objectives.description: Explain how a character set maps characters to numeric codes stored in binary.
explanationUnits: Character sets and internal binary representation
materialTitles: The character code and the drawn glyph are different things

objectives.description: Explain standard ASCII as a 7-bit character set.
Explain extended ASCII as an 8-bit character set.
Explain why Unicode supports a much wider range of characters than ASCII.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Character sets and internal binary representation

leadVisual.title: The character code and the drawn glyph are different things

coreExplanation: A character maps to a numeric code, then an encoding stores the code as bits or bytes.
Decode using the agreed mapping, storage boundaries and original order.
A glyph is a drawn shape; a digit character is not the same stored value as an integer.

teachingBlocks.text: A character is an abstract item such as A, 5 or a space. A character set identifies the available characters; a coded character set assigns numeric codes to them. An encoding specifies how these codes are stored as bits or bytes. A font supplies the visible glyph shapes when the text is drawn.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow meaning through to a visible glyph
Worked round trip: A5 followed by a space
headers: Eight-bit storage with a leading zero

teachingBlocks.title: Encode, store and decode in order
items: Look up A, 5 and space in that order. With one byte per character the file contains 01000001 00110101 00100000.
The reader uses the agreed one-byte convention to obtain codes 65, 53 and 32.
The same ASCII mapping recovers A, then 5, then the space. Changing the order or dropping the space changes the text.
The selected font draws the recovered characters. Changing the font changes their shapes without requiring different ASCII codes.

teachingBlocks.text: The numeric integer 5 stored as an unsigned byte is 00000101. The character “5” under ASCII is code 53, stored here as 00110101. Arithmetic on a numeric value and displaying a digit character are different uses of data. Lesson 058 revisits this distinction when selecting data types.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish a digit character from a number

teachingBlocks.text: A code has meaning only under an agreed mapping and encoding. A bit sequence alone cannot identify the intended text. In these exercises all required codes are supplied; learn the method rather than a table of memorised codes.
teachingBlocks.title: State the decoding requirement

knowledgeUnits.heading: ASCII

leadVisual.title: ASCII capacity

coreExplanation: Standard ASCII has seven-bit codes: 128 possibilities, numbered 0–127.
The repertoire includes printable characters and control codes.
A leading zero may pad a seven-bit ASCII code for byte storage.

teachingBlocks.text: Standard ASCII uses seven bits for each code, allowing 2⁷ = 128 codes numbered 0–127. Some represent letters, digits and punctuation; others are control codes, so 128 codes does not mean 128 printable symbols.
teachingBlocks.title: Count codes from zero

teachingBlocks.text: Seven-bit code 1000010 has value 64 + 2 = 66. If the supplied ASCII table says 66 is B, it decodes to B. In a system storing each ASCII code in a byte it is 01000010; the extra leading zero does not create a different ASCII character.
teachingBlocks.title: Decode a code at the correct width

teachingBlocks.text: ASCII can represent basic English text efficiently, but its limited repertoire cannot cover all writing systems. An agreement on standard ASCII ensures that the same supported code is interpreted consistently by different systems.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect capacity to suitability

knowledgeUnits.heading: Extended ASCII

leadVisual.title: Same bits, different agreed tables

coreExplanation: An eight-bit extension has 256 possible codes and 128 extra positions beyond ASCII.
Different extensions may assign different characters to the same extra code.
Both systems must agree on the character mapping.

teachingBlocks.text: An eight-bit extension can use 2⁸ = 256 code values, 0–255. It normally retains the original ASCII assignments in the lower half and uses the extra values for more characters. The extension adds 128 code positions, not another 256.
teachingBlocks.title: Extend the available code space
Worked mismatch using two supplied example tables

teachingBlocks.text: These two rows are an illustrative pair of mappings, not named real code pages. A sender using Table A encodes Aé as bytes 65, 128. A receiver using Table B decodes the same bytes as A€. No transmitted bit changed: the systems disagreed about the mapping. Using the same agreed table restores Aé.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate a mapping mismatch from corrupted data

teachingBlocks.text: “Extended ASCII” does not name one universal table. Different eight-bit code pages use the extra positions differently. A single extension also still has too few code positions for a wide multilingual repertoire.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify the remaining limitations

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unicode

leadVisual.title: Three separate layers

coreExplanation: Unicode assigns code points across a broad shared repertoire.
An encoding such as UTF-8 or UTF-16 determines the stored code units and bytes.
State the encoding before estimating text size.

teachingBlocks.text: Unicode gives a much larger shared repertoire for characters from many writing systems and assigns code points to them. Code points are conventionally written as U+ followed by hexadecimal digits. A code point is a number identifying a character; it is not by itself a rule saying how many bytes to store.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate repertoire, code point and encoding

teachingBlocks.text: For this supplied example, A中 encoded in UTF-8 has bytes 41 E4 B8 AD. A UTF-8 decoder recovers U+0041 and U+4E2D, then the characters A中. The two characters use four bytes in total. A font must also contain suitable glyphs to display them.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow a multilingual round trip

teachingBlocks.text: UTF-8 and UTF-16 are encodings of Unicode code points. UTF-8 uses a variable number of bytes; UTF-16 uses one or two 16-bit code units for a code point. “Unicode always uses 16 bits per character” is therefore incorrect. The exact UTF-8 bit-construction algorithm is an optional extension, not needed to explain the distinction.
teachingBlocks.title: Avoid a fixed-width misconception

teachingBlocks.text: A shared character repertoire supports consistent multilingual exchange; the sender and receiver must still use compatible encodings. Without a stated encoding and text, character count alone is insufficient to calculate a Unicode file’s byte size.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect purpose to storage

materialTitles: Decode every pixel at its original position

objectives.description: Distinguish image resolution from screen resolution.
Explain colour depth as bits per pixel and the number of available colours.
materialTitles: Compare colour depth at a fixed image resolution

objectives.description: Calculate uncompressed bitmap pixel-data size and convert units.
Explain how image resolution affects stored detail and file size.
Explain how colour depth affects colour accuracy and file size.

objectives.description: Explain why vector graphics scale without pixelation.
Justify bitmap or vector representation for a given task.

knowledgeUnits.heading: How a bitmap image is stored

leadVisual.title: Decode every pixel at its original position

coreExplanation: A bitmap contains an ordered pixel grid and the information needed to interpret it.
Each pixel stores one colour value; its position matters.
Distinguish pixel-data size from the complete file size.

teachingBlocks.text: A bitmap stores an ordered rectangular grid of pixels. Each pixel is one position in that grid and has one selected colour value. The file stores codes for these values; a palette may map short codes to colours, or a format may store colour components directly.
teachingBlocks.title: Rebuild an image from ordered values

teachingBlocks.text: The supplied diagram is a 10-column, 6-row bitmap with two bits per pixel and a four-colour palette. Read row by row from the top left. The second row contains codes 00 01 01 00 00 00 01 01 00 00. Use the palette to replace each code with its colour while keeping its position. Repeating this for all six rows reconstructs the shown grid.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete the code-to-pixel procedure

teachingBlocks.text: The header supplies information needed to interpret the data, such as width, height and colour depth. Here the width tells the reader to start a new row after every ten codes. The palette tells it which colour each code selects. A format can store other header information too; never assume every real header has the same fields or size.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why the metadata is needed

teachingBlocks.text: There are 10 × 6 = 60 pixels, each needing two bits. The pixel data is 120 bits = 15 bytes. This count excludes the header and palette. The same 120 bits cannot be reconstructed correctly without the agreed dimensions, pixel order and colour mapping.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the reconstructed data

knowledgeUnits.heading: Colour depth

leadVisual.title: Compare colour depth at a fixed image resolution

coreExplanation: n bits per pixel allows 2ⁿ colour codes.
Increasing depth can preserve finer colour or tonal differences.
At fixed dimensions, raw pixel-data size is proportional to colour depth.

teachingBlocks.text: Colour depth is the number of bits used for one pixel’s colour code. With n bits there are 2ⁿ possible codes. One bit allows two colours; two bits allow four; four bits allow sixteen. The bits select one colour for a pixel, not several colours at once.
teachingBlocks.title: Count possible colour values

teachingBlocks.text: The diagram uses the same 8 × 8 source pattern in every panel. Only the number of available grey levels changes. With 1, 2 and 4 bits per pixel, the raw pixel data uses 64, 128 and 256 bits: 8, 16 and 32 bytes respectively. Dimensions and pixel count stay fixed.
teachingBlocks.title: Change one variable at a time

teachingBlocks.text: More levels can represent smaller tonal differences, reducing visible banding when the source contains such differences. Doubling the depth from 2 to 4 bits doubles the raw data size but increases the possible colours from 4 to 16. Doubling bits does not merely double the colour count.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain quality and size together

teachingBlocks.text: A two-colour diagram may need only one bit per pixel. A photograph with many shades may benefit from more colour values. Raising the depth of an existing low-depth file adds representational capacity; it does not recover colours that were discarded earlier.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose depth for the content

knowledgeUnits.heading: Image resolution

leadVisual.title: Two grids

coreExplanation: Stored image resolution specifies the pixel grid, independent of screen resolution.
At fixed depth, raw data size is proportional to width × height.
More captured pixels may retain detail; enlargement cannot restore absent source detail.

teachingBlocks.text: Image resolution here means the dimensions of the stored pixel grid, such as 640 × 480 pixels. This is 640 columns and 480 rows, giving 307,200 pixels. A screen has its own pixel grid; showing an image on a larger screen does not change the image’s stored resolution.
teachingBlocks.title: Name the grid being measured
Worked comparison at a fixed depth of 8 bits per pixel

teachingBlocks.text: Capturing the same scene with more suitably measured pixels can preserve finer spatial detail. Doubling both dimensions gives four times as many samples and four times the raw data at the same depth. It does not merely double the file size.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect sampling density to detail

teachingBlocks.text: Enlarging a stored bitmap instead copies or interpolates its existing pixel values. It cannot recover original scene detail that was never captured. Nearest-neighbour enlargement exposes square blocks; interpolation may smooth the boundaries but does not recreate the missing measurements.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate new capture from enlargement

knowledgeUnits.heading: Uncompressed bitmap file size

leadVisual.title: Size calculation units

coreExplanation: Raw pixel bits = width × height × colour depth.
Divide bits by eight before applying byte prefixes.
Add stated overhead in consistent units; do not double a fixed header when depth doubles.

teachingBlocks.text: For an uncompressed bitmap under the stated simplified model, pixel-data bits = width × height × bits per pixel. Divide by eight for bytes. If an actual format adds a header, palette or row padding, include these only when their sizes or rules are supplied; compression requires a different calculation.
teachingBlocks.title: State the storage model
Worked file size: 640 × 480 pixels, 8 bits per pixel, 54-byte header
items: 307,200 + 54 = 307,254 bytes. Assume no palette, padding or other overhead for this calculation.
At 16 bits per pixel, data becomes 614,400 bytes. With the same 54-byte header the whole file is 614,454 bytes, not twice 307,254.

teachingBlocks.text: When dimensions, depth and overhead are specified, this is an exact count. Real compressed image sizes cannot be found from dimensions and depth alone because content and compression settings affect the stored size.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the result within its assumptions

knowledgeUnits.heading: How a vector graphic is stored

leadVisual.title: One drawing list, reconstructed and scaled

coreExplanation: Vector files store object descriptions and properties in a drawing list.
Coordinates, dimensions, style and drawing order determine the rendered result.
Choose defining properties appropriate to each object type.

teachingBlocks.text: A vector graphic stores descriptions of objects and their properties in a drawing list. The renderer interprets these descriptions to produce a visible image. Unlike a bitmap, the source does not have to list a colour for every output pixel.
teachingBlocks.title: Define the representation
Complete drawing list for the diagram
Render the list on a 60 × 45 canvas
items: Origin (0, 0) is at the top left. x increases to the right; y increases downwards. Coordinates and thickness use the same arbitrary drawing units.
The rectangle extends from x = 10 to 50 and y = 10 to 30. Fill that area blue.
Draw the horizontal line from (10, 30) to (50, 30), with a black stroke of width 2 centred on the line.
The line is drawn last, so it lies over the rectangle’s lower edge. Swapping overlapping objects can change which parts remain visible.

teachingBlocks.text: Different objects require different defining properties: a circle can use a centre and radius; a polygon can use a sequence of vertices. Colour, fill, line thickness and position are common properties. Include enough data to reconstruct the intended object instead of merely naming its shape.
teachingBlocks.title: Generalise the drawing-list method

knowledgeUnits.heading: Bitmap and vector enlargement

leadVisual.title: Enlargement mechanisms

coreExplanation: Enlargement of a bitmap uses its existing pixel grid.
Vector geometry can be recalculated at the output size.
Justify a choice using content, scaling and editing requirements.

teachingBlocks.title: Scale the supplied drawing list by a factor of two

teachingBlocks.text: The vector renderer recalculates the objects from their descriptions for the required output size. Its geometry therefore retains smooth shapes under enlargement. A screen still displays a rasterised result on pixels: the advantage concerns the scalable source representation, not the absence of display pixels.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why scaling differs

teachingBlocks.text: A bitmap has a fixed source grid. Enlarging it must copy or interpolate that grid, so edges can become blocky or blurred. A vector description instead continues to define the edge geometrically at the new size. Neither representation guarantees a smaller file in every case: complexity and encoding also matter.
teachingBlocks.title: Compare the mechanisms
Choose a representation from the requirement
rows: Stores the many sampled colour variations directly.
Logo used on a small icon and a large sign
Simple shapes can be redrawn at both sizes without enlarging a fixed source grid.
Individual objects and precise geometry remain available for editing.
The deliberately designed pixel grid is part of the intended appearance.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Analogue sound and the sampling process

leadVisual.title: Four measurements become four stored codes

coreExplanation: Sampling chooses times; quantisation chooses levels; encoding stores their binary codes.
Decode using the same code mapping, width, order and sampling rate.
Quantisation and finite sampling limit how closely a recording can represent the analogue source.

teachingBlocks.text: An analogue sound signal varies continuously with time and amplitude. Digital storage contains discrete measurements: sampling chooses equally spaced times, quantisation chooses from a finite set of amplitude levels, and encoding assigns a binary code to each chosen level.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate three stages

teachingBlocks.text: This small model uses four samples per second and three bits per sample. There are eight allowed levels −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Round each measurement to the nearest allowed level; an exact halfway case would round upwards, and values beyond the range would clip to the nearest endpoint. None of the measurements below needs a tie or clipping rule.
teachingBlocks.title: Define a complete teaching model

teachingBlocks.text: The stored stream is 001 011 110 111, in time order: four samples × three bits = 12 bits of sample data. The code mapping is an explicitly defined offset code, not three-bit two’s complement and not a claim about a real audio file format. The −3 level has code value 1, so it is 001.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve the mapping and order
Decode and reconstruct
items: Split the stream into three-bit groups: 001, 011, 110, 111.
Convert codes to values 1, 3, 6, 7 and subtract 4, giving −3, −1, 2, 3.
At 4 Hz, place those levels at 0, 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 seconds.
A playback system uses timed levels to construct an analogue output. It cannot recover the exact original values −3.2, −0.6, 1.6 and 2.7 or all changes between sample times from these codes alone.

teachingBlocks.text: The brown line is a simplified continuous source trace; blue points show the quantised levels at the sample times. The trace’s straight segments are a teaching model, not a claim about the shape of every sound wave. Lesson 016 connects this data model to microphones, ADCs, DACs and speakers.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect data to devices

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sampling rate

leadVisual.title: Compare rate with the amplitude grid held fixed

coreExplanation: Sampling rate specifies samples per second per channel and controls time spacing.
At fixed duration, resolution and channel count, raw sound size is proportional to rate.
Upsampling an existing recording cannot restore uncaptured source information.

teachingBlocks.text: Sampling rate is the number of samples taken per second per channel, measured in hertz (Hz). Rate determines the spacing in time: at 4 Hz the interval is 1/4 second; at 8 Hz it is 1/8 second. Keep the amplitude levels unchanged when comparing the effect of rate.
teachingBlocks.title: Change timing independently of amplitude levels

teachingBlocks.text: In the diagram, both rows sample the same defined one-second analogue trace at the same three-bit resolution. The 4 Hz row takes four values; the 8 Hz row takes eight and captures additional changes between the earlier sampling times. This illustrates greater time detail during capture; it does not imply that doubling the rate always audibly improves every source.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the controlled comparison
Worked uncompressed sound size
items: Duration 5 s; rate 16,000 Hz; resolution 16 bits per sample; one channel (mono). Exclude headers and compression.
Doubling rate to 32,000 Hz doubles data to 320,000 bytes. Keeping 16,000 Hz but using two channels also gives 320,000 bytes.

teachingBlocks.text: In general, raw sound bytes = duration × sampling rate × bits per sample × channels / 8. Use seconds and samples per second consistently. Sampling rate is not the connection’s transfer bit rate; Lesson 012 uses the resulting data volume when reasoning about streaming.
teachingBlocks.title: Generalise and connect

teachingBlocks.text: Resampling an existing recording at a higher rate computes extra values from stored samples. It does not make new measurements of the original source or recover detail already lost during capture.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate recapture from upsampling

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sampling resolution

leadVisual.title: Compare level spacing at unchanged sample times

coreExplanation: n bits per sample supports 2ⁿ amplitude levels.
More levels over the same range can reduce quantisation error.
At fixed sample count, raw data size is proportional to bits per sample.

teachingBlocks.text: Sampling resolution is the number of bits used for each amplitude sample. With n bits there are 2ⁿ codes and therefore up to 2ⁿ distinguishable levels. Keep the amplitude range and sample times fixed to isolate the effect of resolution.
teachingBlocks.title: Change amplitude precision independently of timing
Quantise the same four measurements at the same times

teachingBlocks.text: Both models cover the same input amplitude range −4 to +4, with allowed reconstruction levels explicitly shown. Smaller gaps between levels can reduce quantisation error; an individual sample can still quantise to the same value at both resolutions. The number and timing of samples do not change.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the accuracy improvement precisely

teachingBlocks.text: Four samples require 4 × 2 = 8 bits at two-bit resolution or 4 × 3 = 12 bits at three-bit resolution. In practical settings, moving from 8 to 16 bits per sample doubles raw size at fixed rate and duration, but increases the number of possible levels from 256 to 65,536.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect resolution to capacity and size

teachingBlocks.text: More bits in an existing file cannot restore amplitude differences previously rounded away. The benefit comes from retaining finer measurements when capturing or preserving higher-precision source data.
teachingBlocks.title: State the boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why files are compressed

leadVisual.title: Same link, fewer bits

coreExplanation: Fewer bits can reduce storage and transfer time.
The benefit depends on the data, method and overhead.
Consider exact recovery as well as size and processing cost.

teachingBlocks.text: Compression represents data using fewer stored bits when the method can exploit its structure or discard acceptable information. Smaller files need less storage and fewer transmitted bits. Compression itself does not increase the physical connection’s bit rate.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect a smaller file to a practical need

teachingBlocks.text: Suppose a link carries 8,000,000 bits each second and overhead is ignored. A 2,000,000-byte file contains 16,000,000 bits and needs two seconds. Compressing it to 1,000,000 bytes reduces transfer time to one second at the same link rate. Encoding and decoding may also cost processing time.
teachingBlocks.title: Work through a transfer example

teachingBlocks.text: Compression is useful for limited storage, downloads and streaming. The method must suit the data and whether exact recovery is required. No lossless compressor can guarantee a smaller result for every input; headers, tables or references can outweigh the savings.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the trade-off

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossless and lossy compression compared

leadVisual.title: Recovery test

coreExplanation: Lossless decoding restores the original data exactly; lossy decoding cannot restore discarded information.
Choose lossless when exactness or an editable master is required.
Justify any lossy choice using both the size constraint and acceptable quality.

teachingBlocks.text: Lossless compression can reproduce every original data value exactly after decoding. Lossy compression discards some source information, so its decoded result is an approximation. Judge the recovery of the original data, not whether a user notices a difference.
teachingBlocks.title: Use reversibility as the deciding test
Choose a method for a stated purpose
rows: Source code or text that must remain exact
Changing even one character may alter the meaning or program.
Preserves all source values for later edits and exports.
Photograph preview with a tight transfer budget
Some fine image information may be sacrificed if the resulting quality is acceptable.
Smaller data may justify some signal approximation when intelligibility remains adequate.

teachingBlocks.text: Lossless does not mean “uncompressed”, and lossy does not mean “always visibly damaged”. A photograph can use either approach. A file extension alone is less useful than a stated encoding method and settings when deciding whether exact recovery is possible.
teachingBlocks.title: Avoid labels without a mechanism

knowledgeUnits.heading: Run-length encoding (RLE)

leadVisual.title: Trace every run and count every stored field

coreExplanation: RLE stores a count and value for each consecutive run and decodes them in order.
Count both fields and any supplied overhead when judging savings.
Short runs or limited count fields can reduce or reverse the benefit.

teachingBlocks.text: Run-length encoding replaces a consecutive run of identical values with a count and the value. The order of runs must remain unchanged. Here a pair stores an eight-bit count followed by an eight-bit character code; the human-readable notation 4A is shorthand for those two fields.
teachingBlocks.title: Define the encoded format

teachingBlocks.text: Scan AAAABBCCCCCCCCDD from left to right. Count until the value changes, emit that count and value, then start the next run. The result is (4,A), (2,B), (8,C), (2,D). Decoding repeats each value its stated number of times and concatenates the runs, recovering all 16 original characters in the same order.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete both directions
Count storage under the stated format

teachingBlocks.text: The counts above exclude any header and assume count/value fields are unambiguous. AAABAA must encode as (3,A), (1,B), (2,A); merging the A runs would move or lose B. An eight-bit unsigned count has maximum 255, so a run of 260 As must split, for example into (255,A), (5,A), under this format.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep order and field limits

teachingBlocks.text: RLE is effective for long uniform bitmap runs or other repeated adjacent data. A detailed or noisy image with frequent changes may contain mostly short runs. Its encoded size can grow. If the original pixels use one bit each but each run needs an eight-bit count plus one-bit value, compare with that nine-bit pair cost, not the character example’s sixteen bits.
teachingBlocks.title: Transfer the method to bitmap data

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossless compression and different file types

leadVisual.title: Text dictionary decoding

coreExplanation: A lossless format must retain everything needed to reverse its encoding.
Text references must preserve literals, separators and order as well as repeated strings.
For media, state exactly what is reconstructed and account for metadata or reference overhead.

teachingBlocks.text: Lossless methods replace redundancy with an exact reversible description. RLE is one example. Other methods can reference repeated strings or patterns; they must also store enough information for the decoder to interpret the references.
teachingBlocks.title: Move from runs to repeated structures
Complete text dictionary model
rows: Reference 1 means the exact string RED.
REF(1), SPACE, REF(1), SPACE, LITERAL(BLUE), SPACE, REF(1)
RED + space + RED + space + BLUE + space + RED

teachingBlocks.text: Typed REF and LITERAL tokens keep a reference distinct from an ordinary digit or word. Every space is explicitly retained. The dictionary, markers, separators and any header also need storage. This model demonstrates exact recovery; without a specified binary token format it does not establish a byte saving.
teachingBlocks.title: Make the format unambiguous
Lossless methods across media
rows: RLE of identical adjacent pixel codes
Each original pixel value at its position
RLE of repeated adjacent numeric samples
Every original sample value in time order
One shared object definition with references and positions
The defined objects, properties and placement

teachingBlocks.text: A small sound model contains 12, 12, 12, 12, 13, 13, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9. Store runs (4,12), (2,13), (6,9). With an eight-bit count and eight-bit sample value, the original 12 × 8 = 96 bits becomes 3 × 16 = 48 bits, excluding headers. Expanding the runs exactly restores all twelve values. Real audio often has little adjacent repetition; this example proves the mechanism, not that RLE is generally the best audio compressor.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete a numerical sound example

teachingBlocks.text: For a vector drawing, define one five-point star S with its geometry and fill, then place references to S at (10,20), (40,20) and (70,20). The renderer can reconstruct the three identical objects at those positions. This can reduce repeated object descriptions. It preserves the drawing model and appearance under these assumptions; rewriting the object list does not guarantee restoration of the original file’s byte sequence. Byte-for-byte file compression must preserve that sequence too.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish drawing reuse from exact file recovery

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossy compression and different file types

leadVisual.title: Irreversible reconstruction

coreExplanation: Lossy methods permanently discard some source information.
State the kind of detail sacrificed and why the result meets the use case.
Exact text, geometry or editable masters require preservation of the relevant source data.

teachingBlocks.text: Lossy compression trades exact recovery for a more compact approximation. A codec may discard fine visual differences or parts of an audio signal judged less noticeable. The precise mechanism depends on the method; removing every second sample or merely changing a filename is not a general description of audio compression.
teachingBlocks.title: Describe the loss and its purpose

teachingBlocks.text: A simple image model maps original grey values 100, 101, 102, 103 to the single stored representative 102. After decoding, all four become 102. The decoder cannot know which pixel was originally 100 or 103. The example demonstrates irreversible value reduction; whether the complete file becomes smaller depends on how the reduced values and metadata are encoded.
teachingBlocks.title: Show why information cannot be recovered

teachingBlocks.text: For bitmap photographs, reducing less noticeable fine detail can lower the amount of data needed while retaining acceptable appearance. Stronger loss may create visible artefacts. Lossless bitmap compression instead restores all original pixel codes. For sound, a lossy method may remove or simplify signal information judged less audible; lossless sound compression restores all original digital sample values.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply the distinction to images and sound

teachingBlocks.text: Ordinary text and programs normally require exact characters, so lossy alteration is unsuitable. Simplifying a vector drawing by deleting small shapes or reducing coordinate precision also changes its geometry; sharing an unchanged object definition does not itself introduce that loss.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply the distinction to text and vectors

teachingBlocks.text: Keep a lossless master when future editing matters. Choose a lossy delivery copy only when its size advantage and quality are appropriate to the task. Increasing resolution later cannot reconstruct information that was discarded during compression.
teachingBlocks.title: Make a justified choice

knowledgeUnits.heading: Networking creates shared access; LAN and WAN describe scope

leadVisual.title: LAN and WAN describe network scope

coreExplanation: Link each network benefit to a shared resource or a management process and its consequence.
LAN and WAN describe scope and control; neither guarantees speed or a particular carrier.

teachingBlocks.text: Networking devices connect systems so authorised users can share files, printers, storage, applications and an internet connection. Networks also support communication, collaboration, central account management and central backup.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: A benefit needs a cause and a consequence. For example, storing one managed copy of an examination file on a server allows authorised users to access the current version and lets administrators back it up centrally.

A LAN covers a limited geographical area such as one building or site and is normally owned or managed by one organisation. A WAN covers a large geographical area, links separate sites or LANs and commonly uses telecommunications-provider infrastructure. These terms do not guarantee a particular speed.

teachingBlocks.title: From a shared resource to a measurable benefit
items: Forty library terminals need the same catalogue and one printer. Separate copies would need separate updates; separate printers would duplicate hardware.
Terminals request the managed catalogue and submit print jobs over the local network. Access permissions determine which users may change records.
A catalogue update is available to authorised clients without copying it to every terminal. Sharing the printer reduces the number of printers needed.
A network does not automatically provide permissions, current backups or uninterrupted service. Those require configuration and maintenance.

teachingBlocks.text: The library site is a LAN. A link joining this site to two libraries in other cities forms part of a WAN. The WAN may use provider-owned fibre while each site uses both Ethernet cables and WiFi. Area and control classify scope; the carrier and measured data rate answer different questions.
teachingBlocks.title: Change the scale without changing the definition

knowledgeUnits.heading: Network models describe who requests and who provides

leadVisual.title: Client-server and peer-to-peer assign different roles

coreExplanation: A client requests a service; a server provides and manages it. Peers may do both.
Justify a model using control, availability, scale, administration and cost.

teachingBlocks.text: In a client-server model, clients request services or resources and one or more servers provide and manage them. Server roles may include authentication, file storage, web hosting, printing and backup.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: In a peer-to-peer model, each peer may request and provide resources directly. No dedicated server is required, but accounts, security, backup and availability are distributed across peers.
A justified choice links the scenario to number of users, trust, central control, required availability, administration and cost. A topology name cannot replace a model choice.

teachingBlocks.title: Follow a service request and its response
items: Terminal T asks the catalogue server for the record with book ID 104. The terminal is the client for this exchange.
The server receives the request, checks the applicable access rules, retrieves the record and prepares a result.
The server sends the record to T, which displays it. A different request could update a record if the user has permission.

teachingBlocks.text: For four trusted colleagues occasionally sharing non-critical photographs, peer-to-peer can avoid buying and administering a dedicated server. Each person shares selected files from their own computer. A file becomes unavailable when its providing peer is switched off, and backup responsibility remains distributed. If central accounts, reliable shared availability and uniform backup become requirements, the model should be reconsidered.
teachingBlocks.title: A contrasting model choice

teachingBlocks.text: A server is a role, not a guarantee of one physical box or one level of reliability. One computer can provide several services; several servers can support a service. A client-server network may use a star or mesh link pattern. Lesson 008 examines those patterns separately.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep roles separate from layout

workedExample.title: Choose a model for shared accounts

knowledgeUnits.heading: Thin and thick describe where the client work happens

leadVisual.title: Thin and thick clients place processing in different locations

coreExplanation: Thin and thick describe how much application work occurs on the client.
Client-server can use thin or thick clients; offline work also needs local software and data.

teachingBlocks.text: A thin client relies mainly on a server for processing and/or storage. It can use lower-specification hardware and supports central software management, but it depends heavily on the server and network.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: A thick client performs more processing locally and normally stores more applications or data locally. It can continue more work when disconnected, but updates, security and maintenance are distributed across devices.
Thin/thick is not a synonym for client-server/peer-to-peer. It describes processing placement within a system design.

teachingBlocks.title: Trace the same editing task with different processing locations
rows: The terminal sends the user’s keystrokes or commands to a remote application.
The local application receives and processes the input.
The server runs most application processing and retains the working data.
The client CPU and memory perform substantial application processing.
The terminal receives output to display; the server may save the file.
The client displays the result and may save locally or send a file to a server.
The dependent remote session is interrupted.
Local work can continue if its program, data and required permissions are available locally.

teachingBlocks.text: For the 40 library terminals, a thin-client application can centralise application updates and reduce local processing requirements, but the server and connection must support the simultaneous sessions. For an engineer running CAD at a site with intermittent connectivity, choose a thick client with the application and authorised working files stored locally; synchronise completed files when connected. A powerful local CAD client can still request central accounts and files in a client-server model.
teachingBlocks.title: Make a complete choice and test its limits

knowledgeUnits.heading: The topology is the link pattern

leadVisual.title: Bus, star and full mesh

coreExplanation: Topology is the link pattern; explain the actual path and relevant failure point.
A full mesh connects every pair; a partial mesh does not. Four full-mesh nodes need six links.

teachingBlocks.text: A bus connects devices to one shared backbone. A signal travels along the common medium and attached devices inspect it.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: A star gives each end device a separate link to one central switch. A frame travels from the source to the switch and then from the switch to the destination link.

A mesh provides multiple interconnections. A full mesh connects every node pair directly; partial meshes retain several, but not all, possible links. Alternative connected routes may remain after one link fails.

A hybrid combines two or more topology patterns. In the example, end devices form stars around S1 and S2, while S1, S2 and S3 form a mesh. A frame is a unit of LAN data; switches forward it on selected links. Assume a loop-free forwarding path, with a spare path available after a failure.

Data is sent in structured units rather than as an entire file moving as one indivisible object. At this level, an IP packet contains addressing information and data for delivery between networks. On an Ethernet link, a frame carries data with link-level addressing such as source and destination MAC addresses. Lesson 011 uses these addresses to distinguish local forwarding from routing.
teachingBlocks.title: Enough packet and frame vocabulary to follow a path
Connect each structure to how a transmission travels
rows: Attached devices share one backbone; signals travel along it. The addressed receiver accepts the relevant frame.
Few backbone cables, but shared traffic contends for access. A backbone break or faulty termination can disrupt the shared segment.
A host sends to the central device. With a switch and a known destination port, the switch forwards through that port.
Each host needs its own cable. A host-link failure isolates that host; centre failure removes the connection through that centre.
Every pair of nodes has a direct link; forwarding can also use an available multi-link route.
Many links provide alternatives at greater cabling, interface and management cost.
A partial mesh supplies some alternate links. A hybrid combines layouts, such as local stars joined by meshed links.
Check the actual graph: a “mesh” label does not prove that every node survives every failure.

teachingBlocks.text: A bus terminator absorbs signals reaching an end of the cable and reduces reflections that would interfere with the signal. It does not choose destinations. In a four-node full mesh, list AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD: six links. Counting three neighbours at each of four nodes gives twelve ends, so divide by two: 4 × 3 / 2 = 6. In general, N distinct nodes need N(N − 1)/2 undirected pairwise links.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain termination and count links

knowledgeUnits.heading: A good choice connects structure to consequence

leadVisual.title: A working path after one link fails

coreExplanation: Trace every successive link; distinguish a failed link, end device and central device.
State the spare-path activation assumption and weigh resilience against extra cost.

teachingBlocks.text: A star usually isolates one end-device cable failure, but the central switch is a single point of failure for that star.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: A bus uses less cable but shares the backbone and traffic; a backbone break can divide or stop the network.
A mesh can offer alternative routes, but extra links and ports increase cost, installation and management.
A hybrid can match different areas, but its failure behaviour depends on the constituent topologies and the links joining them.

teachingBlocks.title: Complete the A-to-C failure analysis
items: A and B connect separately to S1; C and D connect separately to S2. Inter-switch links are S1–S2, S1–S3 and S2–S3. Assume forwarding initially selects S1–S2 and can activate the spare route without loops.
A → S1 → S2 → C uses the two host links and the direct inter-switch link.
Remove S1–S2. The available route becomes A → S1 → S3 → S2 → C, if the configured network activates it.
Remove A–S1 instead: A has no remaining link. Remove S1: A and B both lose their only attachment. The inter-switch mesh cannot repair either missing host attachment.

Choose this hybrid when surviving an inter-switch link failure justifies extra links, interfaces and configuration. Add separate resilience for the centre or host links only if the requirements demand it.

A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

knowledgeUnits.heading: Cloud computing provides remote resources through a network

leadVisual.title: A cloud request crosses local and provider infrastructure

coreExplanation: Cloud computing supplies computing resources as a service through a network.
Follow client request, remote processing or storage, and returned result.

teachingBlocks.text: Cloud computing provides storage, processing, applications or platforms from remote infrastructure accessed through a network. The organisation uses the service without operating every physical server locally.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: A client sends a request across its local network and the internet to provider infrastructure. A virtual server or managed service performs the requested processing or storage operation and returns the result.
Cloud describes where computing resources are provided and accessed; it does not mean that data has no physical location. The resources run on physical provider or organisation-controlled hardware.

teachingBlocks.title: Follow a cloud order-processing request
items: A shop enters order 501 in a browser. Its application sends the order through the shop connection to a hosted application.
Provider computing executes the application; managed storage retains the order. The client uses those resources through a network interface rather than owning every underlying server.
The service returns an accepted-order result. The shop should distinguish that acknowledgement from a form that has only been typed locally.
More processing or storage can be provisioned as demand grows, subject to the service’s capacity, configuration and charges. Cloud resources are not unlimited or automatically free.

teachingBlocks.text: Cloud computing includes remotely provided processing, applications and storage. Simply copying a file to any other computer does not establish all the management and on-demand service features associated with a cloud platform. The client still needs a suitable access connection and permission to use the service.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the term to the resources

knowledgeUnits.heading: A public cloud uses shared third-party provider infrastructure

leadVisual.title: A public cloud uses shared provider infrastructure

coreExplanation: Public cloud uses a provider’s infrastructure to serve multiple customers.
Shared infrastructure does not imply public access to customer data.

teachingBlocks.text: A public cloud is operated by a third-party provider. Its underlying physical resources serve multiple customers, while virtualisation, accounts and permissions provide logical separation between customers.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: Public cloud describes provider control and multi-customer tenancy. It does not mean that files are open to the public; authentication, permissions and encryption are still required.

Because the provider owns and operates the shared platform, a customer can obtain resources without purchasing all of the underlying hardware but accepts greater dependence on the provider's service and controls.

In a public cloud, a third-party provider offers services to multiple customers using its infrastructure. Customer workloads and data need logical separation and access control; shared provider infrastructure does not mean every customer may read everyone else’s files. A shop can obtain capacity without first purchasing and running its own server estate.
teachingBlocks.title: Shared infrastructure and controlled access

teachingBlocks.text: The benefit is a smaller initial infrastructure commitment and the ability to obtain more resources when needed. The trade-off is ongoing charges and dependence on the provider’s service, terms and security arrangements. A traffic surge may increase both the allocated capacity and the bill. Evaluate those consequences against the shop’s workload instead of assuming public means insecure or free.
teachingBlocks.title: Evaluate a changing workload

knowledgeUnits.heading: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

leadVisual.title: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

coreExplanation: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation and can be on-site or hosted.
Greater control still requires administration, capacity planning and recovery arrangements.

teachingBlocks.text: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation. It may be operated by that organisation on its own premises or hosted and managed on its behalf by another provider.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: Private describes single-organisation tenancy and the potential for greater control or configuration. It does not require every server to be in the organisation's building.

Dedicated infrastructure can support control or compliance requirements, but it usually brings greater cost or management responsibility and still requires authentication, permissions, encryption and backup.

A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation. It may run in the organisation’s own data centre or be hosted and operated for it by a third party. “Private” therefore describes exclusivity and control, not a requirement that all equipment sits inside the office or that access uses the public internet.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish tenancy from location

teachingBlocks.text: A research organisation with specialised access rules may choose a dedicated private cloud to control configuration and resource use. It must still fund capacity and skilled administration, directly or through a hosting contract. Dedicated infrastructure can reduce sharing with other customers, but poor permissions, failed hardware and absent backups remain possible. The choice requires both the control requirement and the cost of delivering it.
teachingBlocks.title: Make the control–cost trade-off explicit

knowledgeUnits.heading: Cloud benefits and risks must be connected to dependence

leadVisual.title: An internet-hosted cloud: benefits and dependence

coreExplanation: Explain benefits alongside network and provider dependence.
Recovery requires usable retained data, an available service and checks for missing or duplicated work.

teachingBlocks.text: Benefits can include access from different locations, collaboration, elastic capacity, reduced local hardware, provider maintenance and geographically redundant infrastructure.
teachingBlocks.title: Establish the concept

teachingBlocks.text: Drawbacks can include dependence on broadband and the provider, recurring cost, less direct control, migration difficulty, service outage, data-location/compliance concerns and exposure if accounts or provider controls fail.

A choice depends on sensitivity, required control, expected demand, staff expertise, budget, connection resilience and legal requirements. Cloud storage is not automatically a complete backup strategy.

teachingBlocks.title: Recover the order service with a known backup boundary
items: At 12:00 the shop verifies a recoverable backup held independently of the live provider service. Order 501 was confirmed at 12:05. At 12:10 the service becomes unreachable.

If another independent connection reaches the service, investigate the shop’s access path. If the provider has an outage, changing only the shop’s connection cannot restore that failed provider service. Confirm status rather than assume the cause from one failed browser request.
Use the agreed offline form with temporary unique order references and timestamps. Tell staff these records have not yet been accepted by the cloud application.
The 12:00 backup recovers the captured state, not automatically order 501 or later work. Restore to an available approved service and verify records and access before normal use.

Check which later orders were confirmed or retained elsewhere. Match temporary references and acknowledgements before entering missing records, avoiding duplicate orders. Resume normal submission once the service is verified.

teachingBlocks.title: Choose a response that addresses the actual failure
rows: A working independent connection may restore access.
It does not repair the provider.
Provider recovery or a prepared alternate service is needed.
A backup alone is data, not a running replacement application.
Recover a verified independent backup and reconcile later records.
Changes absent from every retained record cannot be recreated merely by restoring the backup.
