knowledgeUnits.heading: Monitoring and control systems compared

leadVisual.title: Use the same measured quantity to compare systems

coreExplanation: Monitoring measures and reports; control applies an action to the process.
A closed-loop controller uses returned measurements to guide further action.

teachingBlocks.text: Monitoring obtains information about a physical condition and records, displays or reports it. A warning can be part of monitoring: it tells someone that a condition requires attention but does not necessarily regulate that condition. Control applies an output that changes the process. In closed-loop control, new measurements guide the next corrective action.
teachingBlocks.title: Classify the whole task, not merely the presence of output
Three cold-store arrangements use the same measurement
rows: Monitoring with an alert: the sound does not itself cool the store.
Switch cooling on under the stored rule; measure again and stop when required.
Closed-loop temperature control: an actuator changes the measured condition.

teachingBlocks.text: Identify the physical quantity being regulated. A sounder is an output device and can be an actuator in an alarm system, but sounding it does not by itself close a loop that reduces workshop noise. Similarly, an operator could react to a displayed temperature, but that does not establish automatic temperature control by the computer.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why a report is not itself correction

knowledgeUnits.heading: Named sensors and their uses

leadVisual.title: Choose the measurement before the response

coreExplanation: Match temperature, pressure, infra-red or sound sensing to the required physical input.
Separate a sensor’s measurement from the controller’s response rule.

teachingBlocks.text: A sensor responds to a physical quantity and supplies a corresponding signal. Select it by the quantity required, not by the name of the larger machine. Temperature, pressure, infra-red and sound sensors are the four named types used here. A signal can be analogue or already digitised by a sensor module; conversion is needed only where an analogue signal must enter a digital processor.
teachingBlocks.title: Match a physical quantity to a signal
Make and justify a sensor choice
headers: What the reading tells the system
rows: Whether the measured temperature has reached the switching condition.
Stop an air pump at a tyre-pressure target
The actual pressure; motor running time alone cannot establish that pressure.
Detect interruption of a directed IR beam
Whether the specified beam reaches the receiver. A transmitter supplies the beam in this arrangement.
A signal related to the detected sound level, which can be compared with the chosen limit.

teachingBlocks.text: A pressure sensor measures pressure; force and pressure are related but should not be used as interchangeable labels without the device context. An infra-red beam receiver is also not the same mechanism as a passive detector responding to changes in incoming thermal radiation. Name the signal that the stated arrangement actually measures.
teachingBlocks.title: Avoid replacing the measurement with a guess

teachingBlocks.text: In the beam example, first establish that the beam is received. An object interrupts it, the receiver’s signal changes, and the controller applies the specified alert or counting rule. When the beam is restored the signal returns. Whether to count once, sound continuously or reset an alarm is a control rule, not information supplied by the sensor type alone.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete one detection and recovery

knowledgeUnits.heading: How sensors, a microprocessor and actuators form a control system

leadVisual.title: Assign each responsibility in the pump example

coreExplanation: Trace sensor → conversion if needed → processor comparison → output driver → actuator → physical effect.
A command and the actual outcome are different; new sensing checks the result.

teachingBlocks.text: The sensor measures, the processor decides and the actuator acts. A sensor signal is converted to digital data when necessary before the processor compares it with a stored target or rule. The resulting output signal usually operates suitable driving circuitry; it does not imply that the processor can directly supply a heater’s or motor’s power.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow information and physical power separately
Complete a tyre-inflation control example
items: Target pressure is 220 kPa. The pump is initially off. Turn it on while the measured pressure is below 220 kPa; switch it off at or above the target. Assume a working sensor, driver and pump.
The pressure sensor reports 200 kPa. Convert its signal if necessary. The processor compares 200 with 220 and commands the driver to power the pump motor.
The motor operates the pump, adding air and increasing actual pressure. The motor is the actuator in the stated assembly.
The next reading is 215 kPa, so pumping continues. A later reading of 220 kPa causes the controller to switch the pump off.
The measured target has been reached and the pump is off. Continued measurements can detect a later change rather than assuming pressure remains correct forever.

teachingBlocks.text: ADC and DAC should not be inserted mechanically into every block diagram. An analogue input needs digitisation; an already digital sensor output does not need an additional external ADC for that same signal. A switched motor or relay can use a digital command and driver; an actuator interface requiring an analogue command may use a DAC. State the actual signal requirement.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose conversion from the interface

knowledgeUnits.heading: The importance of feedback

leadVisual.title: Return the actual outcome to the controller

coreExplanation: Feedback is returned measurement of the actual condition, including unchanged outcomes.
Use the supplied rule and previous state; disturbances and faulty measurements can change the result.

teachingBlocks.text: Feedback returns information about the actual measured condition to the controller. It is used to compare the outcome with a target or switching rule and determine the next output. A reading that has not changed can be valuable feedback when an actuator is ineffective. Feedback does not require that the attempted action already succeeded.
teachingBlocks.title: Measure what happened, not what was commanded

teachingBlocks.text: Begin with a single threshold: switch a heater on below 20 °C and off at or above 20 °C. Readings 18, 19, 20 produce ON, ON, OFF. Continued sensing matters because an open door can cool the room again. The exact action follows the stored rule; the sensor does not choose it.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow an ordinary closed loop

teachingBlocks.text: A two-threshold variant turns on below 18 °C and off at or above 20 °C. Between those boundaries it keeps its previous state. The initial state is OFF. The readings below are supplied observations, not values predicted by a thermal simulation.
teachingBlocks.title: Trace both warming and cooling
The same middle reading can require different states
Use feedback to reason about faults
headers: Likely consequence under the stated rule
rows: Heating restarts from the new measurement.
The controller keeps receiving a low reading even if the room warms.
It may keep heating; the measurement is no longer reliable evidence of actual temperature.
A working sensor keeps reporting the actual low temperature.
The controller can continue commanding heat, but feedback alone cannot repair the actuator.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Recognise six gate symbols and apply their functions

leadVisual.title: Six symbols with exact input and output connections

coreExplanation: Recognise NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR and XOR by their shapes and output rules.
Output circles invert; XOR’s extra input curve does not denote inversion.

teachingBlocks.text: A logic gate maps binary input values to a binary output. In these examples 1 represents TRUE/high and 0 FALSE/low; each scenario must say what those values mean for its inputs. NOT has one input. The other five named gates each have two inputs, even when a whole circuit has three or more independent variables.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the input and output connections
Build the basic rules before their variants
items: Invert one input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. Its triangular symbol has an output inversion circle.
The output is 1 only for 11. For 01, one required condition is missing, so the output is 0.
The output is 1 when either or both inputs are 1. The 11 case is included.
Evaluate AND or OR first, then invert the whole result at the output bubble. Inverting one input is a different circuit.
Exactly one of the two inputs must be 1. The output is 1 for 01 and 10, and 0 for 00 and 11. The extra curved input line distinguishes its symbol from OR.

teachingBlocks.title: Use a decisive row to distinguish rules
rows: OR = 1, XOR = 0. An example with 10 cannot distinguish them.
NAND or AND with B inverted?
NAND = 1; A AND NOT B = 0. Moving the inversion changes the function.
NOR = 1 while OR = 0. The bubble complements the whole result.

teachingBlocks.text: Use AND, OR and NOT words with brackets in the following expressions. Other texts may use a dot for AND, a plus for OR, an overbar or ¬ for NOT, and ⊕ for XOR. A logical plus is not ordinary binary addition. The equality sign in Q = A AND B describes a Boolean relationship, not a pseudocode assignment statement.

leadVisual.title: All two-input cases

coreExplanation: List all 2^n input combinations exactly once, then evaluate the rule for each row.
State input order and include both accepted and rejected cases.

teachingBlocks.text: A truth table lists every possible combination of independent binary inputs and the resulting output. With n independent inputs there are 2^n combinations. One input gives two rows; two give four; three give eight. The number of gates or intermediate wires does not create extra independent input combinations.
teachingBlocks.title: Enumerate inputs before calculating outputs
Construct AND, then NAND, without memorising a sequence
items: Write 00, 01, 10, 11 once each. Keep that order for every output column.
00 fails both conditions; 01 and 10 each fail one; 11 satisfies both. AND therefore gives 0, 0, 0, 1.
Complement each completed AND result, obtaining 1, 1, 1, 0. Inversion comes after the AND operation.
There are four distinct rows, every row has one output and the 11 result matches the NAND rule.

teachingBlocks.text: For NOR, OR first gives 0,1,1,1 and inversion gives 1,0,0,0. For XOR, compare the two input values in each row: they differ only at 01 and 10. The comparison table above collects these independently derived results. The complete NOT example below uses only two rows because its one input has only two states.
teachingBlocks.title: Extend the method to every named gate

teachingBlocks.text: An output sequence such as 1,0,0,0 is meaningful only with its input order. Omitting a zero-output row would lose information about rejected cases. To challenge a proposed table, choose a row that separates the correct rule from the claimed rule, then still check that all rows are present.

Preserve each AND, OR and NOT relationship with explicit brackets. In the door example, D = 1 means a valid request and C = 1 means the lock condition is active; permission is 1 exactly when D is 1 and C is 0.
teachingBlocks.title: Translate the complete condition
Connect words, expression, circuit and table
items: A valid request and an inactive lock give P = D AND (NOT C). Both conditions are required.
C feeds NOT first. That result and D feed a two-input AND. Label the output P; the small circle belongs on NOT’s output, before AND.
List DC as 00, 01, 10, 11. Calculate NOT C, then P. Check each P against the original permission condition.
NOT (D AND C) returns 1 for DC = 00, granting permission without a valid request. One counterexample disproves equivalence.

teachingBlocks.text: For three conditions, keep two inputs per gate. A lamp rule “S is on and both U and V are off” becomes L = S AND ((NOT U) AND (NOT V)). Build NOT U and NOT V, combine them with AND, then combine that intermediate result with S. This whole circuit has three independent inputs and eight rows, although each AND gate still has two inputs.

Read the existing Circuit B
items: The XOR receives A and B: X = A XOR B. The NOT receives C: Y = NOT C.
The AND receives X and Y: Q = X AND Y. Substitute both definitions to obtain Q = (A XOR B) AND (NOT C).
For ABC = 010, X = 1 and Y = 1, so Q = 1. For ABC = 011 the XOR stays 1 but Y becomes 0, so Q becomes 0.
Calculate the same intermediate columns for all eight rows, as in the complete example below. The accepted rows are 010 and 100.

teachingBlocks.text: A NAND at the end would invert the entire AND result; an input NOT would invert only its own incoming signal. leadVisual.title: The equality rule as an actual circuit

coreExplanation: AND the conditions in each output-1 row, then OR all accepted-row terms.
Draw the actual two-input gate circuit and verify both output-1 and output-0 rows.

teachingBlocks.text: An output-1 row states a complete accepted input condition. Use an unmodified variable for each input 1 and its NOT form for each input 0. AND those conditions to select that one row. OR the terms for all accepted rows so that any accepted condition can produce the output. This constructs a valid expression without needing algebraic simplification.
teachingBlocks.title: Why one row becomes one AND term

teachingBlocks.text: The equality example has accepted rows AB = 00 and 11. The first term is (NOT A) AND (NOT B); the second is A AND B. Their OR gives the full rule. The circuit in the visual overview makes the two branches visible. NOT (A XOR B) is another valid implementation using the six taught gate types; an additional single XNOR symbol is not needed.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete the two-input construction

teachingBlocks.text: Connect inverted A and inverted B to the first AND. Connect unchanged A and B to the second AND. Join those outputs with OR and label its output Q. The four rows give 1,0,0,1; both rejected rows remain 0. A single matching row would not establish the whole equality rule.
teachingBlocks.title: Wire and verify the two-input circuit
A second source table: three independent inputs
Construct the circuit for the three-input table
items: Only 001 and 101 have Q = 1. Row 001 requires NOT A, NOT B and C; row 101 requires A, NOT B and C.
T1 = ((NOT A) AND (NOT B)) AND C. T2 = (A AND (NOT B)) AND C. Each three-condition term uses two cascaded two-input AND gates.
Q = T1 OR T2. Draw the two term circuits and join their outputs with a two-input OR. Repeated A, B and C labels carry the same respective input values.
The circuit gives 0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0 in ABC order 000–111. Checking all six rejected rows is necessary; a missing NOT could otherwise accept unwanted cases.

teachingBlocks.text: A shorter expression (NOT B) AND C happens to implement this table because both values of A are accepted whenever B = 0 and C = 1. The unsimplified construction is already correct. Recognise the shorter form only by checking all rows; do not delete a variable merely to make a diagram smaller.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Von Neumann architecture and the stored program concept

leadVisual.title: Processor and shared memory

coreExplanation: A stored program computer holds its instructions in memory. The processor fetches these instructions, decodes them and carries out the specified operations. Loading another instruction sequence changes the task the computer performs.

The basic Von Neumann model uses one memory for instructions and data. The processor contains a control unit, an arithmetic and logic unit and registers. Buses connect the processor to memory and input/output interfaces; instructions and data share transfer paths.

workedExample.title: A program and its data in one store

knowledgeUnits.heading: General-purpose and special-purpose registers

leadVisual.title: Register roles

coreExplanation: Registers are small, fast storage locations inside the processor. A general-purpose register can hold operands and intermediate results; a special-purpose register has a defined role. In CPU architecture, ACC has the designated accumulator role and appears with the special-purpose registers. In the syllabus's example assembly model, ACC is also the only register available for general data operations; IX supplies an index offset.

During instruction processing, several registers are needed at once: one identifies the next instruction, one retains the current instruction, and others support memory transfers. Status flags record conditions such as zero, carry, sign or overflow, depending on the processor; they are not the complete arithmetic answer.

leadVisual.title: A memory read and a memory write use different data directions

coreExplanation: Address bus: Selects a memory location or addressed interface. In the basic processor-controlled model, the address travels outwards from the processor. Data bus: Carries instructions and data. Reads return values to the CPU; writes send values from the CPU.

The control bus coordinates operations. READ and WRITE travel from the CPU; interrupt requests can travel towards it. The collection is bidirectional, but each individual signal line has its own defined direction.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Factors affecting processor performance

leadVisual.title: A cache hit avoids a main-memory read

coreExplanation: Processor type: Instruction sets and internal organisation affect work per cycle, pipelining and cache use. Clock frequency alone cannot rank different designs. Core count: Independent tasks or parallel parts can run concurrently. Sequential dependencies and communication overhead limit the gain. Clock and data bus: A faster clock provides more cycles per second; a wider data bus transfers more bits at once. Neither removes every memory or I/O delay.

Cache keeps copies of recently or frequently needed instructions and data near the processor. A hit avoids a slower main-memory access. More capacity helps when it retains useful parts of the working set; access patterns and hit rate matter as well as size.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Fetch using register-transfer notation

leadVisual.title: Instruction fetch: address and value transfers

coreExplanation: In this notation, [PC] means the contents of PC and [[MAR]] means the contents of the memory location whose address is in MAR. The arrow points towards the destination. MAR ← [PC] therefore copies the next instruction address into MAR.

The CU issues a memory-read signal; the instruction from the selected location travels to MDR and is copied to CIR. PC advances to the next sequential address. For these examples each instruction occupies one location, so the increment is one. Some fetch operations can overlap; the instruction must reach MDR before it can be copied from MDR to CIR.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Purpose, causes and applications of interrupts

leadVisual.title: Event → useful response

coreExplanation: An interrupt is a request or event requiring the processor to suspend its normal instruction sequence and transfer control to a handler when the request is accepted. This supports response to asynchronous events without continually polling every device.

Requests may originate from hardware, such as a device completing input/output or a timer expiring, or from software requesting a system service. Exceptional conditions such as an arithmetic error also require processor attention. The precise treatment of faults depends on the processor; the basic taught sequence considers interrupt checks at instruction boundaries.

coreBlocks.title: Why an interrupt is useful

knowledgeUnits.heading: Detection, ISR and restoration of context

leadVisual.title: Save the interrupted context before running the ISR

coreExplanation: Detect: After the current instruction finishes, check pending enabled requests. Priority and enable rules decide acceptance; another request may remain pending. Save context: Preserve the return address and the state needed to resume. Service: Load the appropriate Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) address into PC and run it, acknowledging or clearing the request as required. Restore and resume: Restore saved state and continue the interrupted work.
The ISR must preserve registers as required by the system’s interrupt mechanism. Servicing an event must not corrupt values the interrupted program will use later.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assembly language and machine code

leadVisual.title: Three representations

coreExplanation: Machine instructions are encoded as binary patterns understood by a particular processor. An instruction contains an opcode and, where required, operand information. Assembly language provides readable mnemonics and symbolic names for the same low-level operations.

An assembler translates assembly source into machine code for its target instruction set. An ordinary mnemonic instruction corresponds to a machine instruction; labels and data declarations organise the source and are not additional operations for the processor to execute. Source for a different instruction set is not automatically interchangeable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Applying both passes of an assembler

leadVisual.title: A complete symbol table resolves a forward reference

coreExplanation: Pass one: Assign locations and record labels with their addresses in a symbol table. Advance the location counter by each instruction or data item’s size; report duplicate definitions. Pass two: Use the completed table to resolve symbolic operands, translate mnemonics into opcodes and emit machine instructions and data.

A forward reference names a label defined later in the source. The completed first pass makes its address available to pass two. A label still undefined after that pass is an error. The diagram’s one-word instructions and starting location are explicit example assumptions.

leadVisual.title: Trace fields

coreExplanation: Start a trace from the supplied PC, register values, memory contents and input. Fetch the instruction at PC, apply its exact operation, then record the resulting state. Record a row whenever an instruction executes; a loop therefore repeats rows for the same instruction address.

Use the branch condition produced by the preceding compare operation. JPE jumps when that comparison was True; JPN jumps when it was False. A skipped instruction has no trace row. END terminates execution and returns control to the operating system, rather than fetching the following data declarations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Instruction groups in the example instruction set

leadVisual.title: Five syllabus groups

coreExplanation: Group an instruction by the operation it performs. Movement instructions copy a value, arithmetic instructions calculate a value, and input/output instructions transfer character data between the program and its environment.

Control instructions alter the sequence of execution. JMP does so unconditionally; JPE and JPN depend on a comparison result. CMP and CMI are compare operations: they compare values without themselves jumping. END terminates the program and returns control to the operating system.

leadVisual.title: Resolve the index, copy the value, then store a copy

coreExplanation: Immediate #15, B00001111 and &0F supply the same value in denary, binary and hexadecimal forms. A bare address instead directs an instruction to memory.
LDX: Add IX to the address operand, then read the contents at that effective address. MOV IX: Copy ACC into IX, not IX into ACC. STO: Copy ACC into memory while leaving ACC unchanged.
A copy does not consume its source. LDX 400 with IX = 2 reads location 402; STO 450 then saves a copy at 450 while the original value remains at 402.

leadVisual.title: Operation forms

coreExplanation: ADD / SUB: Combine ACC with an immediate operand or directly addressed contents; retain the result in ACC. INC / DEC: Increase or decrease the named ACC or IX register by one.

CMP / CMI: CMP compares with an immediate or direct operand; CMI uses an indirect operand. Neither replaces ACC. JPE / JPN: JPE jumps when the comparison was True (equal); JPN jumps when it was False (not equal). JPN does not mean negative.
IN: Read one character and put its ASCII value in ACC. OUT: Output the character represented by ACC: 65 produces A, not the printed digits 65. END: Return control to the operating system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Logical, arithmetic and cyclic shifts

leadVisual.title: Track every bit through a one-place shift

coreExplanation: State the word width, direction and number of positions before shifting. Each panel starts from the same original byte; the panels are not successive instructions.

Logical: Insert 0 and discard outgoing bits. LSL #n and LSR #n shift ACC logically by n positions. Arithmetic: For two's complement, copy the sign bit when shifting right. A left shift inserts 0, like logical left, but may overflow. Cyclic: Wrap the outgoing bit to the opposite end; the number of 1 bits is unchanged.
A left shift multiplies a signed value by a power of two only when the result remains representable. Arithmetic right shift of a negative odd value rounds towards negative infinity: -105 becomes -53.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Labels for instructions and data

leadVisual.title: Two label forms

coreExplanation: The form <label>: <opcode> <operand> names the address of an instruction. The operand is omitted for an instruction that does not require one, such as END. A branch can use an instruction label as its target.

The form <label>: <data> names a location containing the given data. The label denotes the location's address, not its contents. Loading or storing through the label accesses that location; program execution must end or branch before falling into data declarations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why an operating system is needed

leadVisual.title: Applications request services through the operating system

coreExplanation: An operating system is system software that manages resources and supplies services to applications. Its graphical or command-line user interface lets users request operations.

Application: The editor requests a named file operation; it still owns the task-specific editing behaviour. Operating system: Check whether the operation is permitted and coordinate shared storage access. Device services: A driver and hardware perform the transfer, so every application need not implement its own storage controller.

coreBlocks.text: An operating system is system software that manages resources and supplies services to applications. Its graphical or command-line user interface lets users request operations.
coreBlocks.title: The OS provides shared services
A Save request crosses layers
items: The editor requests a named file operation; it still owns the task-specific editing behaviour.
Check whether the operation is permitted and coordinate shared storage access.
A driver and hardware perform the transfer, so every application need not implement its own storage controller.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Memory management

leadVisual.title: Allocate, protect and release main memory

coreExplanation: Memory management records which parts of main memory are allocated and which remain available.

Allocate: Reserve working space when a process starts or needs more memory. Protect: Check access so one process cannot freely overwrite another process's instructions or data. Release: Make a finished process's allocation available for reuse.
Allocation answers where a process can store data; protection answers whether access is permitted. RAM allocation does not save a file permanently.

knowledgeUnits.heading: File management

leadVisual.title: Opening a saved timetable

coreExplanation: File management maintains the organisation of files and directories, with information such as names, locations, sizes and ownership. It supports operations including creation, opening, reading, writing, renaming and deletion.

When an application supplies a path, the OS locates the corresponding file and coordinates the requested operation with storage services. File organisation gives programs a consistent way to retrieve data without needing to know the physical position of each stored block.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security management

leadVisual.title: One file, different permissions

coreExplanation: Security management authenticates users and enforces access rights. Authentication establishes an identity, for example by checking credentials; permissions determine which resources and operations that identity is allowed to use.

An OS can restrict a student to reading a shared document while allowing a teacher to modify it. An authenticated login therefore does not grant unrestricted access. Logging activity and applying security updates can also support protection of the computer system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Hardware and peripheral management

leadVisual.title: A queue, driver and buffer solve different printing problems

coreExplanation: Hardware management coordinates input, output and peripherals. Device drivers translate general OS requests into commands for particular devices, giving applications a consistent interface.

Queue: Keep requests waiting until the device is available. Buffer: Hold data temporarily during transfers between components operating at different rates. Interrupt: Notify the OS of completion or a need for attention so it can arrange a response.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Process management

leadVisual.title: A waiting process lets another ready process use the core

coreExplanation: A process is a program in execution. The OS records its state and schedules which ready process receives processor time. Switching on one core gives the appearance of simultaneous progress.

Retain context: Keep enough execution state to resume correctly. Schedule another process: Give the core to a ready process while the first cannot usefully continue. Make the waiting process ready: When its event completes, it can be selected to run again. Being ready does not mean it immediately owns the core.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Disk formatter

leadVisual.title: Disk formatter: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A disk formatter prepares a storage medium or volume with the file-system structures needed to organise files. Formatting establishes an empty organisational structure; it does not install all application software or restore a previous user's documents.

Reformatting an existing volume can make its current files inaccessible. A storage fault or a missing file is therefore not a reason to format a disk automatically; preserve needed data and choose the utility appropriate to the problem.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Virus checker

leadVisual.title: Virus checker: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A virus checker scans files, memory or activity for evidence of malware, using methods such as known signatures and suspicious behaviour. Its detection information needs updating as new threats are identified.

Detected items may be quarantined so they cannot run, removed, or repaired where that is possible. Detection does not guarantee that every new threat is found, and removing malware does not necessarily recover data it has already damaged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Defragmentation software

leadVisual.title: Rearrange file blocks without changing the file

coreExplanation: Relocate blocks: Move separated parts of a file into fewer, more contiguous groups; consolidate free space where possible. Reduce seeking: The magnetic drive’s head can move less while reading the file, reducing access delays.

The file’s logical contents stay the same. The performance explanation depends on mechanical seeking: an SSD has no moving read head, so routine HDD-style defragmentation is not the same treatment for an SSD.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Disk contents analysis and disk repair

leadVisual.title: Disk contents analysis and disk repair: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: Disk contents analysis can report how storage space is being used. Disk checking and repair tools examine file-system consistency and may detect problems such as lost allocation information or unreadable sectors.

A repair utility attempts supported corrections and can mark unsuitable areas to avoid further use. It cannot guarantee recovery from physical damage. Analysing a disk does not mean erasing it, and a recoverable backup remains valuable if repairs fail.

knowledgeUnits.heading: File-compression utilities

leadVisual.title: File-compression utilities: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A file-compression utility encodes data in a representation that can use fewer bits. Smaller files can require less storage space and less time to transfer over a connection with a given data rate.

A general-purpose archive utility uses lossless compression so decompression restores the original file exactly. The reduction depends on the data: an already compressed or poorly compressible file may shrink very little or even gain overhead. Compression alone does not create a recovery copy or encrypt the contents.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Back-up software

leadVisual.title: A saved recovery version can outlive loss of the working file

coreExplanation: Copy: Create recoverable copies of files or system data, using a separate recovery destination. Schedule and retain: Select changed files and keep suitable versions so an earlier state can be restored. Restore and check: Test that the saved copy and recovery procedure actually work after loss, corruption or failure.

A copy on the same failing disk does not protect against that disk’s failure. Only changes present in the chosen backup can be recovered from it; a completed copy job alone is not proof of successful restoration.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Program libraries and routine calls

leadVisual.title: Use the routine’s contract to supply input and interpret its result

coreExplanation: A program library is a collection of routines or modules other programs can use, such as mathematical functions or image-reading operations.

Inputs: Use the specified name, argument order, data types and conditions. Result: Know what is returned and use it correctly in the surrounding program. Integration: Test the caller: a correct routine can still be called with inappropriate data.

Suitable documented, tested libraries reduce implementation and testing effort and provide specialist operations. Those benefits depend on the chosen library; they are not guaranteed for every downloaded file.

leadVisual.title: Static copies and a separate shared library

coreExplanation: Linking model: Static; Arrangement: Required library code is incorporated into the built executable.. Linking model: Dynamic; Arrangement: A DLL remains separate; routines are linked at load time or as needed during execution..

Less duplication: Compatible applications can use one library, reducing repeated disk copies and allowing loaded code to be shared in memory. Calling executables can be smaller. One compatible correction: Update the library without recompiling each caller; running programs may need a restart or reload. Compatibility matters: The interface and behaviour must remain compatible. Missing or incompatible DLLs can prevent loading or cause failures, so updates need checking.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assembly source to target instructions

leadVisual.title: A small assembly routine

coreExplanation: Assembly language represents processor instructions using mnemonics and operands. An assembler converts a program written in that notation into the machine-code instruction encodings for its target processor; it does not translate high-level source such as Java.

The output may be a complete machine-code program or an object-code module that still requires linking. A linker combines modules and resolves references between them before a complete executable can be loaded. The instruction set determines which mnemonics and encodings are valid.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compilation before execution

leadVisual.title: Build and run are separate operations

coreExplanation: In the native compilation model, a compiler translates high-level source as a whole program or compilation unit into machine code before that code executes. Object-code modules can be linked into a complete executable. Some compilers instead target an intermediate representation, as in the Java example in the next lesson.

Translation diagnostics identify detected source problems. A source correction must be translated again before the built program reflects that correction. Successful compilation does not prove that the algorithm is correct or prevent every run-time error.

Object-code modules can be linked into a complete executable. Some compilers instead target an intermediate representation, as in the Java example in the next lesson.
coreBlocks.title: Translate before executing

coreBlocks.text: Translation diagnostics identify detected source problems. A source correction must be translated again before the built program reflects that correction. Successful compilation does not prove that the algorithm is correct or prevent every run-time error.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translation during execution

leadVisual.title: Execution order is not just page order

coreExplanation: In the high-level interpretation model, an interpreter translates and executes statements as execution proceeds rather than first producing a separate permanent native executable for the complete source program. The interpreter itself is software running on the computer.

Execution follows control flow. A loop can cause the interpreter to process the same statement repeatedly; a branch can skip statements. An error encountered during execution can stop progress at that point. Partial execution and immediate feedback are useful when investigating a developing program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare approaches and justify a choice

leadVisual.title: Compare matching factors

coreExplanation: Choose by the required workflow rather than calling one translator universally better. An interpreter can provide immediate feedback while individual statements or incomplete program sections are tested. The environment must still support the source language and the required operations.

A native compiled executable avoids translating the original source on every run and can be distributed without that source. It can suit repeated execution or delivery to end users. A separate build is needed after source changes, and the produced native code must suit the target platform.

Interpretation can add execution overhead and normally requires the interpreter and an executable form of the program's source or intermediate code to remain available. Real tools may combine techniques, so a justified exam answer links the specified translation model to a concrete requirement instead of making an unconditional speed claim.

leadVisual.title: What a coding prompt can show

coreExplanation: An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) brings programming tools into one working environment. While code is entered, context-sensitive prompts suggest suitable identifiers, keywords, members or parameters based on the current position and language context.

A prompt can reduce typing and help a programmer recall a routine's interface. The programmer must still select the intended operation and supply meaningful arguments; a syntactically available suggestion may be inappropriate for the problem.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dynamic syntax checking

leadVisual.title: From a highlight to a correction

coreExplanation: Dynamic syntax checking examines source as it is entered and highlights violations of the language's rules, such as an incomplete expression or a missing keyword. Feedback before a full run helps the programmer locate and correct an error early.

An inline diagnostic can describe the detected problem and indicate its source location. Read the message with the surrounding statement to investigate its cause. A reported location can be where a problem becomes detectable rather than where the original mistake was made.

Syntax checking does not establish that the program solves its intended task. For example, a legal subtraction can still be wrong when the specification requires addition, so expected results and execution evidence are also needed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pretty-printing and code folding

leadVisual.title: Presentation tools do different jobs

coreExplanation: Pretty-printing presents source in a consistent readable form, for example by indenting nested blocks and applying syntax colouring to keywords or other language elements. This helps a programmer recognise structure and spot suspicious formatting or missing elements.

Expanding and collapsing code blocks reveals or hides sections in the editor so attention can be focused on the relevant part of a large program. Folding changes the display only: hidden statements still belong to the program and execute whenever control flow reaches them.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Single stepping, breakpoints and inspection

leadVisual.title: Pause before the line, then inspect its effect

coreExplanation: Debugging connects an unexpected program state to the statement that caused it. Compare a predicted result with the observed result.

Tool: Single stepping; What it lets you do: Execute one statement, then inspect its effect before the next runs.. Tool: Breakpoint; What it lets you do: Pause at a selected location, normally before that statement executes; choose a point just before the suspect operation.. Tool: Variable / expression inspection; What it lets you do: Read current values while paused; evaluating an expression does not execute OUTPUT.. Tool: Report window; What it lets you do: Read program output, run-time errors and diagnostic messages..

Predict: Write the expected state at the suspect line. Step and compare: Run that statement once. If a value is wrong, inspect the operation and its inputs. Correct and retest: Fix the cause, restart from the initial state and compare the new output with the expectation.

Explain why both data and the computer system need security.
explanationUnits: Protect the data and its processing system
materialTitles: A clinic cannot open its records

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security, privacy and integrity

leadVisual.title: Classify the consequence

coreExplanation: Data security protects information against unauthorised access, loss or damage. Privacy concerns the appropriate collection, use and disclosure of personal information. Data integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and consistency, including avoiding incorrect changes during processing or transfer.

These concepts can be affected separately. Restricting access does not make an incorrect value true, and copying a record perfectly does not make its disclosure appropriate. Identify the property affected from what happened to the data, not simply from the presence of a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Protect the data and its processing system

leadVisual.title: Two independent protection targets

coreExplanation: A system must remain available to authorised users and must execute trusted operations. Malware, stolen credentials or damaged hardware can disrupt processing or expose data even when a separate file copy has been protected.

Data also needs protection wherever copies are stored or transferred. A secured computer cannot prevent disclosure from an unencrypted removable drive that has already been lost. Combine system controls with protection of the data and recoverable copies.

leadVisual.title: Establish an identity before checking what that identity may do

coreExplanation: Account: Associates a distinct identity with permissions and an activity record. Separate accounts help attribute actions. Password: Secret knowledge used to authenticate that claimed identity against the stored verifier.
A successful login does not grant every permission. Hard-to-guess passwords and limits on repeated attempts reduce guessing, but a disclosed password can still be misused.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create and verify a digital signature

leadVisual.title: Digital signature: sender and receiver

coreExplanation: The sender applies a hash algorithm to a message to produce a digest, then signs that digest using the sender's private key. In the simplified signing model, this is described as encrypting the digest. The sender sends the message together with the digital signature.

The receiver uses the sender's public key to verify the signature; in the simplified model, decrypting the signature recovers the sender's digest. The receiver also hashes the received message with the same algorithm and compares the digests. A match supports the claimed origin and shows that the signed content has not changed, provided the public key is correctly associated with the sender.

A digital signature does not make the message unreadable. Confidentiality requires encryption separately. Signing the digest must not be confused with sending the private key or merely appending an unprotected checksum.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Biometric authentication

leadVisual.title: Capture and match a biometric

coreExplanation: Biometrics use a physical or behavioural feature, such as a fingerprint, iris, voice or typing pattern. A sensor captures the feature and software extracts a template that is compared with an enrolled reference.

A sufficient match authenticates the identity claim. False acceptance can admit an impostor, while false rejection can deny a legitimate user. Sensors and protected templates are needed, and a compromised biological feature cannot be replaced as easily as a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Firewalls on a PC and at a network boundary

leadVisual.title: Traffic decisions and firewall placement

coreExplanation: A firewall checks incoming and outgoing traffic against configured rules, for example rules about addresses, ports, protocols or connection state. It allows permitted traffic and blocks disallowed traffic; it may also log decisions.

A host firewall runs on one computer. A network firewall filters traffic passing through a network boundary. Neither arrangement guarantees that all harmful content is detected: permitted traffic can still carry a deceptive message or malicious download, and poorly chosen rules can leave unwanted access open.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-virus software

leadVisual.title: Respond to a suspicious executable

coreExplanation: Anti-virus software scans files, memory or activity for known virus signatures and suspicious behaviour. On detection it can block execution, isolate a file in quarantine, or remove the malicious code.

Detection information must be updated as new threats are identified. Quarantine prevents normal use of a suspicious file while preserving it for review. New or concealed malware may escape detection, so a successful scan does not prove that every file is safe.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-spyware software

leadVisual.title: After detecting a keylogger

coreExplanation: Anti-spyware looks for software that covertly monitors activity or collects information. It can detect a monitoring component, stop it, quarantine it or remove it. Detection may be included within a broader anti-malware product.

Removing spyware reduces further collection but cannot retrieve information already sent to a third party. Exposed credentials may need replacing, and the entry route should be addressed to reduce reinfection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine controls for different risks

leadVisual.title: A travelling employee's computer

coreExplanation: Encryption changes readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. It protects the confidentiality of stored or intercepted copies; the authorised application needs the correct key to recover readable data.

Choose controls by mechanism. Login authentication checks identity, a firewall filters connections, anti-malware addresses malicious software, and encryption protects content outside normal access paths. Combining these controls reduces different risks without assuming that any one control replaces the others.

leadVisual.title: An infected host can carry replication to other files

coreExplanation: Attach: Virus code attaches to or modifies a host file or program. Execute: Running the infected host can run the virus. Replicate: The virus can infect further files; a payload may corrupt, delete or disrupt data.
Shared files, networks and downloaded attachments can carry infected hosts to another computer. Avoid executing untrusted files and maintain detection software to reduce the risk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Spyware monitors and discloses

leadVisual.title: The collection and disclosure route

coreExplanation: Spyware covertly monitors activity or collects data, for example by logging keystrokes or recording the screen. Collected information may be sent to a third party, exposing private details or credentials.

Its defining feature is covert collection, not necessarily self-replication. Anti-spyware can address the installed component, while controlled installation and caution with downloads reduce entry opportunities.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unauthorised access by hackers

leadVisual.title: Entry route and consequence

coreExplanation: In this security context, a hacker gains or attempts unauthorised access to a system or its data. Weak credentials, exposed services or unpatched vulnerabilities can provide an entry route.

The resulting access may permit disclosure, alteration or disruption. Strong authentication reduces impersonation, software patches address known vulnerabilities, and access rights limit what a compromised account can do.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Phishing persuades the user

leadVisual.title: Phishing succeeds by persuading a person to act

coreExplanation: Impersonation: A message claims to come from a trusted person or organisation. Unsafe action: Urgency or a pretext encourages disclosure, a link click or another unsafe action. Credential capture: A linked fake sign-in page can collect the supplied password.

Verify a request through an independently obtained contact or known website. Filtering and training reduce exposure. Multi-factor authentication can reduce the impact of a stolen password, but does not make every deceptive request harmless.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match precautions to the threat

leadVisual.title: Choose from the mechanism

coreExplanation: A useful precaution interrupts a specific route or reduces a specific consequence. Explain that link: patching repairs a known software weakness, permission restrictions reduce exposure, and independent verification challenges a deceptive request.

Controls reduce risk rather than eliminate every possible incident. Combining prevention, detection and recovery allows a response when one measure fails. Choose controls appropriate to the system and explain what remains outside each control's role.

objectives.description: Describe encryption and decryption as protection for data confidentiality.
materialTitles: From readable data to a protected copy
An encrypted archive on a lost drive

objectives.description: Apply access rights to data operations and explain their limits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Encryption and decryption

leadVisual.title: From readable data to a protected copy

coreExplanation: Encryption applies an algorithm and key to plaintext, producing ciphertext. Decryption applies the corresponding algorithm and correct key to recover the original readable information. An intercepted or stolen encrypted copy should be unintelligible to someone without the required key.

Protect the key separately from the encrypted copy. Encryption does not decide which logged-in user may edit a record, prevent deletion of ciphertext, or prove that the source data was true. Its main role here is confidentiality.

workedExample.title: An encrypted archive on a lost drive

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply access rights to data

leadVisual.title: Personnel-file permissions

coreExplanation: Access rights associate users or roles with permitted actions on a resource. Read permits viewing, modify permits alteration, and delete permits removal. A service checks the requested operation against these permissions after identifying the user.

Least privilege gives a role only the rights needed for its work. Restricting read access supports confidentiality; restricting changes supports integrity. Rights on a server do not protect an unencrypted copy outside that server, and authorised users can still make mistakes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Validation and verification answer different questions

leadVisual.title: A source mark of 46 is entered as 64

coreExplanation: Validation tests whether input satisfies stated rules and is reasonable for its purpose. Verification checks whether information has been entered, copied or transferred accurately relative to its source. Both reduce the acceptance of errors and so help maintain data integrity.

A plausible wrong value can pass validation, and two copies of a false original can agree. Neither process proves that the source is true. Use both when a system needs acceptable values and faithful copying.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Range and limit checks

leadVisual.title: Apply the written bounds

coreExplanation: A range check applies both a lower and an upper bound, such as 0 <= Mark <= 75. Test both endpoints as well as values outside them; the stated rule decides whether the bounds are inclusive.

A limit check applies one upper or lower bound, such as FileSize <= 10 MiB. It does not introduce a second bound that was not specified. Choose a range when both ends matter and a limit when the requirement supplies one bound.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Format and length checks

leadVisual.title: Code rule: two uppercase letters, then four digits

coreExplanation: A format check tests a required pattern, for example two uppercase letters followed by four digits. A length check tests the number of characters, for example exactly six. The two checks ask different questions about the same string.
A six-character value can still have the wrong format. Check the complete pattern and the specified character count, preserving leading zeros when a code is a string.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Presence and existence checks

leadVisual.title: Stored customer IDs: C102, C107, C115

coreExplanation: A presence check requires an entry rather than a blank required field. An existence check looks for the supplied value in a specified stored lookup or file, such as checking that a customer identifier belongs to an existing customer.
A value can be present but absent from the lookup. Define which field is required and which stored set supplies valid identifiers; do not confuse these checks with a format test.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and check an identifier's check digit

leadVisual.title: Weighted check digit: a complete calculation

coreExplanation: A check digit is derived from the other digits in an identifier and stored with them. On entry or scanning, the system repeats the stated calculation and compares the expected check digit with the supplied digit. A mismatch causes rejection or re-entry.

Use the algorithm given in the question: different schemes use different weights and moduli. For the example here, multiply the four data digits by 3, 1, 3, 1 and choose a final digit that makes the total a multiple of 10. Some errors can still produce the same check digit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Verify entered data

leadVisual.title: Source code: BK209

coreExplanation: For a visual check, a person compares the entered value with the original source and investigates differences. It is a comparison with a source, not simply a judgement that the value looks reasonable.

For double entry, the value is entered independently twice and the computer compares the entries. A mismatch is flagged for correction or re-entry. Agreement still cannot establish that the original source is correct, and repeating the same mistake can evade detection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use parity on a byte

leadVisual.title: Build an even-parity byte

coreExplanation: A parity bit is chosen so the total number of 1 bits, including that bit, has the agreed even or odd parity. The examples use seven data bits and one parity bit to form an eight-bit transmitted group.

The receiver counts the 1s and compares the result with the agreed convention. Any odd number of flipped bits changes parity and is detected. An even number of flips can leave parity unchanged; the check alone cannot identify the incorrect bit or prove the byte is correct.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use row and column parity

leadVisual.title: Locate a single-bit error by intersection

coreExplanation: Block parity organises transmitted groups into rows, applies a parity bit to each row, and adds a parity row or byte for the columns. The receiver checks parity in both directions using the agreed convention.

If exactly one bit has changed, the failing row and failing column intersect at that bit, allowing it to be located and corrected by flipping it. Multiple errors may be ambiguous or undetected; four flipped corner bits in a rectangle leave every affected row and column parity unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and compare a checksum

leadVisual.title: An eight-bit sum checksum

coreExplanation: The sender calculates a value from a data block using an agreed checksum algorithm and sends it with the data. The receiver applies the same algorithm to the received block and compares its result with the transmitted checksum.

A mismatch indicates an error and can trigger rejection or retransmission. A match means no error was detected by that checksum; different data can produce the same value. Use the stated algorithm rather than assuming that all checksums are simple sums.

objectives.description: Explain why joining a professional ethical body supports professional practice.
explanationUnits: BCS, IEEE and the value of membership

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why computing professionals need ethics

leadVisual.title: From specialist knowledge to an informed decision

coreExplanation: Ethics concerns principles about right and wrong conduct. A computing professional makes decisions that can affect other people's safety, privacy, opportunities and resources. Users may lack the technical knowledge or access needed to detect an unsafe system or challenge its design, so technical power brings responsibilities.

Professional ethics helps guide decisions when interests conflict or a rule does not settle what should be done. Its purposes include protecting the public interest, promoting honest and competent work, maintaining trust and making professionals accountable for foreseeable effects of their decisions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Professional duties and legal compliance

leadVisual.title: Recognise the professional duty

coreExplanation: A professional should work within their competence, report limitations honestly, protect confidential information and consider effects on the public. Conflicting interests should be disclosed so that advice can be evaluated fairly. For example, a paid relationship with a supplier can influence a recommendation even when that recommendation is technically possible.

Law sets enforceable requirements; ethical judgement also considers what is responsible in the particular circumstances. An employer's instruction or the absence of an explicit legal prohibition does not remove a professional's duty to consider harm. A defensible response records the concern, seeks appropriate guidance and proposes an action that addresses it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: BCS, IEEE and the value of membership

leadVisual.title: Membership support and its purpose

coreExplanation: BCS is the British Computer Society. IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. These professional bodies provide codes of conduct or ethics that express standards expected of members. A shared code gives a practitioner a reference when explaining a professional concern to an employer or client.

Joining can provide continuing professional development, technical information and contact with experienced peers. These help members maintain competence and obtain guidance when a problem exceeds their experience. Membership also brings expectations of conduct and accountability through the body's professional processes, supporting public confidence in the profession.

A code supports judgement but cannot guarantee that every member acts ethically. Membership does not replace the law, remove personal responsibility or automatically certify every product a member develops.

leadVisual.title: School trip location sharing

coreExplanation: Begin with the actual decision: what is someone proposing to collect, disclose, change or conceal? Identify direct stakeholders, such as users and employees, and others affected indirectly, such as families or the wider public. Different groups may have different interests in the same system.

Connect each stakeholder to a relevant responsibility. A school handling location data has duties towards pupils' privacy as well as safety. Naming 'society' without explaining a connection is too vague to support a judgement. Benefits and harms are parallel possibilities to investigate; one is not automatically the cause of the other.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare ethical and unethical actions

leadVisual.title: Compare the consequences of two actions

coreExplanation: Explain consequences through a cause-and-effect link: the action changes what happens to a stakeholder. For example, disclosing a known defect allows a client to avoid relying on unsafe output; concealing it can lead the client to make a harmful decision with misplaced confidence.

Consider both courses of action. Acting ethically can have an immediate cost, such as delay or extra testing, while preserving safety and trust. Acting unethically may produce a short-term advantage but can cause harm, complaints, loss of confidence or professional consequences. State consequences supported by the situation rather than assuming that every outcome is certain.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify a proportionate response

leadVisual.title: Build a supported judgement

coreExplanation: Use evidence to weigh the stated purpose against the effects on people. Compare a realistic alternative that could meet the purpose with less intrusion or risk. Proportionality means the action should be appropriate to the need and no more intrusive or harmful than necessary to achieve it.

A conclusion should identify an action and explain why it is justified. Relevant safeguards might include limiting collection and retention, restricting access, correcting inaccurate information or providing a way to challenge a decision. A safeguard needs a mechanism linked to the particular risk, and it may reduce rather than eliminate that risk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why software needs copyright protection

leadVisual.title: Ownership and permission perform different roles

coreExplanation: Writing software takes time, skill and investment, while copying a finished program can cost very little. Copyright legislation gives the rights holder enforceable control over protected expression such as original source code and documentation. This allows unauthorised copying or distribution to be challenged and enables creators to grant permissions and obtain revenue from their work.

Copyright protects the expression of a program rather than every underlying idea or mathematical method. A licence grants permission for specified acts under conditions; buying a copy normally does not transfer ownership of its copyright. A user should establish the applicable permissions before copying, modifying or redistributing software, taking account of any relevant legal exceptions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Free software and the Free Software Foundation

leadVisual.title: Four freedoms in use

coreExplanation: The Free Software Foundation (FSF) promotes software freedom. Its approach gives users freedoms to run a program for any purpose, study and change it, redistribute copies, and distribute modified versions. Access to source code is necessary for studying how the program works and making useful changes.

Free refers to these freedoms, not necessarily a zero price. A copy or support service can be sold while the user retains the freedoms granted by a free-software licence. Some licences use copyleft conditions to preserve freedoms in distributed derivatives; not every free-software licence imposes the same redistribution conditions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Open source and the Open Source Initiative

leadVisual.title: Check rights as well as source access

coreExplanation: The Open Source Initiative (OSI) maintains the Open Source Definition and approves licences that satisfy its criteria. Open-source licensing includes access to source code and permission to modify and redistribute the software. Merely allowing users to look at source code is insufficient if the licence prohibits the necessary uses or redistribution.

FSF and OSI are organisations, not two individual licences. Many licences satisfy both free-software and open-source criteria. Their emphasis differs: the FSF stresses users' freedoms, while the OSI evaluates licences against open-source criteria. For a real choice, read the licence's obligations, such as keeping notices or conditions on distributing modified work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Shareware: evaluate before continued use

leadVisual.title: A trial has terms and a continuation decision

coreExplanation: Shareware is distributed so users can try software before paying for continued or complete use. A trial may expire after a stated period or restrict features until a licence is purchased. The exact trial terms determine what use and copying are permitted.

This approach can reduce the risk of buying an unsuitable program because a user can test it on their own system. However, a successful trial is not a permanent entitlement, and shareware does not automatically include source code or permission to modify it. Budget for any required payment and check what happens when the trial ends.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Commercial and proprietary software

leadVisual.title: Separate user permissions from the price of a copy

coreExplanation: Commercial software is developed or supplied as a business activity. A supplier may earn income from licences, subscriptions, support or other services. Commercial and proprietary are not synonyms: a business can sell free or open-source software, while proprietary software can sometimes be offered without payment.

A proprietary licence commonly permits specified use while limiting copying, modification or redistribution. Terms may specify the number of users or devices, duration and support arrangements. Paid support can be useful when it is actually included in the agreement; payment alone does not guarantee support, source access or unrestricted installation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose a licence from the requirements

leadVisual.title: Match a requirement to a licence feature

coreExplanation: Identify the organisation's required acts before selecting software: running it on the intended devices, modifying source, distributing copies or obtaining support. Then compare those needs with the permissions, costs and obligations of the offered licences. A cheap option is unsuitable if its terms prohibit a required act.

A justification connects a stated requirement to a licence feature and its consequence. Check practical limits as well: source modification needs skilled staff, a trial needs a continuation plan, and supplier support needs agreed scope and availability. There is no single licence category that is best for every organisation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: What artificial intelligence does

leadVisual.title: Identify the task

coreExplanation: Artificial intelligence (AI) enables computer systems to perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as interpreting language, recognising patterns, reasoning or making predictions and decisions. A system may use expert-written rules or a model learned from data to infer an output for a new input.

An AI system does not have to be a physical robot, conscious or human-like in every respect. A recommendation service can use AI entirely in software. Conversely, recording information or performing a fixed arithmetic calculation does not by itself demonstrate AI. Identify the interpretation, inference or decision task being performed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: From input to an AI-assisted action

leadVisual.title: Follow a maintenance prediction from input to use

coreExplanation: Describe an application as a connected chain. State the input information, what the AI infers or recognises, the resulting output and how that output is used. 'AI is used in medicine' names an area but does not explain an application; interpreting a scan to flag a possible abnormality gives a task and a use.

Outputs can guide a person or control an action. A fraud-detection model may flag a payment for an investigator, while an autonomous controller may select an action from sensor readings. Confidence, reliability and consequences determine how much checking or human intervention is appropriate. A prediction can be useful without being certain.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Social effects: access, fairness and privacy

leadVisual.title: Look beyond an overall accuracy figure

coreExplanation: Social impacts concern how people live, participate and are treated. Speech recognition can improve access for someone unable to type, and translation can help people communicate. The benefit depends on whether the system works adequately for its users, including different accents, languages or disabilities.

Biased or unrepresentative data can contribute to unequal error rates and unfair decisions. Collecting personal information also creates privacy risks. Explain who benefits or is harmed: a hiring system that rejects qualified applicants unfairly changes their opportunities. Testing across affected groups, limiting unnecessary collection and providing human review or appeal can reduce specific risks.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Economic effects: productivity, work and cost

leadVisual.title: Account for more than one cost

coreExplanation: Economic impacts concern resources, production, costs and employment. An AI tool may process routine cases more quickly, reduce waste or predict failures before expensive disruption. Link the saving to the activity: an early equipment warning may allow planned maintenance during a quiet period rather than an emergency shutdown.

Costs include developing or buying the system, obtaining and maintaining suitable data, operating hardware and training staff. Incorrect decisions can create rework or losses. Automation may reduce demand for some tasks while creating or changing roles in supervision, maintenance and specialist support; workers may need retraining. A productivity gain does not mean every worker or business benefits equally.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Environmental costs and potential savings

leadVisual.title: Compare application savings with the system footprint

coreExplanation: Training and operating AI models uses computing equipment and electricity, and cooling may require water or additional energy. Manufacturing and replacing hardware also uses materials and produces waste. Emissions depend partly on the energy supply, so identical computation can have different environmental consequences in different settings.

An AI application can also reduce resource use: optimising delivery routes may reduce fuel consumption, adjusting heating to occupancy may reduce energy waste, and detecting faults may prolong equipment life. Compare these savings with the system's own operation and hardware lifecycle. The result depends on the scale of use and the alternative being replaced, not on an assumption that all AI is environmentally beneficial or harmful.

leadVisual.title: Evaluate a proposed deployment

coreExplanation: Start an evaluation by identifying the AI task and the decision it influences. Develop relevant benefits and drawbacks through effects on named stakeholders or resources. Reach a supported judgement using the supplied constraints. State a suitable safeguard or alternative and explain the risk it addresses. Human oversight needs a workable review process and competent reviewers; writing 'a human checks it' does not establish that errors will be caught. A conditional recommendation should say which evidence or conditions would make deployment acceptable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: From repeated facts to linked tables

leadVisual.title: Store shared patient facts once

coreExplanation: A file-based approach keeps data in files managed by individual applications. Repeating a patient's address in appointment and billing files uses extra storage. If only the billing copy is updated, the two applications may report different addresses for the same patient.

A relational design can store the address in Patient and put PatientID in related records. Applications retrieve the shared fact through that relationship. Central queries, constraints and access controls also reduce isolated retrieval and duplicated control code; the benefits depend on the design and its enforcement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Entities, tables, records and fields

leadVisual.title: From an entity to its stored representation

coreExplanation: An entity is a type of real-world object or concept about which data is stored, such as Patient. A table represents occurrences of that entity. One row is a record, also called a tuple; it describes one particular patient.

An attribute is a named property of the entity, such as PatientName. A field is the corresponding column in its table. Distinguish the property from one value: PatientName is the field, while 'Imani' is a value in a particular record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose keys for identification and retrieval

leadVisual.title: Keys answer different questions

coreExplanation: Candidate key: A minimal field or combination that uniquely identifies a record. Primary key: The chosen candidate; values must be unique and not null. Composite key: Uses several fields, with every component needed for uniqueness.

Secondary key: Another retrieval route, such as Town; it need not be unique. Foreign key: References a key in another table. A patient identifier may therefore recur across several appointment records.

coreBlocks.title: Retrieve and relate records

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read relationship cardinality in both directions

leadVisual.title: Read each relationship in both directions

coreExplanation: Relationship cardinality describes how many occurrences on one side may be associated with an occurrence on the other. Read the business rule in both directions before choosing one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.

If a student can join several clubs and a club can have several students, the relationship is many-to-many. A Membership table records each student-club association and gives two one-to-many relationships. The pair of identifiers can be its composite key when each membership occurs only once.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Prevent references to missing records

leadVisual.title: A reference must reach an existing record

coreExplanation: Referential integrity requires each non-null foreign-key value to match an existing referenced key value. If an appointment names PatientID 99 but no such patient exists, a declared foreign-key constraint can reject that appointment.

Updates and deletions must also preserve valid links. Deleting a referenced patient can be rejected, or handled by an explicitly defined referential action. A nullable foreign key may be null where the design allows no association; it must not hold an arbitrary unmatched identifier.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use an index to find matching records

leadVisual.title: An index provides another access path

coreExplanation: An index is an additional lookup structure associated with one or more fields. It relates indexed values to record locations so the DBMS can find matches without inspecting every table row in suitable queries.

An index on Town can help retrieve all patients in York even when Town is not unique. The index occupies storage and must be maintained when indexed data changes. It improves an access path; it does not replace the table or guarantee that stored facts are correct.

coreExplanation: Extract entity types from the facts that the organisation needs to store, then identify each entity's key and relevant attributes. In this clinic, each appointment involves exactly one patient and one doctor. A patient or doctor may have many appointments. Appointment therefore stores both foreign keys, and its separate AppointmentID allows the same patient to visit the same doctor on different occasions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: 1NF: one value in each field

leadVisual.title: 1NF: expand a repeating group

coreExplanation: Identify it: Several product entries stored together in one order field form a repeating group. Separate rows: Give each product line its own row, keeping the order and customer information needed to interpret it. Check 1NF: Every field value is atomic and no repeating group remains.

Assume each product occurs once at most per order and UnitPrice is its current fixed price. (OrderID, ProductID) identifies a line. Customer and product details still repeat; 1NF alone does not remove those dependencies.
