knowledgeUnits.heading: Data management and the data dictionary

leadVisual.title: Metadata describes the data

coreExplanation: A DBMS provides software services to store, retrieve and update database data. It maintains a data dictionary containing metadata: information about the database's tables, fields, types, lengths, keys and constraints rather than the ordinary records themselves.

When a table or query is defined, the DBMS can consult that metadata to check field names and permitted structures. Maintaining definitions centrally reduces the risk that separate applications use conflicting assumptions about the same stored data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent the organisation's data

leadVisual.title: Translate a business rule into a model

coreExplanation: Data modelling identifies the entities, attributes and relationships required by an organisation. It starts from the information and business rules, such as whether one appointment may involve several doctors, rather than from how bytes will be arranged on disk.

A DBMS modelling tool can help create and inspect the relationships before they are implemented as tables. The designer must still confirm that the model matches the stated requirements; software cannot infer every business rule from field names.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define the logical schema

leadVisual.title: A logical schema describes organisation

coreExplanation: The logical schema specifies the logical organisation of the database: its tables, attributes, data types, keys, relationships and constraints. Programs can use these definitions without knowing the physical disk locations of individual records.

A model of pupils and groups can become Pupil(PupilID, PupilName, GroupID) and TutorGroup(GroupID, GroupName), with specified primary and foreign keys. The schema is the design being defined; the data dictionary stores metadata describing that design.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Enforce valid values and relationships

leadVisual.title: Check a change before accepting it

coreExplanation: Integrity constraints restrict invalid or inconsistent database changes. A primary key identifies records uniquely, a foreign key checks a declared reference, and field types or validation rules restrict values to a permitted domain.

For an examination database, a rule can require Mark to be between 0 and 100 and CandidateID to refer to an existing candidate. The DBMS rejects changes violating those rules. A plausible but incorrectly transcribed mark can still pass them, so integrity constraints do not establish factual truth.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assign access rights to users and groups

leadVisual.title: Permit operations according to user roles

coreExplanation: Database security restricts who can access stored information and which operations are permitted. After authentication establishes identity, access rights can allow reading selected data while denying insertion, modification or deletion.

Rights may be assigned to an individual account or to a group representing a role. A school can give Tutors access to contact information and the Finance group permission to update fees. Group membership must be maintained when responsibilities change.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Back up and recover a consistent database

leadVisual.title: Prepare, protect, restore and check

coreExplanation: Schedule: Choose backup frequency for the acceptable interval of data loss. Protect: Keep a consistent recovery copy outside the same failure as the live database; restrict access to sensitive records. Recover: Restore a suitable backup. Where supported, replay later transaction logs to the chosen recovery point. Test: Periodically restore to check the copies and the procedure.
A backup is a saved database state; recovery is the process of making a suitable consistent state usable again.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use the developer interface

leadVisual.title: Build the objects and interfaces users need

coreExplanation: A DBMS developer interface supplies tools for constructing database objects and applications. A developer can define tables and constraints and build forms or reports that use the database without manually implementing every interface component.

For a school admissions form, the developer chooses the fields, configures validation and links controls to the appropriate data. The resulting form collects a new pupil record. Designing that form is distinct from the query processor carrying out its eventual data request.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a query through the query processor

leadVisual.title: Turn a SQL request into a result

coreExplanation: Interpret and check: Check the statement’s syntax and references against table definitions. Plan: Choose a suitable execution plan, considering available indexes. Execute: Locate, filter and return the requested records while permissions and integrity rules apply.
An overdue-loans query needs data access, not a rebuilt data-entry form. The developer interface creates application objects; the query processor carries out the submitted data request.

objectives.description: Explain the role of DDL in creating and changing database structure.
materialTitles: Distinguish a new attribute from a new value

objectives.description: Explain the role of DML in querying and maintaining stored data.
Explain SQL as the industry-standard language for DDL and DML.
explanationUnits: SQL expresses both kinds of operation
materialTitles: SQL includes both DDL and DML

knowledgeUnits.heading: DDL changes structure

leadVisual.title: Distinguish a new attribute from a new value

coreExplanation: Data Definition Language defines and modifies database structure. It can create a database, define a table's attributes and constraints, or alter an existing table definition. These operations determine what data the database can store.
Creating a Loan table does not add a particular loan record. Similarly, adding DueDate changes the permitted structure for loan records rather than choosing the date for one member's loan.

knowledgeUnits.heading: DML retrieves and maintains records

leadVisual.title: DML works with records

coreExplanation: Data Manipulation Language works with records in the defined structure. SELECT retrieves specified information. INSERT INTO adds records, UPDATE changes stored field values, and DELETE FROM removes records.

A query can produce a result table without altering the stored rows. Updating one member's phone number changes data while leaving the Member field definitions intact. These are both DML operations in the syllabus classification.

knowledgeUnits.heading: SQL expresses both kinds of operation

leadVisual.title: SQL includes both DDL and DML

coreExplanation: Structured Query Language (SQL) is the industry-standard language used for both DDL and DML. The DBMS interprets SQL statements and carries out their requested changes or queries. DDL and DML describe roles within SQL rather than two alternative database products.

Determine the category from the requested effect, not from the word 'change' alone. A SQL statement that changes a column's definition is structural; one that changes the current value in that column operates on data.

explanationUnits: Read the supplied statement before explaining it
materialTitles: Read what each SQL clause asks for

objectives.description: Explain how identifiers, types, operators or literal values affect a supplied statement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read the supplied statement before explaining it

leadVisual.title: Read what each SQL clause asks for

coreExplanation: A SQL statement must be interpreted from the actual identifiers, conditions and values supplied. In a retrieval statement, SELECT identifies output expressions, FROM identifies the source and WHERE restricts rows. A changed field list can alter the columns without changing which records qualify.

Read a definition statement by identifying the object created or altered, its field types and its constraints. Quoted text literals represent values rather than field names. Explain the effect of the operator or limit given; recognising a keyword alone does not determine the result.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create a named database

leadVisual.title: Create the database before defining its tables

coreExplanation: CREATE DATABASE creates a named database in a DBMS that supports this SQL operation. The name is an identifier, not a quoted data value. Creating the database does not by itself define its tables or populate records.

After creating SchoolLibrary, the developer selects that database in the chosen DBMS interface and defines its tables. The interface command for selecting a database varies between products; the SQL statement below expresses the required creation operation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose data types and define fields

leadVisual.title: Choose a type from the meaning of a value

coreExplanation: Choose a field type from the meaning and range of its values. CHARACTER stores fixed-length character data; VARCHAR(n) stores text up to the specified maximum length. INTEGER represents whole numbers, REAL represents values with a fractional part, and BOOLEAN represents true or false.

DATE and TIME represent calendar dates and times of day separately. Field names and types appear inside the CREATE TABLE brackets, separated by commas. A numeric-looking identifier may still need a text type when leading zeroes or non-arithmetic meaning must be preserved.

workedExample.title: Create a referenced table before its child

knowledgeUnits.heading: Alter an existing table definition

leadVisual.title: ALTER TABLE adds a field to the definition

coreExplanation: ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table. To add Email to the Student definition, identify the existing table and supply the new field name and type after ADD. Existing student records remain present.

In this example the added Email field is nullable and has no default, so existing records initially have no supplied email value. Setting an email for one student is a later UPDATE operation. The new attribute and the value in one occurrence are separate changes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the primary key

leadVisual.title: A primary key identifies each record

coreExplanation: A PRIMARY KEY constraint declares the chosen identifier for a table. The key must distinguish every record and cannot be null. Write the selected field inside PRIMARY KEY brackets in the CREATE TABLE definition.

A composite primary key lists all fields needed for identification, for example PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID) in Membership. The combination must be unique; either component may recur in other combinations. Choose the key from the stated business rules.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare the referenced relationship

leadVisual.title: Declare which field references which key

coreExplanation: FOREIGN KEY names the field or fields in the current table; REFERENCES names the related table and referenced key. In Student, FOREIGN KEY (TutorID) REFERENCES Tutor(TutorID) declares which parent identifier each non-null tutor reference must match.

Create the referenced table and key first when using this teaching sequence. The child field may repeat when many students share a tutor. A foreign-key declaration enforces the link; it does not automatically assign a tutor or create the missing parent record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the result columns and source

leadVisual.title: SELECT chooses the output columns

coreExplanation: SELECT lists the fields or expressions required in the result, while FROM names the source table. Returning MemberName alone does not return MemberID or Active. Reading a result leaves the original Member records unchanged.

Use the Member and Loan data in this lesson to trace each request. Each example states any required ordering explicitly; without ORDER BY, a DBMS need not return records in insertion or primary-key order.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Filter rows using a Boolean condition

leadVisual.title: WHERE: both conditions must be true

coreExplanation: WHERE retains only records for which the condition is true. Combine comparisons with AND when all conditions must hold, or OR when an alternative is sufficient. Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit in compound expressions.
The Loan example requires an unreturned loan and a fee of at least 3. Loan 202 has a sufficient fee but is returned; loan 201 is unreturned but its fee is only 2. Neither satisfies both conditions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sort the returned records

leadVisual.title: ORDER BY rearranges the result rows

coreExplanation: ORDER BY arranges result rows by the specified field or expression. ASC means increasing order and is the default; DESC means decreasing order. Sorting changes result presentation rather than the stored values.

Multiple sort fields are applied in sequence: sort by the first field, then use the next field for ties. The example sorts fees from largest to smallest and uses LoanID ascending to make any equal-fee ordering predictable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Form groups before calculating group results

leadVisual.title: GROUP BY forms one group per key value

coreExplanation: GROUP BY places records sharing the grouping values into the same group. An aggregate can then calculate one result for each group. Grouping loans by MemberID lets COUNT(*) report the number of loans for each represented member.

Include non-aggregated selected fields in GROUP BY so each returned value has a defined meaning for the group. ORDER BY can subsequently arrange the grouped results; it does not create the groups. A member with no Loan row does not appear in a grouping of Loan alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match records from two tables with INNER JOIN

leadVisual.title: INNER JOIN returns matching row pairs

coreExplanation: An INNER JOIN combines row pairs satisfying its ON condition. Here Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID connects each loan to its member. Qualify shared field names with the table name to make the intended reference unambiguous.

A member with two loans contributes two joined rows, while a member with no matching loan contributes none. WHERE may further filter the joined rows. These AS SQL tasks use at most two tables; use an explicit INNER JOIN and a separate ON matching condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate SUM, COUNT and AVG

leadVisual.title: Aggregates calculate over the selected records

coreExplanation: Expression: SUM(Fee); What it includes: Adds non-null fees.. Expression: COUNT(Fee); What it includes: Counts non-null fees.. Expression: COUNT(*); What it includes: Counts rows, including rows with a null Fee.. Expression: AVG(Fee); What it includes: Mean of included non-null fees..

For fees 2, 4, 6, 0, 3, SUM is 15, COUNT(*) is 5 and AVG is 3. SUM, AVG and COUNT(Fee) ignore null fees. Zero is a known value and stays included. Without GROUP BY, the query gives one overall aggregate result for the selected records.

coreBlocks.title: Select the aggregate
rows: Counts rows, including rows with a null Fee.

coreBlocks.text: For fees 2, 4, 6, 0, 3, SUM is 15, COUNT(*) is 5 and AVG is 3. SUM, AVG and COUNT(Fee) ignore null fees. Zero is a known value and stays included. Without GROUP BY, the query gives one overall aggregate result for the selected records.
coreBlocks.title: Distinguish null from zero

workedExample.title: Calculate the same result by hand

knowledgeUnits.heading: Insert values into named fields

leadVisual.title: INSERT INTO adds a new record

coreExplanation: INSERT INTO adds a record. Name the target fields and supply the corresponding VALUES in the same order. Text literals use single quotes; numeric and Boolean values are written according to their types.

Check the new primary key and any foreign-key values before insertion. The library example adds MemberID 5 with the name Elena and Active TRUE. It does not alter an existing member's record, and it must fail if that primary key is already present.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Delete only the intended records

leadVisual.title: DELETE FROM removes the selected row

coreExplanation: DELETE FROM removes complete records from the named table. WHERE selects the records to remove. To remove the completed loan with LoanID 204, match that identifier rather than a member identifier shared by several loans.

Without a WHERE condition, deletion targets all rows in the table, subject to constraints. Check the intended rows first with a corresponding SELECT. Removing a referenced parent may be rejected by foreign-key constraints; this example removes the child Loan record.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change fields while keeping the record

leadVisual.title: UPDATE changes a field in the selected record

coreExplanation: UPDATE names the table, SET supplies the new field values, and WHERE selects the affected records. Updating Returned to TRUE for LoanID 203 leaves that loan's identity, member and fee in place.

A missing or incorrect WHERE condition can affect unintended records. Decide whether the business task requires changing a value or removing a record, then verify both the affected rows and the values that should remain unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 1: Information representation

leadVisual.title: Three questions for every representation

coreExplanation: Recover meaning using a stated representation, then show the calculation or reconstruction and check its boundary.

teachingBlocks.title: Retrieve a method and produce evidence
rows: Explain 2ⁿ patterns versus maximum 2ⁿ − 1; convert prefixes through bytes.
Convert both ways; decode signed values; show carries or borrows and judge overflow.
Use supplied codes to encode and decode a string; distinguish a code point from its stored bytes.
Reconstruct the grid or object list, calculate data size, and justify scaling behaviour.
Quantise numerical measurements, encode and decode them, then calculate raw data size.
Decode every run or reference and compare the complete stated storage costs.

teachingBlocks.text: In the independent tasks below, first name the width, representation and any storage assumptions. A familiar bit pattern can have different meanings; a repeated source can still grow after encoding. Check your intermediate steps before opening the answers.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a consistent checking method

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 2: Communication

leadVisual.title: Four independent diagnosis tasks

coreExplanation: Justify designs from their constraints and trace packets, frames and responses through named devices.
Calculate buffer and subnet decisions with supplied values; distinguish failed dependencies before proposing recovery.

teachingBlocks.text: A mobile museum terminal retrieves an exhibit record from a hosted service. Diagnose the complete system by locating each responsibility: local access, onward link, addressing, remote service and returned content. A correct name must be connected to the stated requirement or failure.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the section as one system
Follow the request and identify evidence
rows: Choose LAN/WAN scope, client-server/P2P roles, thin/thick processing, topology and carrier from separate requirements.
A suitable service model does not create a spare physical link or guarantee radio coverage.
WNIC → WAP → switch; MAC and known ports guide local frames, while routers handle other networks.
A device, cable or central switch can fail; shared half-duplex collision handling has a separate scope.
Use the prefix to choose local/gateway delivery; distinguish scope from assignment; resolve the domain before requesting a resource.
DNS success, network delivery and an existing server resource are different conditions.
Compare arrival and playback rates, current reserve and capacity; follow the hosted request and response.
A finite buffer cannot cover an indefinite deficit. A backup captures only retained state and requires a usable recovery service.

teachingBlocks.text: Use the four Section 2 diagnosis questions below to test design, forwarding and collision behaviour, rate calculations, and address-to-resource flow. For revision, return to Lessons 007–014 when a step depends on a label you cannot yet explain.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply the complete chain

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 3: Hardware

leadVisual.title: Section 3 application route

coreExplanation: Trace physical and data changes before assigning a fault or choosing hardware.
Use the full rule, actual state and all input combinations when checking control and logic.

teachingBlocks.text: An environmental recorder measures conditions, stores observations and controls a pump. Diagnose it by separating the physical measurement, data representation, temporary workspace, persistent files and corrective action. A component’s name alone does not demonstrate that the full system is working.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the hardware responsibilities
Choose evidence that separates possible faults
rows: A saved reading returns after restart but an unsaved edit disappears.
Separate non-volatile saved data from volatile working memory.
A burst can be accepted but a sustained excess eventually blocks transfer.
Compare waiting content and finite capacity; apply the full-buffer policy.
A motor receives a command but the pressure stays unchanged.
The command is not the physical outcome; use actual feedback and investigate the actuator.
An alarm triggers under a supposedly rejected input.
Translate the stated condition, trace intermediate logic and identify a counterexample.

teachingBlocks.text: Use the three hardware diagnosis tasks and the retained logic task below. Return to Lessons 015–020 to reconstruct any missing physical stage or Boolean relationship. The logic task’s complete eight-row answer is a check on the supplied expression, not a substitute for independently deriving the table.

Understand address, data and control buses.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 5: System software

leadVisual.title: Retrieve the complete S5 chain

coreExplanation: Separate the job from the software responsible for it: the OS coordinates resources, utilities perform maintenance or protection tasks, and libraries supply reusable code. Explain the actual operation before claiming a benefit.

Track what is translated, when execution occurs and which environment is required. Match compilation or interpretation to the workload, follow Java through bytecode and the JVM, and use IDE evidence to check behaviour rather than assuming a successful translation proves correctness.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 6: Security, privacy and data integrity

leadVisual.title: Visual overview · Section 6: Security, privacy and data integrity

coreExplanation: Distinguish data security, privacy and integrity.
Explain the need for data and computer-system security.
Understand user accounts/passwords, digital signatures, biometrics, firewall, antivirus, anti-spyware and encryption as security measures.
Understand virus, spyware, hackers, phishing and pharming threats.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 7: Ethics and ownership

leadVisual.title: Retrieve the complete S7 reasoning

coreExplanation: Explain why specialists owe duties to affected people, then use the actual decision to identify stakeholders and compare the consequences of ethical and unethical actions. Professional membership supplies standards and development; it leaves the individual responsible for applying them.

For software ownership, distinguish copyright from the permissions in a licence. Compare free-software freedoms, open-source criteria, trial limits and commercial terms against the required use. For AI, describe the task performed before assessing its effects on people, costs and resources.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 8: Databases

leadVisual.title: Retrieve and apply the S8 methods

coreExplanation: Start with the information and business rules: identify entities, choose candidate and primary keys, then show relationship cardinalities. Diagnose repeated data and dependency problems before decomposing tables into 3NF. Retain foreign keys that allow the original facts to be reconstructed.

Connect the design to its DBMS implementation. The dictionary describes fields and constraints; access rights and recovery procedures protect use and availability. Read or write DDL to define the structure, and DML to retrieve or maintain records. Trace SQL against the actual data, including join matches, grouped totals and the rows targeted by a maintenance condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose detail according to the purpose

leadVisual.title: Two purposes, different relevant facts

coreExplanation: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while retaining the essential features of a problem or system. What counts as essential depends on the purpose: a journey planner needs connections and travel times, whereas a vehicle-painting system may need colours.

A simpler representation reduces the information a designer must consider and makes the important relationships easier to understand. It can also reduce the data and processing needed by the solution. Omitting a detail that changes the required result makes the model unsuitable, even if the model becomes smaller.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Produce and check an abstract model

leadVisual.title: Model for checking a particular copy

coreExplanation: Start by stating what the model must answer. Select the objects, properties and relationships needed for that answer, and represent them with a suitable table or diagram. Record assumptions so the intended limits of the model are clear.

For a library's loan-availability check, a copy identifier and its current loan status can be enough. A title alone cannot distinguish two copies with different availability. Test the representation with one available copy and one borrowed copy before deciding that it captures the required distinction.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate responsibilities

leadVisual.title: Decompose a library loan into responsibilities

coreExplanation: Decomposition breaks a complex problem into smaller sub-problems. Each part has a clear responsibility; together, the parts must satisfy the original requirements.

Name responsibilities: For a loan: identify the copy, check availability, record the loan and report the outcome. Connect the parts: Agree the data passed between modules and the conditions under which each is used. Check completeness: Every requirement must be handled. Avoid an arbitrary list of screens or repeated names for the whole task.
Smaller parts are easier to understand, implement and test. Agreed interfaces also allow designers to work on separate parts.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Specify an ordered solution

leadVisual.title: A rectangular floor area

coreExplanation: An algorithm is a solution to a problem expressed as a sequence of defined steps. The order and meaning of the steps must be clear enough to carry out the intended task. Steps may include decisions and repeated actions, so a defined sequence does not mean that every execution follows one straight path.

For a rectangular area, obtain the two dimensions before multiplying them and report the product afterwards. 'Find the area' describes the goal but does not supply the calculation. Conditions also need precise operators: 'at least 18' includes 18 and every greater age, not just the single value 18.

objectives.description: Write pseudocode using the three basic constructs of sequence, selection and iteration (repetition)
explanationUnits: Repeat with a defined stopping rule
Place a decision inside a repeated task
materialTitles: A mark selects one of two outcomes
Select a result at an inclusive boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Execute dependent operations in order

leadVisual.title: A sequence with a dependency

coreExplanation: Sequence executes instructions in their written order. A later calculation may depend on an earlier input or assignment, so moving operations can change the result or read an unassigned variable. Follow dependencies when placing statements.

For a price calculation, input the quantity before multiplying it by the unit price, then add any fixed charge before outputting the final amount. Declarations can appear first to document types, but they do not perform those calculations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the correct branch

leadVisual.title: A mark selects one of two outcomes

coreExplanation: Selection chooses operations according to a Boolean condition. In IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF, a true condition selects the THEN block and a false condition selects the ELSE block. Execution continues after ENDIF once the selected block finishes.

Write a condition that matches the exact boundary in the requirement. A pass mark of at least 50 uses Mark >= 50. Mark = 50 would accept only the boundary value and reject higher marks; Mark > 50 would incorrectly reject 50 itself.

workedExample.title: Select a result at an inclusive boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Repeat with a defined stopping rule

leadVisual.title: Choose a loop from the requirement

coreExplanation: Iteration repeats a block of operations. A FOR loop is suitable when the number of repetitions is known. A WHILE loop tests a condition before the body, so it may execute zero times. A REPEAT ... UNTIL loop tests after the body and therefore executes at least once.

Initialise totals or counts before the loop, update them inside the loop, and put a final aggregate output after the loop. A condition-controlled loop must make progress towards stopping. In a countdown, decreasing Count eventually makes Count > 0 false.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Place a decision inside a repeated task

leadVisual.title: Count passes from ten marks

coreExplanation: The three constructs cooperate in a complete solution. Counting passes begins with an initialisation, repeats input and a decision for each mark, and finishes with one output. Indentation shows that the decision is inside the loop while the final output is outside it.

Read each new mark during its iteration. Increase the count only on the qualifying branch and leave it unchanged otherwise. This arrangement counts qualifying inputs rather than counting all iterations or checking one old input repeatedly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Document a solution in structured English

leadVisual.title: Age classification in structured English

coreExplanation: Structured English expresses an algorithm using controlled natural-language steps and clear grouping. State the operations in order, identify both outcomes of a decision and make the scope of any repetition explicit. It should leave the same computational choices determined as pseudocode does.

A flowchart shows that control structure with symbols and directed lines, while pseudocode uses statements and indentation. Changing notation should not change the accepted inputs or results. Trace a value on each side of a boundary when comparing two representations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use symbols and arrows consistently

leadVisual.title: Standard flowchart symbols

coreExplanation: Use terminators for start and end, parallelograms for input and output, rectangles for processing, and diamonds for decisions. Arrowheads indicate the next operation. Label the outgoing decision paths consistently, for example Yes and No, so the truth value selects an unambiguous route.

A loop needs a return path to its condition or repeated body, according to when it tests. Paths that rejoin must not imply that both selection branches execute. Inspect the arrow direction at the final output as well as at the decision; an output cannot follow an end terminator.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write pseudocode from a flowchart

leadVisual.title: A loop returns to its condition

coreExplanation: Begin at the start symbol and follow the arrows. Translate each input, process and output into its corresponding statement. At a decision, retain the full expression and place each path's operations in the appropriate block. Declare suitable types for the data used by the resulting program.

In the displayed countdown, a false condition goes directly to the final message. A true condition outputs the current value, decreases it and returns to the same test. That control flow corresponds to WHILE, with the message placed after ENDWHILE.

workedExample.title: Recover a loop from directed paths

knowledgeUnits.heading: Draw a flowchart from a written algorithm

leadVisual.title: Four inputs contribute to one total

coreExplanation: When drawing from structured English or pseudocode, identify the sequence, branch boundaries and loop boundaries before choosing symbols. Put a complete condition in every decision and show where execution continues after each path. Convert implicit loop control into visible initialisation, a condition and an update where needed.

A FOR loop that totals four values can be drawn using Index initialised to 1, a decision Index <= 4 and an increment after each addition. The false path outputs the final total. This expands the loop notation while preserving exactly four input operations.

coreExplanation: Start from the result: Name the required outcome and its preconditions. Expand an unresolved step: Replace it with operations that achieve the same result. Continue to programmable detail: Stop when no remaining action requires the programmer to invent a missing rule.

Decomposition identifies smaller sub-problems; refinement develops the internal detail of a solution. For an average, specify how inputs are read, how Total is updated and when division happens. For the diagram’s algorithm, N must be positive.

Logical conditions define where an algorithm takes an action or accepts a value. Test the value at the boundary and nearby values on either side. For an integer age requirement of at least 18, 17 must fail while 18 and 19 must pass.

Why a pupil count needs INTEGER
items: 0, 1, 2, 3, ... represent complete pupils. Zero can represent an empty class.
18.6 pupils cannot describe a count of people.
-3 is still a valid INTEGER; it can represent a score change.

teachingBlocks.title: The thermometer reads 20.0: choose the type
items: The current value happens to be a whole number.
The sensor can also report fractional readings, such as 18.6.

rows: Valid: it is a whole number.

INTEGER suits a task that stores only whole numbers of grams.

What counts as one character?
items: '7' and '@' are characters too; CHAR is not limited to letters.
' ' contains one space. It is different from the empty string, which contains no characters.

rows: Single quotes identify CHAR. One character is stored; the quotes are delimiters.

teachingBlocks.text: A database row is also often called a record. Here TYPE describes a record value in a program. It does not create a database table or a persistent file. Defining MemberRecord once allows First and Second to hold two different members.

Initialise fields before reading them; changing one field preserves the others.
Saving values in record fields does not make them persistent between runs.

teachingBlocks.text: Use dot notation to identify a field, for example Member.YearGroup. INPUT can save a new value directly into that field; an assignment can update it; OUTPUT reads its current value. Updating one field leaves the other fields unchanged.
teachingBlocks.title: Select one field with dot notation

teachingBlocks.text: In the example, the name and current year group are inputs. FeesPaid is explicitly initialised to FALSE, and YearGroup increases by one. Saving data into a record means storing values in its fields. Keeping the record after the program finishes requires a separate file operation.
teachingBlocks.title: Read, change and retain the intended data
Trace a field update
items: Write 12 into Member.YearGroup. Name and FeesPaid retain their existing values.

teachingBlocks.title: Diagnose the destination
rows: The destination is a record; the supplied value is STRING.
Quoted text is not a BOOLEAN value.
OUTPUT Member.YearGroup before input or assignment
No value has been established for this field.
Supply a starting value before reading it.

A whole-record assignment requires a compatible record type; the later field assignment still selects just one destination.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the complete examples

objectives.description: Use array terminology correctly.
explanationUnits: Distinguish the array, an element and an index
materialTitles: An array index selects a cell; it is not the stored value

objectives.description: Identify an array's indices and lower and upper bounds.
explanationUnits: Use inclusive lower and upper bounds

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish the array, an element and an index

leadVisual.title: An array index selects a cell; it is not the stored value

coreExplanation: An index selects an element; it is not the stored value.
All elements have the declared element type, and an access must use the correct number of indices.

teachingBlocks.text: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type, stored under one identifier. An index selects a particular element. In Ages[4], Ages names the array and 4 is the index; the value stored in that element might be 17 and is independent of its index.
teachingBlocks.title: One collection, many selected values

teachingBlocks.text: A one-dimensional array uses one index. A two-dimensional array uses two indices to locate each element. The element type applies to every position, and a declared element must receive a value before an algorithm relies on that value.
teachingBlocks.title: Dimensions and element types
Read Ages[4] <- Ages[3] + 3
items: Index 4 is valid, so replace its old value 17 with 18.
The values at indices 3, 5, 6 and 7 stay 15, 16, 15 and 18.

teachingBlocks.text: Two cells can store equal values while remaining different elements. Index expressions such as Index + 1 are allowed only when they produce a valid integer index. An array declaration provides a fixed set of positions but does not supply the data shown in a trace: those values must be given or assigned.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish storage from initial data

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use inclusive lower and upper bounds

leadVisual.title: Check capacity and access

coreExplanation: Capacity is upper bound − lower bound + 1 for each dimension.
Multiply dimension lengths for 2D capacity; check every index against its own inclusive bounds.

teachingBlocks.text: The lower bound is the smallest permitted index and the upper bound is the largest. For inclusive bounds L and U, the number of elements is U − L + 1. Cambridge declarations specify these bounds explicitly; an array does not always start at zero or one.
teachingBlocks.title: Count both endpoints

teachingBlocks.text: A complete traversal visits each permitted index and stops before exceeding the upper bound. Accessing an out-of-range index is invalid. In two dimensions, both indices must satisfy their own bounds, and capacity is the product of the two dimension lengths.
teachingBlocks.title: Check each dimension separately
Derive the capacity of ARRAY[3:7]
items: 7 − 3 gives four gaps between five positions.

teachingBlocks.title: Choose a complete traversal
rows: Starting at 1 reads positions that do not exist.
Visit both rows, and all four columns per row.
Accepting a valid row does not make column 4 valid.

teachingBlocks.text: A statement can be out of range even if its result would have a suitable data type. Check the index before accessing the element; attempting the read and checking afterwards is too late.
teachingBlocks.title: Protect the access itself

explanationUnits: Input, store and total a 1D array

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use one index for one independent position

leadVisual.title: Match a task to a position

coreExplanation: Choose a 1D array when one index locates each retained value.
Declare sufficient bounds and one element type; initialise elements before reading them.

teachingBlocks.text: Choose a one-dimensional array when one index identifies each item, such as a test number selecting one mark. The declaration must provide enough positions and an element type suitable for all values. For four whole-number marks, DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:4] OF INTEGER gives one element per test.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose one independent position

teachingBlocks.text: An array retains individual values for later indexed access. If a task requires only a running total, a total variable alone may be enough; retaining an array is justified when later processing needs the original marks, for example displaying the third test mark after all inputs have been read.
teachingBlocks.title: Retain values when later work needs them
Choose storage from the required result
rows: Output only the sum as values arrive
A total and one input variable can suffice.
Earlier individual values are not needed again.
Find a total, then revisit any particular mark
The original marks must remain available.
Store one pupil name and their payment state
These are different attributes of one item, not interchangeable marks.

teachingBlocks.text: Initialisation is a separate task. To give every declared STRING element an empty starting value, assign "" to each valid index in a loop. Do not use Names[1 TO 3] <- "": a range is not an individual element access.
teachingBlocks.title: Initialise every value that will be read

knowledgeUnits.heading: Input, store and total a 1D array

leadVisual.title: Keep the accumulator while the index advances

coreExplanation: Initialise Total once before the loop; input and accumulate within valid bounds.
Place the final total output after the loop; indexed elements remain available for later access.

teachingBlocks.text: Initialise Total once before the traversal. Each iteration inputs a value into Marks[Index], then adds that same element to Total. FOR Index <- 1 TO 4 visits both bounds, and NEXT Index closes the count-controlled loop. No DO keyword is used in this FOR form.
teachingBlocks.title: Store before processing the element

teachingBlocks.text: Keeping the final OUTPUT after the loop produces one total for all four elements. OUTPUT Marks[3] then demonstrates that the third value remains available. Moving Total <- 0 inside the loop would discard the contributions from earlier elements.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the accumulated state
Trace the first two inputs
items: Total is 0 and Index begins at 1.
Store 6 at Marks[1], then add it: Total becomes 6.
Store 9 at Marks[2], then add it to the existing total: Total becomes 15.
After four iterations Total is 26. The later read of Marks[3] still gives 4.

teachingBlocks.text: INPUT Marks[Index] both obtains and stores a value. INPUT Value would require a separate Marks[Index] <- Value assignment. The loop-control variable selects a new destination each time; reusing Marks[1] would overwrite one cell instead of retaining four inputs.
teachingBlocks.title: Avoid losing the collection

teachingBlocks.text: A total adds the data values. A count adds one for each qualifying item. A maximum keeps the greatest value seen. All can traverse the same array, but they need different update rules and sometimes different initial values.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the operation before writing the loop

workedExample.title: Store four marks and report their total

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count values that meet a condition

leadVisual.title: Three different results from 6, 9, 4, 7

coreExplanation: Initialise a counter to zero and increase it by one only on the qualifying branch.
Test the threshold itself, no qualifying values, and all qualifying values.

teachingBlocks.text: A conditional count measures how many items satisfy a rule. Initialise Count to zero before traversing the stored marks; add one only when the current mark meets the threshold.
teachingBlocks.title: Count qualifying items

teachingBlocks.text: The requirement is at least Threshold, so equality qualifies. Keep the input pass and processing pass separate here to show that the stored values can be revisited.
teachingBlocks.title: Make the condition match the requirement

teachingBlocks.text: Count <- Count + Marks[Index] would add the qualifying marks, producing 16 in this example. The required result is the number of qualifying marks, 2. No qualifying values must leave the initial count at zero; if all four qualify, the result must be four.
teachingBlocks.title: Check what the accumulator means

knowledgeUnits.heading: Find a maximum and a minimum

leadVisual.title: Minimum trace on the same four readings

coreExplanation: Initialise an extreme from a supplied element, then compare the remaining elements.
Use > for a maximum and < for a minimum; a zero initial maximum fails on all-negative data.

teachingBlocks.text: An extreme is the greatest or least supplied value. Copy the first element into each candidate, then inspect the remaining elements so the candidate always represents a value encountered in the data.
teachingBlocks.title: Start with a real member of the data

teachingBlocks.text: Use separate comparisons for Largest and Smallest. Replacing a candidate only for a strict improvement is sufficient when the required outputs are the values rather than their positions.
teachingBlocks.title: Replace the candidate only when necessary

teachingBlocks.text: Zero is a valid initial total, but it is not a valid maximum candidate for an all-negative collection. Initialising from the first element makes Largest a value that actually occurs. Every later comparison keeps the greatest value encountered so far.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why the initial value works

teachingBlocks.text: For a minimum, initialise Smallest from the first element and update when a later element is smaller. Equal values need no replacement when only the extreme value is required. These four-element examples always contain data; if an optional active-count model allows no items, report that there is no extreme instead of reading element 1.
teachingBlocks.title: Handle the paired operation and its boundary

objectives.description: Write pseudocode to declare and process 1D and 2D arrays.
explanationUnits: Traverse rows with a nested loop
Calculate row, column and whole-table totals
materialTitles: Input six scores and output two row totals
One matrix, three kinds of total

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assign a meaning to each dimension

leadVisual.title: Rows are horizontal; columns are vertical

coreExplanation: A 2D element needs two valid indices with stated meanings.
Choose the element type for the stored value, not for the row or column labels.

teachingBlocks.text: Choose a two-dimensional array when two independent positions identify an element. In Scores[Row, Column], let rows represent pupils and columns represent tests. DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:2, 1:3] OF INTEGER stores six scores, with the first index selecting the pupil and the second selecting the test.
teachingBlocks.title: Give each dimension a stable meaning

teachingBlocks.text: Rows run horizontally across a displayed table and columns vertically down it. Scores[2,3] is the second pupil's third test score, not the third pupil's second test. State each dimension's meaning before writing code so every reference uses the same convention.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the coordinate in the declared order
Locate Scores[2,3]
items: Within that row, choose test column 3.
The value is 6; neither index is the mark itself.

teachingBlocks.text: All six cells still have one element type, INTEGER. Two dimensions do not mean two different data types. A name, an age and a paid flag belong in a record; a score for each pupil and test fits this 2D array.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish dimensions from field types

knowledgeUnits.heading: Traverse rows with a nested loop

leadVisual.title: Row totals for the diagram

coreExplanation: For each row, reset its total, visit every column, then output the completed row total.
Close the inner loop before advancing the outer loop.

teachingBlocks.text: The outer loop chooses Row; the inner loop visits every Column for that row. With ascending bounds, the visit order is (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), then (2,1), (2,2), (2,3). The column loop restarts from 1 for each new row, so the second row is not traversed backwards.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete the inner loop for one row

teachingBlocks.text: RowTotal is reset at the start of each outer iteration because each row needs a separate total. Input and addition occur inside the inner loop, while OUTPUT RowTotal occurs after NEXT Column but before NEXT Row. To calculate column totals, choose a column in the outer loop and vary the row in the inner loop instead.
teachingBlocks.title: Reset and output at the correct level
Trace the row boundary
rows: Reset to 0, then input 8 and add: 8

teachingBlocks.text: NEXT Column completes the current row. NEXT Row advances to the next row and re-enters the inner loop at column 1. Output inside the inner loop would report six partial totals; output after both loops would report only the final RowTotal. The placement follows the number of required results.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the code from the outputs

workedExample.title: Input six scores and output two row totals

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate row, column and whole-table totals

leadVisual.title: One matrix, three kinds of total

coreExplanation: For a column total, hold the column fixed and vary the row.
Reset once per required group; a grand total is reset once for the whole table.

teachingBlocks.text: The same stored table can answer several questions. A row total groups columns for one row; a column total groups rows for one column. The index meanings remain Row, Column in both traversals.
teachingBlocks.title: Hold the group index fixed

teachingBlocks.text: A grand total belongs to the whole data set, so initialise it once before input begins. Accumulate each of the six inputs exactly once; do not add them again during the later column-total traversal.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish per-group and whole-table state
Same matrix, different questions
rows: Reset before both loops; output after both loops.

teachingBlocks.text: The input loop and the processing loop do not have to use the same nesting order. First store all six values in row order. Later, a column-total pass can hold Column fixed while Row changes. Scores[Row, Column] keeps the same index meaning throughout.
teachingBlocks.title: Change traversal without changing the data model

teachingBlocks.text: For column 1, add 4 then 8 to obtain 12. Reset before column 2, then add 7 and 1 to obtain 8. Resetting inside the row loop would repeatedly erase earlier rows; failing to reset between columns would mix different column totals.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the first two groups to test the nesting

objectives.description: Write and trace a bounded linear search.
explanationUnits: Compare each element with the search value
materialTitles: Stop at the first match; guard the index when no match exists

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare each element with the search value

leadVisual.title: Stop at the first match; guard the index when no match exists

coreExplanation: Compare consecutive elements; an unsorted array does not require sorting first.
State whether the result is an index or a found flag, and use an unambiguous absence convention.

teachingBlocks.text: A linear search checks elements sequentially against a target value. This version searches a 1-based five-element array, reports the first matching index and uses 0 to mean not found. The sentinel is valid because 0 is outside the declared array bounds.
teachingBlocks.title: Specify what the search returns

teachingBlocks.text: Index begins at the lower bound. A mismatch advances it by one; a match saves the current index in Position. The next loop condition stops once Position is nonzero or Index exceeds 5. Array access occurs inside the guarded loop body, so an unsuccessful search never reads Values[6].
teachingBlocks.title: Advance until the required result is known
Search the unsorted values for 4
items: 9 is not 4, so advance to 2. A larger value does not rule out a later match.
Position is no longer 0, so stop. The second 4 at index 4 is not inspected.

teachingBlocks.text: For an unsorted collection, a mismatch tells us only about the checked element. Returning the first match is a stated choice. A task requesting every match would need a different result and stopping rule, rather than silently reusing this first-match version.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the requirement and stopping rule together

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace found and not-found paths

leadVisual.title: Boundary checks

coreExplanation: Initialise index and result before every search.
Guard the element access and include the upper bound; test first, last, absent and duplicate cases.

teachingBlocks.text: The complete algorithm first inputs five values and a target, then initialises the search state. Position starts at 0 for each new search, preventing a previous result from being mistaken for the result of this target. The loop conditions refer only to scalar state; they do not depend on short-circuit evaluation to protect an array subscript.
teachingBlocks.title: Initialise a fresh search

teachingBlocks.text: Test a match at the first position, a match at the final position, an absent target and repeated matching values. An absent target causes five comparisons and finishes with Index equal to 6 and Position still 0. A match at index 5 leaves Position at 5 and performs no sixth comparison.
teachingBlocks.title: Test both ends and the absent path
Final comparison when target 7 is absent
rows: Only the scalar index has advanced.
Index <= 5 is FALSE; no Values[6] read occurs.

teachingBlocks.text: A compound condition that reads Values[Index] can be unsafe if it assumes the language will skip one operand. This version tests only Index and Position in the loop header, and performs the element read inside the guarded body. It does not need an assumed short-circuit rule.
teachingBlocks.title: Put the array read behind the bounds check

teachingBlocks.text: The first match takes one comparison; an absent value needs all five. Counting actual comparisons explains why early stopping can save work without introducing a new search algorithm.
teachingBlocks.title: Optional connection: compare the work done

objectives.description: Write and trace an ascending bubble sort using adjacent comparisons and a complete swap.
explanationUnits: Trace adjacent comparisons and complete passes
Use a swap flag and a shrinking bound
materialTitles: Bubble sort: array after each complete pass
Control state for the diagram input
First pass uses every updated pair

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace adjacent comparisons and complete passes

leadVisual.title: Bubble sort: array after each complete pass

coreExplanation: Bubble sort compares adjacent elements, using the updated array for the next comparison.
Use a temporary value for a complete swap; one ascending pass fixes the greatest active value at the right.

teachingBlocks.text: An ascending bubble sort compares neighbouring elements from left to right and swaps them if the left value is greater. After the first full pass, the largest value is at the final position. Further passes repeat the process over the remaining unsorted prefix.
teachingBlocks.title: One comparison moves one neighbouring pair

teachingBlocks.text: Every swap preserves both original values: save the left value in Temp, copy the right value into the left position, then copy Temp into the right position. The diagram records the state after each pass, always with exactly seven elements. Equal adjacent values need no swap.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve both values through a swap
Swap left 6 and right 2
items: Keep 6 in Temp before any overwrite.
The left cell now contains 2; Temp still contains 6.
The right cell now contains 6. Both input values are preserved.

teachingBlocks.text: After each comparison the greater of that pair is on its right. Comparing that position with the next neighbour carries the greatest value encountered further right. At the end of the pass the greatest value in the active prefix is in its final position. The other values may still be unsorted.
teachingBlocks.title: Why a completed pass fixes one position

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a swap flag and a shrinking bound

leadVisual.title: Control state for the diagram input

coreExplanation: Reset Swapped once per pass, set it after any swap, and compare only through Last − 1.
Reduce Last after each pass; stop after a no-swap pass or when fewer than two active positions remain.

teachingBlocks.text: Last starts at the upper bound and Swapped starts TRUE so the first pass runs. Reset Swapped to FALSE at the start of each pass and set it TRUE only when a swap occurs. A completed pass with no swaps proves that the remaining adjacent pairs are already ordered.
teachingBlocks.title: A flag records the whole pass

teachingBlocks.text: The inner loop stops at Last − 1 because it also accesses Index + 1. Reducing Last after each pass avoids comparing the sorted suffix again. For the diagram input, pass 3 creates the sorted order; pass 4 makes no swaps and terminates this implementation. Final outputs occur after sorting has finished.
teachingBlocks.title: Shrink the part still needing work

teachingBlocks.text: First understand a fixed-pass version: for seven elements, six left-to-right passes are sufficient even in reverse order. The supplied version retains the same adjacent-swap rule but avoids needless work by shrinking Last and stopping when a completed pass has no swaps.
teachingBlocks.title: Move from the basic algorithm to the optimisation
Read the two levels of control
items: Last > 1 means at least two active positions remain; Swapped permits another pass.
Set Swapped to FALSE before the first comparison.
Index ends at Last − 1 so Index + 1 never exceeds Last. Any swap sets Swapped TRUE for the rest of this pass.
Reduce Last. Stop if no swap occurred or only one active element remains.

teachingBlocks.title: Useful challenges
rows: One pass, six comparisons, no swaps in the seven-element version.
No swaps; retain all seven equal values.
Repeated passes are needed; each fixes one more position.
Swap when the left value is smaller; preserve the same bounds and all duplicates.

materialTitles: READ preserves, WRITE replaces, APPEND extends
Save, close, extend, close, then read back

objectives.description: Write pseudocode to handle text files consisting of one or more lines.
explanationUnits: Write a new file and append a line
Read lines with an end-of-file check
Save, extend and read the data back
Read one file while writing a transformed copy
materialTitles: An empty line is data; end of file is a position
Save, close, extend, close, then read back
Independent starting file: Ada, blank, Bo
Copy text and label blank lines

knowledgeUnits.heading: Select the correct file mode

leadVisual.title: READ preserves, WRITE replaces, APPEND extends

coreExplanation: Files retain data between executions.
READ loads, WRITE creates or replaces, APPEND extends; a quoted filename is a STRING identifier.

teachingBlocks.text: Files retain data on secondary storage so it can be reused after a program terminates or transferred to another program. Keeping names only in variables or arrays does not provide this persistence. A text file stores a sequence of lines that can be processed in order.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep data beyond one execution

teachingBlocks.text: OPENFILE selects how a program will use the named file. READ permits reading existing lines. WRITE creates a file or replaces existing contents. APPEND adds at the end while retaining existing contents. Select the mode from the task: replacing a report and extending a log require different modes.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose whether old lines must survive

teachingBlocks.text: A STRING such as "Names.txt" identifies the file; it is not its contents. READFILE transfers one line from storage into a STRING variable. A second read replaces that variable with the next line unless the program stores or processes the previous value.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish filename, contents and working variable
Open mode controls what may happen next
rows: Opening replaces any previous contents, even before the first new line is written.
New lines follow the old lines.

teachingBlocks.text: Open one file in only one mode at a time. Close it before reopening in a different mode. In the following examples, required input files exist and file access succeeds; missing-file and permission handling belong to the chosen programming environment.
teachingBlocks.title: State the conditions of the examples

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write a new file and append a line

leadVisual.title: Fresh list and later extension

coreExplanation: Open an output once before writing its sequence, then close it afterwards.
Use APPEND to preserve earlier lines; repeated opening FOR WRITE discards them.

teachingBlocks.text: WRITEFILE writes the supplied STRING as a line in an open text file. The complete example opens Names.txt FOR WRITE, inputs three lines, writes each line and closes the file. Existing contents are replaced, so this operation suits creating a fresh list.
teachingBlocks.title: Create the intended complete output

teachingBlocks.text: To extend that list, use APPEND instead. Input a new line, open the same file FOR APPEND, write the line and close the file. Closing completes the file operation and releases the file. When copying between files, use different names so opening the output FOR WRITE cannot erase the input.
teachingBlocks.title: Extend it without erasing earlier lines
Create, close, then extend
items: Open Names.txt FOR WRITE once. This replaces Old if it existed.
Input and write Ada, Ben and Cy on separate iterations.
Finish the writing session; the saved list has three lines.
Input Dia, open FOR APPEND, write it and close. The saved list now has four lines.

teachingBlocks.text: The simple writing example uses a fixed three-iteration FOR loop because the number of input lines is known. A later reading program uses EOF because the number of saved lines need not be known in advance. The two loop choices follow different information available at the start.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the loop from the task

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read lines with an end-of-file check

leadVisual.title: An empty line is data; end of file is a position

coreExplanation: Open FOR READ; test NOT EOF before each READFILE; process the STRING line and close after the loop.
A blank line contributes one read; an empty file contributes zero.

teachingBlocks.text: After OPENFILE in READ mode, check EOF before each READFILE. READFILE copies the next line into a STRING variable and advances the file position. EOF becomes TRUE when there are no further lines to read. CLOSEFILE finishes access after the loop.
teachingBlocks.title: Read only when another line exists

teachingBlocks.text: A blank line is still a line and can be read as an empty string. It is different from reaching the end of the file. The example outputs and counts every line, including blank ones. For an empty file, the loop body is skipped and the count remains zero.
teachingBlocks.title: A blank value is still a successful read
EOF and the current line are different facts
rows: Skip the body; output count 0 after closing.
Next line is empty, followed by Bo
Read the empty string, count it, then test again.
Bo is the final unread line

teachingBlocks.text: A WHILE loop can perform zero reads and so handles an empty file naturally. Reading once before the first EOF test would assume a first line exists. An empty line does exist; an empty file has no line to return.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the pre-condition loop

knowledgeUnits.heading: Save, extend and read the data back

leadVisual.title: Save, close, extend, close, then read back

coreExplanation: A complete save-and-load example writes data, closes, reopens, reads and shows the result.
Opening alone does not save data; reopening FOR READ does not erase it.

teachingBlocks.text: Use one named file throughout a complete lifecycle. Start with Names.txt containing Old. Opening FOR WRITE replaces Old; three writes create Ada, an empty line and Bo. Close before changing the access mode.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect saving to a later read

teachingBlocks.text: Append Cy in a second writing session, close again, then reopen FOR READ. The reading loop processes all four lines and reports the count after closing the file.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the stored file at each boundary

teachingBlocks.text: The lifecycle below has three separate open/close sessions. A later execution can run the reader alone on the saved file. In this complete demonstration the sessions follow consecutively so every state is visible; reopening FOR READ does not recreate the earlier input array or numeric variables.
teachingBlocks.title: What is retained between sessions

teachingBlocks.text: The deliberately blank second line must survive both the append and the reader. The reader outputs Ada, a blank line, Bo, Cy, then 4. Each successful READFILE increases Count once; the final failed continuation test performs no read.
teachingBlocks.title: Predict before following the program

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read one file while writing a transformed copy

leadVisual.title: Independent starting file: Ada, blank, Bo

coreExplanation: Use distinct source and destination names, guard each read, and apply the condition before writing.
Close both files; empty input must produce the specified empty output.

teachingBlocks.text: Open an existing input file FOR READ and a different output file FOR WRITE. Every input line is read exactly once and produces one output line in this example.
teachingBlocks.title: Read one file and write a different file

teachingBlocks.text: A selection replaces an empty input line with the text [blank]; other lines pass through unchanged. Keeping the input and output names different prevents the output open from destroying the source.
teachingBlocks.title: Transform only the lines selected by the condition
Copy while replacing blank lines
items: Open the existing source FOR READ and a different destination FOR WRITE.
Check NOT EOF, then read the next STRING line.
If the line is empty, write "[blank]"; otherwise write the original line.
Close both files after every source line has been processed.

teachingBlocks.title: Source has Ada, an empty line, Bo
rows: One output line per input line; order unchanged.
The blank line is read but deliberately not written.
The loop is skipped; the newly opened output is empty.

teachingBlocks.text: Do not use the source filename as the destination: opening it FOR WRITE would remove the lines before they can be read. The independent exercise changes the processing decision; it does not change the safe file-opening and EOF structure.
teachingBlocks.title: Protect the supplied input and transfer the method

objectives.description: Explain that an ADT consists of a collection of data and a set of operations on those data.
explanationUnits: Define the data and operations together
Separate an interface from its implementation
materialTitles: Describe an ADT without choosing storage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define the data and operations together

leadVisual.title: A specification includes behaviour

coreExplanation: An ADT combines a collection of data and a set of operations on it.
Define an operation’s effect, result and relevant conditions, not only the stored values.

teachingBlocks.text: An abstract data type is a collection of data together with a set of operations on those data. The specification describes what each operation does and any conditions for using it. For example, a stack specifies adding at the top and removing the most recently added item.
teachingBlocks.title: Data plus permitted operations

teachingBlocks.text: The word abstract separates observable behaviour from representation. A user of an ADT needs to know which item a removal returns and how empty or full conditions are handled. The user does not need to know the array position or pointer updates that implement the operation.
teachingBlocks.title: Specify behaviour independently of storage
Ask enough to use an operation
rows: The existing stack; no new item is supplied.
The most recently added item still present.
That item is removed; earlier items keep their order.
An empty-stack outcome is reported; no item is removed.

teachingBlocks.text: Push, pop, enqueue and dequeue in these lessons are operation names in state descriptions. They are not being introduced as built-in Cambridge pseudocode commands. At AS Level, describe and trace the ADT operations and array representation; writing their implementation pseudocode is not required.
teachingBlocks.title: Scope of the ADT lessons

workedExample.title: Describe an ADT without choosing storage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate an interface from its implementation

leadVisual.title: Specification versus implementation

coreExplanation: The interface describes behaviour; the implementation chooses storage and state variables.
A replacement implementation must preserve the specified operation results and conditions.

teachingBlocks.text: An implementation chooses concrete storage and procedures that satisfy the ADT's rules. An array implementation may use extra INTEGER variables to track active positions. Those variables are implementation details; changing them must not change the specified order in which clients receive data.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose storage that satisfies the behaviour

teachingBlocks.text: A bounded implementation also needs defined behaviour when storage is full or empty. Rejecting a removal from an empty collection prevents an invalid access. Replacing an array implementation with another representation is acceptable only if valid operations still produce the specified results.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate capacity from the abstract order
Compare two implementations
items: Add Red, add Blue, then remove one item.
It must return Blue and leave Red.
Array cells and linked nodes may differ while producing that same result.
Returning Red would change the removal order; it is not this stack behaviour.

teachingBlocks.text: A fixed array has a finite capacity. Its full condition belongs to that bounded implementation; it is not a claim that every possible implementation must have the same capacity. The lessons state pointer conventions explicitly because different valid implementations can use different conventions.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the stated representation

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use LIFO for nested or reversible work

leadVisual.title: A stack removes the most recently added item

coreExplanation: A stack uses LIFO: push and pop act at the top.
Peek reads without removing; use a stack when the latest remaining item must be handled first.

teachingBlocks.text: A stack is a last-in, first-out structure. PUSH adds an item at the top; POP removes and returns the top item. A peek operation, if provided, reads the top item without removing it. Items below the top wait until the items above them have been removed.
teachingBlocks.title: Remove the latest remaining item

teachingBlocks.text: Undo history and nested subroutine calls fit this access order. The latest action is undone first, and the most recent unfinished call returns before an earlier call resumes. Choose a stack because of that ordering requirement, rather than merely because the task stores several items.
teachingBlocks.title: Match the order to the application

teachingBlocks.text: After undoing an action it is no longer in this active undo history. Recording a new action makes that new action the top. The example models Undo only; Redo would require its own stated rules and storage.
teachingBlocks.title: Track the active history

knowledgeUnits.heading: Track the active top in an array

leadVisual.title: Top marks the active stack, even if an old value remains

coreExplanation: With Top as the last occupied index: empty is 0 and full is capacity.
Check limits before changing state; read before decreasing Top on pop.
An allowed value edit preserves Top and the order of other items.

teachingBlocks.text: In this 1-based array model, Top is the index of the last occupied element; Top = 0 means empty. To push, check that Top is below capacity, increase Top and store the new item at that position. To pop, check that Top is above zero, read the top value and decrease Top.
teachingBlocks.title: State the Top convention

teachingBlocks.text: Editing the top item changes its stored value without changing Top. Access to a deeper item must follow the permitted interface, for example temporarily popping the items above it and restoring them in reverse removal order. Removing an item does not require erasing its old cell; positions above Top are inactive.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep membership and value edits separate
PUSH into a 1-based stack
items: If Top equals capacity, reject without modifying the array or Top.
Increase Top by one only on the successful path.
Write the new value into Stack[Top].

teachingBlocks.title: POP from the same stack
items: If Top is zero, report empty without an array read.
Save the value at Stack[Top] for the caller.
Decrease Top by one. The old bytes may remain above the active range.

teachingBlocks.text: This example permits an in-place edit of the active top. A different interface allowing only push and pop needs temporary storage to reach a deeper item. State that interface before choosing the operation; direct access through the backing array is not automatically available to an ADT client.
teachingBlocks.title: Do not invent extra access operations

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add at the rear and remove from the front

leadVisual.title: Service order

coreExplanation: Enqueue at the rear; dequeue from the front.
FIFO preserves the arrival order of the remaining waiting items.

teachingBlocks.text: A queue is a first-in, first-out structure. ENQUEUE adds at the rear and DEQUEUE removes and returns the front item. A new arrival joins behind the items already waiting, so serving the front preserves arrival order.
teachingBlocks.title: Serve the earliest item still waiting

teachingBlocks.text: A first-come, first-served print queue or service desk suits FIFO. The requirement concerns waiting items: a job already removed is no longer in the queue. An ordinary FIFO queue does not automatically move a later urgent job ahead of earlier arrivals; that would require different scheduling rules.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose FIFO only when it fits the rule
Name the ends consistently
headers: Example after A, B, C arrive
rows: D follows C; A remains next.

teachingBlocks.text: The queue describes waiting items. After A is served, the order begins with B; A is no longer a member even if an array cell still contains A. A priority service is a different policy, so a hospital example must explicitly state first-come, first-served before FIFO is justified.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the requirement, not the scenario name

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use front, rear and count consistently

leadVisual.title: Wrap the rear index while preserving arrival order

coreExplanation: Front selects the next removal; Rear is the last insertion position in this model.
Count = 0 is empty; Count = capacity is full. Wrap indices while preserving FIFO.

teachingBlocks.text: This circular array implementation uses Front for the next removal position, Rear for the last occupied insertion position, and Count for the number of active items. Initially Front = 1, Rear = 0 and Count = 0. A successful enqueue advances Rear with wrap-around, stores the item and increases Count; a dequeue reads Front, advances it with wrap-around and decreases Count.
teachingBlocks.title: Use one declared circular model

teachingBlocks.text: Count = 0 means empty and Count = capacity means full. Wrapping from the final index back to 1 reuses positions released by earlier dequeues. An allowed edit changes an active item's value without changing its arrival position or Count. Reading or editing an inactive cell must not turn it into a waiting item.
teachingBlocks.title: Reuse a released position without reordering
Why wrap-around is useful
rows: B and C at indices 2 and 3; index 1 released
Rear has reached the final index.
There are only two waiting items, so one slot is available.
Continuing to index 4 would be invalid.
Wrap Rear to 1 and store D behind B and C.

teachingBlocks.title: Update the correct end
items: Check Count < capacity; advance Rear, wrapping after the upper bound; store the item and increase Count.
Check Count > 0; return the item at Front; advance Front with wrap-around and decrease Count.
Change only the specified active value. Do not move its arrival position or change Count.

teachingBlocks.text: Here Rear means the last inserted occupied position when Count > 0, not the next free position. Count is authoritative when empty. Other conventions are possible, but their initial states and update rules cannot be mixed into this trace.
teachingBlocks.title: Avoid mixing pointer conventions

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace full, empty and reused circular states

leadVisual.title: Read the three state variables together

coreExplanation: Derive active order from Front and Count, not from physical left-to-right storage.
Empty and full operations are rejected before any state change; emptied storage can be reused.

teachingBlocks.text: Use Queue[1:3] with Front as the next removal position, Rear as the last insertion position, and Count as the active length. The initial state is Front = 1, Rear = 0, Count = 0; advance a position after 3 back to 1.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow every successful and rejected operation

teachingBlocks.text: A successful enqueue advances Rear and increases Count. A successful dequeue reads Front, advances Front and decreases Count. This interface also permits editing the front item without changing its position; failed full or empty operations change nothing.
teachingBlocks.title: An empty queue can be reused

teachingBlocks.text: The trace uses capacity 3, indices 1 through 3, and the same Front/Rear/Count convention as the previous unit. Only active values are shown in the logical-order column. Old cell contents have no effect on membership.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the state table

teachingBlocks.text: After the final D is removed, Front = 2, Rear = 1 and Count = 0. This is a valid empty state even though it differs from the initial pointers. The next enqueue advances Rear to 2, placing E at Front; there is no need to reset both pointers.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the empty-to-nonempty transition

teachingBlocks.text: Trying to remove from empty or insert into full must leave all three variables and active values unchanged. Do not advance a pointer first and then discover that the operation was impossible.
teachingBlocks.title: Check before changing anything
