Operations on the starting A → B → C list
Boundary cases change the head or a null link

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent a sequence using nodes and links

leadVisual.title: Follow links, not consecutive array positions

coreExplanation: Nodes store data and links; Head identifies the first node and a null link ends traversal.
Logical order follows links, not consecutive array positions.

teachingBlocks.text: A linked list contains nodes, each holding data and a link to the next node. A head pointer identifies the first node. In the model used here, a link value of 0 means no next node; Head = 0 represents an empty list. The last active node has a null link.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify nodes, head and the null link

teachingBlocks.text: Logical order is determined by links, not by consecutive storage positions. Follow the head and successive links to traverse the list. A linked list suits a sequence that needs insertions or deletions between neighbours because changing links can avoid shifting every following data item, although locating the required node may still require traversal.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow logical order through physical storage

teachingBlocks.text: These links are INTEGER array indices. The value 0 is a null-link convention outside indices 1 through 4, not a node to read. A node at array index 4 can be second in the logical sequence. Directly selecting slot 4 and selecting the fourth item in the list are different tasks.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate a slot address from an ordinal position

teachingBlocks.text: Insertion between known neighbours changes links rather than shifting all later values. Finding a named item still requires checking nodes along the chain unless some additional index has been supplied. Array-backed nodes have fixed total capacity even though their logical order can change.
teachingBlocks.title: State the benefit and the limitation together

knowledgeUnits.heading: Update data and links without losing nodes

leadVisual.title: Preserve the successor before linking the new node

coreExplanation: Insertion links the new node to the old successor before redirecting the predecessor.
An edit preserves links; deletion bypasses the node and releases its storage.

teachingBlocks.text: An array implementation can store Data[Index] and Next[Index] for each node, plus Head and information about unused slots. To insert X at free slot 3 after node 2 in the diagram, first store X and set Next[3] to the old successor 4. Then set Next[2] to 3. The sequence becomes A, X, B, C.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve the successor during insertion

teachingBlocks.text: Editing a node's data leaves its links unchanged. Deleting a middle node makes its predecessor point to the deleted node's successor, then returns the removed slot to the available storage. Deleting the head updates Head instead. The programmer must preserve access to the successor before changing links, or the remaining chain can become unreachable.
teachingBlocks.title: Edit values and remove nodes deliberately
Explain the safe insertion order
items: A at slot 2 currently points to B at slot 4.
Put X in free slot 3 and link it onward to 4.
Set Next[2] to 3. The chain is now A, X, B, C.

teachingBlocks.text: If Next[2] is overwritten first and its old value was not saved, copying that changed value into Next[3] can make the new node point to itself. The old successor B then becomes unreachable from A. Safe order, or explicitly saved state, prevents this.
teachingBlocks.title: Diagnose a lost chain

teachingBlocks.text: The independent cases below all start from the original A → B → C chain. An edit changes data but retains links; a deletion changes reachability before the storage can be reused. The boundary unit next explains why deleting the head needs a different destination for the changed link.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep separate cases separate

knowledgeUnits.heading: Handle the head, tail and empty list

leadVisual.title: Boundary cases change the head or a null link

coreExplanation: Update Head when the first node changes; deleting the tail sets its predecessor’s next link to null.
Deleting the only node makes Head null; empty deletion and insertion without capacity leave state unchanged.

teachingBlocks.text: A node at the head has no active predecessor, so insertion or deletion there updates Head. At the tail, the successor is null. Deleting the only node must make Head null rather than leaving it pointing to a free slot.
teachingBlocks.title: Treat the head and null link explicitly

teachingBlocks.text: Each case below starts from its stated snapshot, independently of the other cases. Assume null = 0 and that released slots are recorded as available. If no slot is free, reject an insertion before changing Data or links.
teachingBlocks.title: Handle one node and no nodes

teachingBlocks.text: For a head insertion, the new node takes the old Head as its successor and Head changes to the new slot. For a head deletion, there is no predecessor node to update: Head takes the old head’s successor. These rules also work when that successor is 0.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the boundary cases
Deletion destinations
rows: Tail C in the same original list
Head A in the same original list

teachingBlocks.text: Deleting from Head = 0 is rejected because no node exists. Inserting into an empty list still needs a free slot: put the value there, give it a null next link and make Head identify it. If no slot is free, reject the insertion before changing Head or any active link.
teachingBlocks.title: Empty list is different from exhausted storage

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check active positions when an array is reused

leadVisual.title: Capacity 4; old cell values are not membership

coreExplanation: Active membership is determined by Top, queue state or the reachable link chain.
Check empty, full and active-position conditions before reading or changing a structure.

teachingBlocks.text: An array-backed stack and queue can contain inactive cells whose old values are still visible in memory. For a stack with Top as the last occupied index, only positions 1 through Top are active. For a circular queue, Count active positions begin at Front and wrap through the array; Rear identifies the last one when Count is positive.
teachingBlocks.title: Membership is part of the representation

teachingBlocks.text: Check representation state before adding, editing or deleting. A full structure cannot accept another item without a specified capacity change; an empty structure cannot supply an item. Value edits preserve membership and order, whereas push/pop or enqueue/dequeue change membership and must update the corresponding state variables.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the operation before modifying state
Compare the membership rules
rows: Indices 1 through Top in this model.
Top and the selected top value.
Count positions beginning at Front with wrap-around.
Front, Rear, Count and logical order.
Nodes reachable by following links from Head.
Head and the complete reachable chain.

teachingBlocks.text: Do not classify a cell as occupied merely because it contains old data. Conversely, storing a new value in an inactive cell does not complete an addition until the state variables or links make it active. The operation must leave one consistent representation, including on rejection.
teachingBlocks.title: Check data and control state together

workedExample.title: Check an edit against active membership

knowledgeUnits.heading: Track free nodes separately from the active list

leadVisual.title: A node belongs to either the active chain or the free chain

coreExplanation: Keep active and free chains disjoint; preserve the old free link before reusing it.
Unlink before releasing; no free node means insertion is rejected without changing the active data.

teachingBlocks.text: A fixed array implementation of a linked list needs a way to find unused nodes. One method links unused positions into a free list with its own Free head pointer. Active and free chains must not share nodes. A null Free pointer means the array has no available slot for another insertion.
teachingBlocks.title: Track two disjoint chains

teachingBlocks.text: To allocate a node, take the position identified by Free and advance Free to that node's old free link before reusing the link for the active chain. To release a deleted node, remove it from the active chain first, link it to the current free head and make it the new Free head. This reuses storage without shifting surviving node data.
teachingBlocks.title: Transfer a node without losing the rest
Allocate a free node
items: Free = 0 means no slot can be allocated. Reject without changing either chain.
Let the allocated slot be the old Free. Advance Free using its old Next link.
Now set the node’s active successor and connect it to the active list.

teachingBlocks.title: Release a deleted node
items: Remove it from the active chain, updating Head or a predecessor as required.
Point the removed node to the current Free head.
Make the removed slot the new free head. Its old data is no longer an active item.

teachingBlocks.text: This free-list model accounts for every array slot exactly once: active or free. After each change, follow both chains to null. Neither should contain a cycle, a repeated node, or a node from the other chain. Free-list management is one chosen array implementation; AS study here is descriptive, not implementation pseudocode.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a representation check

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose dimensions for retained application data

leadVisual.title: Choose dimensions from the required indices

coreExplanation: Choose dimensions from the selectors needed to locate one value.
Use records for named attributes and files when persistence is required.

teachingBlocks.text: Separate the values the application must retain from the order in which it processes actions. A theatre can store one occupancy flag per row and seat in a 2D BOOLEAN array. A separate 1D INTEGER array can store one booking total per performance, because performance number alone identifies each total.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate stored facts from processing order

teachingBlocks.text: Describe the meaning and bounds of each dimension explicitly. Occupied[Row, Seat] uses two indices; Bookings[Performance] uses one. The declaration should follow the data's actual indexing needs. Adding dimensions simply because a system is large creates an unnecessary or misleading model.
teachingBlocks.title: Give every index one meaning
Questions that determine a structure
rows: Do fields describe different attributes of one request?
Use a record for its ID, row and seat.
Does one index select the required value?
Use a 1D array, for example a performance total.
Do row and seat together select the required value?
Use a 2D occupancy array for one performance.
Write the required representation to persistent storage.

teachingBlocks.text: The occupancy model below covers one performance. The separate six-element totals array does not add a performance index to that occupancy array. State the limits of each model; handling every performance’s full seating map would require another explicit arrangement.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the model’s scope honest

workedExample.title: Choose two arrays for a theatre

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify each ADT by its operation order

leadVisual.title: Theatre responsibilities

coreExplanation: Justify a queue by FIFO, a stack by LIFO and a linked list by linked sequence updates.
Describe which data each structure holds and preserve the old state needed for Undo.

teachingBlocks.text: The same theatre can use a queue for booking requests processed in arrival order and a stack for reversing the most recent completed edits. A linked list can represent a running order of acts that frequently receives insertions between known neighbours. Each choice follows a specific access or update requirement.
teachingBlocks.title: Match each responsibility to its operation order

teachingBlocks.text: Explain how the structures cooperate: dequeue a request, use its row and seat to access the occupancy array, and push an undo record containing the previous state after a successful change. The request queue and undo stack contain different items and have different removal orders. Merely naming all three ADTs does not justify a design.
teachingBlocks.title: Store enough information to reverse a change

teachingBlocks.text: A request record and an undo record serve different purposes. A request identifies what the user wants. An undo record retains the location and previous value of a change that actually succeeded. A rejected request must not add an undo entry for a change that never happened.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish waiting work from successful changes
Describe the responsibility of each structure
items: Read and update the requested seat using its two indices.
Retain and later remove the newest successful change with its previous state.
Append an explicit event line without deleting earlier history.

workedExample.title: Follow one booking through the structures

knowledgeUnits.heading: Run a booking, reject a duplicate and undo a success

leadVisual.title: One request: accept or reject, then continue

coreExplanation: A failed booking changes neither seat occupancy nor undo history.
Undo restores the previous value of the latest successful change; record the resulting event explicitly.

teachingBlocks.text: The request queue initially holds R1(1,1), R2(1,1), R3(2,2), in front-to-rear order. Occupied[1:2,1:2] is initially all FALSE; the undo stack is empty and Bookings.txt is an empty existing file.
teachingBlocks.title: State the complete small-system rules

teachingBlocks.text: Each successful booking stores an undo record with request ID, row, seat and PreviousState = FALSE. A rejected request produces no seat change or undo entry. After all requests have been processed, Undo once reverses the latest successful booking.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow success, rejection and undo to final states

teachingBlocks.text: This is a complete conceptual state trace using named ADT operations, not an ADT implementation program. One performance has two rows of two seats. All seats start FALSE. Request and undo capacities are three, sufficient for this example. Each request record contains ID : STRING, Row : INTEGER and Seat : INTEGER; every supplied coordinate is in range.
teachingBlocks.title: Initial conditions and notation
Apply the same rules to each request
items: Dequeue the next request; stop processing when no requests remain.
Leave occupancy and undo history unchanged; append a REJECT event.
Retain its old value in an undo record, set occupancy TRUE, push the undo record, and append an ACCEPT event.
If the undo stack is non-empty, pop its top record, restore that seat’s previous value and append an UNDO event. Otherwise report no change without reading a record.

teachingBlocks.text: The log is an event history, so Undo appends an event rather than erasing the earlier acceptance. This log format records ID, coordinates and outcome for inspection; it is not presented as a complete reloadable seating-file format.

materialTitles: Flowchart: count positives in three inputs

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate structured English

leadVisual.title: Translate each design step

coreExplanation: Translate the stated input, processing and output without changing the rules.
Initialise once, preserve every branch and place repeated actions inside the correct loop.

teachingBlocks.text: Read the whole design before writing statements. Identify the inputs, initial values, processing order and required outputs. Translate a precise action such as increase Count by one into Count <- Count + 1; do not leave the action as an unexplained instruction to process data.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the complete contract

teachingBlocks.text: Consider this design: set a count to zero; read three integers in turn; increase the count for each positive integer; output the final count. Initialisation belongs before repetition, the input and positive-value decision belong inside it, and the final output belongs after it. Indentation makes these responsibilities visible.
teachingBlocks.title: Place each action at the correct level
Build the translation in dependency order
items: Value is the current INTEGER input. Index identifies which input is being processed; Count counts only positive inputs. Their meanings differ even though both counters are integers.
Set Count to 0 once. No positive input has been seen at the start. Declaring Count does not establish that value.
Obtain a fresh Value, test Value > 0 and increment Count only on TRUE. Complete all three inputs, including non-positive ones.
Output Count after repetition. The requirement asks for one completed count, not three intermediate counts.

teachingBlocks.text: Changing the input values is a useful way to challenge the translation. All non-positive values must leave Count at zero; three positive values must give three. A zero input is data, not a stopping signal in this task. A sentinel would need to be explicitly specified.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the meaning as well as the notation

teachingBlocks.text: The basic constructs are introduced in Lesson 053; Lessons 073 and 076–078 explain their precise statement forms. Here the supplied design determines which operations belong together. Do not invent new validation rules or outputs while translating it.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the design boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow every flowchart edge

leadVisual.title: Flowchart: count positives in three inputs

coreExplanation: Preserve both outcomes, the back edge and the path to the final output.
A loop update outside the inner IF executes after either branch.

teachingBlocks.text: A flowchart's arrows specify execution order. A decision requires both outcomes to reach the correct next operation. A backward arrow identifies repetition; determine which state changes before execution returns to the decision. A terminal marks the end of that execution path.
teachingBlocks.title: Read each directed edge

teachingBlocks.text: The flowchart below implements the same three-value design. Count and Index are initialised before the first test. Each completed input advances Index once, including a non-positive value. The loop exits to the final output when Index exceeds three; execution ends after that output.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the repeated and final paths
Map this graph to the direct WHILE implementation
rows: TRUE enters the loop; FALSE reaches OUTPUT Count.
Only the TRUE branch increments Count.
Index <- Index + 1 runs after ENDIF, on either path.
ENDWHILE returns control to the Index test.

teachingBlocks.text: After the third value, Index becomes 4. The next test is FALSE, so no fourth input is read. Moving the Index update inside the positive branch would mean a non-positive input fails to advance the processed-input count.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the exit

teachingBlocks.text: The previous unit expresses the known three inputs with FOR. The direct WHILE version below makes the graph’s initialisation, test and update explicit. Compare their consumed inputs, decisions and final output. This does not require an assumption about the FOR control variable after the loop has ended.
teachingBlocks.title: Recognise an equivalent representation

objectives.description: Declare and initialise constants.
Declare variables with Cambridge data types.
Assign expression values to variables.
materialTitles: Evaluate the right-hand expression before storing its result

objectives.description: Read keyboard input and write console output.
materialTitles: Evaluate the right-hand expression before storing its result

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare variables and constants

leadVisual.title: Declarations and literals

coreExplanation: DECLARE gives a variable its type; initialise it before reading its value.
Use CONSTANT Name = Literal; quoted STRING, quoted CHAR and BOOLEAN literals are different types.

teachingBlocks.text: Use DECLARE Identifier : DataType for a variable. Choose INTEGER for whole-number counts, REAL for values that may have a fractional part, BOOLEAN for TRUE or FALSE, CHAR for one character and STRING for text. A declaration does not provide an initial value.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose names and types

teachingBlocks.text: Declare and initialise a named constant with CONSTANT Identifier = Literal. Its type follows from the literal and its value remains fixed. Use double quotes for a STRING literal and single quotes for a CHAR literal. In this notation a constant declaration uses a literal, rather than an expression involving other identifiers.
teachingBlocks.title: Give constants literal values
Separate three responsibilities
rows: A variable name and permitted data type.
The current value of the declared variable.
A new declaration or a permanent restriction to zero.
A fixed named value supplied by a literal.
A variable that can later store a different rate.

teachingBlocks.text: A meaningful name exposes a value’s role: Quantity is an INTEGER count while ProductCode is a STRING if leading zeros matter and arithmetic is not required. Lesson 058 develops the data types in full, including DATE; this lesson concentrates on using declarations correctly in programs.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose from the meaning of the data

teachingBlocks.text: A constant avoids repeating an unexplained literal throughout a program. Changing its declaration for a different version updates all uses of the name. In Cambridge pseudocode, CONSTANT DoubleRate = TaxRate * 2 is not a valid constant declaration: only a literal is allowed on its right side.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish a fixed value from a computed value

knowledgeUnits.heading: Obtain, assign and output values

leadVisual.title: Evaluate the right-hand expression before storing its result

coreExplanation: Obtain all inputs before calculations that read them.
Assignment evaluates the right side and replaces the left-side variable; OUTPUT displays values.

teachingBlocks.text: Assignment evaluates the expression on the right and stores the result in the variable on the left. Total <- Price * Quantity changes Total; Total = Price * Quantity is a comparison. A later assignment replaces the variable's earlier value. INPUT obtains a value from the keyboard, while OUTPUT writes a value or expression to the console.
teachingBlocks.title: Evaluate before storing

teachingBlocks.text: For a purchase with tax charged per item, read Price and Quantity before using either. Compute Tax <- Price * TaxRate, then multiply the tax-inclusive item price by Quantity. Declaring all identifiers, obtaining the inputs and assigning intermediate results in order prevents undefined values from reaching the calculation.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the purchase dependencies
Read Quantity <- Quantity + 1
items: Add one to that old value.
Replace Quantity with the result. The statement is an update, not a mathematical equality.

teachingBlocks.text: B <- A copies A’s value at that moment. A later assignment to A does not cause B to be recalculated. A variable on the right side must already have a value, even when it is also the destination on the left.
teachingBlocks.title: Copy a value rather than establish a link

teachingBlocks.text: OUTPUT can display several values separated by commas, for example OUTPUT "Total: ", Total. The text is a label and Total supplies the current number. Output does not store a new variable. Constructing a reusable STRING with & is a separate operation taught in Lesson 075.
teachingBlocks.title: Make the report understandable

objectives.description: Assign expression values to variables.
Use arithmetic and logical operators in expressions.
materialTitles: Test both sides of the rule
Convert minutes and test a permitted interval

knowledgeUnits.heading: Evaluate arithmetic and integer division

leadVisual.title: Evaluate before assignment

coreExplanation: Use parentheses to make expression grouping explicit.
For non-negative integers, DIV gives complete groups and MOD the remainder; / gives real division.

teachingBlocks.text: Arithmetic expressions use +, -, * and /. Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction; parentheses override that order. The / operator produces a real division result even when both operands are integers. Choose a REAL destination when a fractional result is possible.
teachingBlocks.title: Evaluate grouped expressions

teachingBlocks.text: DIV gives the integer quotient and MOD gives the remainder. For a non-negative number of minutes, Minutes DIV 60 gives complete hours and Minutes MOD 60 gives minutes left over. The divisor must be non-zero. Parentheses are useful when an expression combines arithmetic operations with a comparison.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate quotient and remainder
Evaluate Total <- 2 + 3 * 4
items: Store 14 in Total. Parentheses around 2 + 3 would instead produce 20.

teachingBlocks.text: For the non-negative integer quantities and positive integer divisors used here, the remainder is at least zero and less than the divisor. This gives two checks: reconstruct the original quantity and check the remainder’s range. DIV is not rounding to the nearest integer, and / may give a fractional REAL result.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the result without repeating the calculation

teachingBlocks.text: All operands must be defined, and a divisor must not be zero. These examples deliberately avoid language-dependent signed-remainder conventions. For a money example, the mathematical amount and a chosen display format such as two decimal places are different requirements.
teachingBlocks.title: State the arithmetic assumptions

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build and test Boolean expressions

leadVisual.title: Test both sides of the rule

coreExplanation: Comparisons produce BOOLEAN results; AND, OR and NOT combine them.
Test each endpoint and both outside regions; use parentheses and complete operands.

teachingBlocks.text: Comparisons =, <>, <, <=, > and >= produce Boolean values. AND requires both conditions to be true; OR is true when either or both are true; NOT reverses a Boolean value. Write each comparison in full, including the identifier on both sides of an interval test.
teachingBlocks.title: Build complete comparisons

teachingBlocks.text: An adult threshold uses Age >= 18, which accepts 18 and every greater age. An inclusive interval from zero to 180 uses (Minutes >= 0) AND (Minutes <= 180). Test both endpoints and outside values. Its complement uses (Minutes < 0) OR (Minutes > 180); replacing AND by OR without changing the comparisons admits every value.
teachingBlocks.title: Test a range and its complement

teachingBlocks.text: The comparison first produces a BOOLEAN. NOT reverses the suspension flag, then AND combines those two truth values. NOT should apply to the intended condition: NOT (Age >= 18 AND NOT Suspended) rejects the whole eligibility rule, not just suspension.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow intermediate Boolean results

teachingBlocks.text: Write both comparisons in full. Minutes >= 0 AND <= 180 leaves the second comparison without an operand. Minutes >= 0 OR Minutes <= 180 accepts every integer: even an out-of-range value meets the other half. Lesson 056 establishes boundary reasoning; here use it inside assignments and program conditions.
teachingBlocks.title: Diagnose a plausible-looking condition

teachingBlocks.text: Do not assume that AND always skips its second operand when the first is false. If an operand could divide by zero or access an invalid array index, put that operation behind a separate IF guard. Logical truth and an implementation’s evaluation strategy are different issues.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep potentially invalid operations behind a guard

workedExample.title: Convert minutes and test a permitted interval

materialTitles: Truncate first, then shift the six possible integer results
Use a numeric function and store one random draw
Apply the supplied string and character interfaces
Positions, counts and concatenation preserve the characters

objectives.description: Use an unfamiliar routine from its supplied interface and definition.
explanationUnits: Apply supplied string and character interfaces
materialTitles: Apply the supplied string and character interfaces

objectives.description: Apply the supplied definitions of string manipulation functions.
explanationUnits: Apply supplied string and character interfaces
materialTitles: Apply the supplied string and character interfaces
Positions, counts and concatenation preserve the characters

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use numeric built-in functions

leadVisual.title: Truncate first, then shift the six possible integer results

coreExplanation: Check the argument type, order and returned type before using a routine.
RAND(N) returns a REAL in [0, N); INT(RAND(N)) + 1 gives integers 1 through N for positive INTEGER N.

teachingBlocks.text: A built-in function is supplied by the language; a library routine supplies reusable operations through an interface. A function call gives arguments in the specified order and supplies a returned value to the surrounding expression. Check the accepted types and the meaning of the result before using it.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the routine contract

teachingBlocks.text: INT(X) returns the integer part of real X. RAND(X), for a positive integer bound X, returns a real value from zero inclusive to X exclusive. INT(RAND(6)) + 1 therefore produces an integer from one to six. The addition shifts the possible values after truncation; RAND(6) alone does not return a die face.
teachingBlocks.title: Build a bounded integer result
Follow the die expression through its stages

teachingBlocks.text: These selected random values illustrate the transformation; they are not predicted outputs of a fresh random call. A call returns one value. Calling RAND again requests another draw, so store a result when two later operations must use the same draw.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate a possible result from a promised result

teachingBlocks.text: INT takes the integer part, rather than rounding to the nearest integer. The non-negative inputs here make the truncation and interval argument explicit. Defining your own function is taught in Lesson 081; using a supplied function only needs its interface and result contract.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the result in an expression

workedExample.title: Use a numeric function and store one random draw

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply supplied string and character interfaces

leadVisual.title: Supplied interfaces for this lesson

coreExplanation: For supplied MID, the third argument is a character count, not an ending position.
Keep STRING and CHAR types distinct; use valid positions and count spaces.

teachingBlocks.text: In examinations, string manipulation functions are supplied; other functions absent from the pseudocode guide are also defined. Read those definitions rather than assuming that a familiar name uses another language's indexing or argument order. The table here supplies the contracts needed for the lesson's examples.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the supplied definitions

teachingBlocks.text: LENGTH(Text) returns a string's character count; MID(Text, Start, Count) takes Count characters beginning at the one-based Start position; RIGHT(Text, Count) takes the rightmost characters. UCASE and LCASE here accept and return a single CHAR. Supply indices and counts valid for the stated string; the examples do not rely on unspecified out-of-range behaviour.
teachingBlocks.title: Track positions and result types
Distinguish a start position from a count

teachingBlocks.text: A STRING of one character and a CHAR are still different declared types. Under the supplied interfaces, UCASE accepts Letter : CHAR, not Word : STRING. A digit such as '7' has no upper-case alternative and is returned unchanged. Space and punctuation count as characters: LENGTH("A B!") is 4.
teachingBlocks.title: Respect type and content

teachingBlocks.text: For the complete program below, Word contains at least four characters and Letter is one CHAR. That makes MID(Word, 2, 3) and RIGHT(Word, 2) valid. LENGTH("") is zero, but do not apply these non-empty slices to an empty string or invent an out-of-range result.
teachingBlocks.title: Give the calls valid inputs

teachingBlocks.text: An unfamiliar name such as TAKE or SLICE does not change the method: read its definition, match arguments in order, determine the return type, then use the result. String functions are supplied in examination questions; learning the interface-reading process is more useful than assuming a language’s familiar indexing rule.
teachingBlocks.title: Transfer to an unfamiliar routine

workedExample.title: Apply the supplied string and character interfaces

knowledgeUnits.heading: Construct strings with concatenation

leadVisual.title: Positions, counts and concatenation preserve the characters

coreExplanation: Use & to concatenate strings; include required spaces or separators explicitly.
Extracted digits remain STRING data; concatenation does not change the source.

teachingBlocks.text: Concatenation joins two STRING values with & to produce one STRING. It can build a label from extracted parts while preserving their character order.
teachingBlocks.title: Join text into a new value
Build the label from CS2046AB
items: MID(Code, 3, 4) returns "2046". It is text, even though all four characters are digits.
Digits & "-" & Suffix produces the new STRING "2046-AB".
Assign that result to Label. The source Code remains "CS2046AB"; OUTPUT Label displays the stored result.

teachingBlocks.text: The & operator joins strings exactly as supplied. It does not insert spaces or separators automatically: "Ada" & "Lovelace" produces "AdaLovelace", whereas an explicit " " preserves the gap. Joining "" adds no characters. Numeric addition uses + and has a different purpose.
teachingBlocks.title: Make every character intentional

teachingBlocks.text: OUTPUT "Label: ", Label displays two values without requiring one combined variable. Label <- "Label: " & Label constructs a reusable string. Do not assume that & implicitly converts an INTEGER to STRING; use a conversion routine only when its interface has been supplied.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish concatenation from multiple-value output

objectives.description: Write IF, ELSE and nested IF statements.
materialTitles: Independent decisions and exclusive alternatives follow different paths

objectives.description: Write a CASE structure.
explanationUnits: Select by the value of one identifier

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write alternatives and nested decisions

leadVisual.title: Independent decisions and exclusive alternatives follow different paths

coreExplanation: An IF/ELSE selects one branch; separate IF statements can both execute.
In nested selection, the outer branch determines whether the inner decision is reached.

teachingBlocks.text: An IF statement executes its THEN block when the condition is true. An optional ELSE block handles the false outcome. ENDIF closes that decision. Two independent IF statements can both execute their blocks; IF with ELSE selects only one of its alternatives.
teachingBlocks.title: Select a branch

teachingBlocks.text: Nesting puts a second decision inside a branch of the first. For adult membership, check Age >= 18 first and check Member only inside the adult branch. Give each IF its own ENDIF and indent consistently so the reader can identify which ELSE belongs to which decision.
teachingBlocks.title: Nest a decision within one branch

teachingBlocks.text: After a chosen IF branch finishes, execution continues after its matching ENDIF. An ELSE attaches to one IF, not to every earlier condition. Indentation and matching ENDIF statements make this visible; a branch that is not selected does not execute its inner tests.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow control after the branch
Four combinations in the membership program

teachingBlocks.text: Two separate IF statements can both be true. That is correct when two independent actions are required, such as counting passes and counting merits. A single classification needs exclusive alternatives: test the highest threshold first, then place the lower-threshold decision in ELSE. At 85, the two programs below intentionally have different output contracts.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose independent or exclusive actions from the requirement

knowledgeUnits.heading: Select by the value of one identifier

leadVisual.title: CASE layout

coreExplanation: Use CASE OF Identifier, labelled values or ranges, and ENDCASE.
Only the first matching clause runs; a final OTHERWISE handles unmatched values.

teachingBlocks.text: Use CASE OF Identifier when alternatives depend on the value of one identifier. Put each value or permitted range before a colon, provide its statements, and close the structure with ENDCASE. OTHERWISE handles a value that matches no listed case; no break statement is needed in Cambridge pseudocode.
teachingBlocks.title: Select from one identifier

teachingBlocks.text: For a menu, Choice 1 opens and Choice 2 saves; every other value reports Invalid. This is clearer than a long series of equality tests on Choice. Use IF for general Boolean conditions or nested rules involving different data, and ensure CASE labels express distinct intended alternatives.
teachingBlocks.title: Give unmatched values a defined route

teachingBlocks.text: CASE clauses are considered in order. After the first matching clause runs, control continues after ENDCASE; later clauses are not executed. There is no fall-through and no BREAK is needed. Keep intended ranges distinct so the case order does not hide a classification mistake.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain what happens after a match

teachingBlocks.text: OTHERWISE must come last when it is present. Without it, a value matching no clause performs no case action and execution continues after ENDCASE. IF remains more suitable for a general Boolean rule involving several different identifiers.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate optional syntax from the task requirement

objectives.description: Write a count-controlled FOR loop.
explanationUnits: Use an explicit step and direction
materialTitles: Total a specified number of integers
A negative step stops before crossing the lower endpoint
The inner loop restarts for each outer value
Visit two rows of three positions

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use inclusive count-controlled bounds

leadVisual.title: Default positive-step cases

coreExplanation: FOR uses every reachable value within inclusive bounds; default STEP is 1.
Initialise totals before, obtain each input inside, and report the completed result after the loop.

teachingBlocks.text: A FOR loop is suitable when the iteration count is known before entering the loop. Write FOR Index <- Start TO End and close it with NEXT Index. With the default step of one, the body uses Start, Start + 1 and so on up to End inclusive. Let the loop manage its control variable.
teachingBlocks.title: Count the values used by the body

teachingBlocks.text: FOR Index <- 1 TO Count performs Count iterations for a non-negative Count. Count zero gives no iterations, and Count one gives exactly one. Initialise an accumulator before the loop; obtain each new value and add it inside; report the total afterwards. A zero-item total remains the initial zero without a special loop branch.
teachingBlocks.title: Place accumulation at the correct level

teachingBlocks.text: For default STEP 1, the number of body executions is End − Start + 1 when Start <= End; otherwise it is zero. With Count 0 in this program, the initial zero is still available for output and no Value input is requested. With Count 1, exactly one input contributes.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the boundary behaviour

teachingBlocks.text: The control variable and bounds are INTEGER values. Do not assign another value to the control variable inside the loop; let FOR and NEXT manage it. A trace should record the values used in the body and not depend on an unspecified final counter value after loop termination.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep loop control separate from data

workedExample.title: Total a specified number of integers

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use an explicit step and direction

leadVisual.title: A negative step stops before crossing the lower endpoint

coreExplanation: STEP changes the control value by the stated integer amount; negative steps descend.
Stop before crossing the bound; the endpoint is visited only when the step reaches it.

teachingBlocks.text: STEP supplies the integer increment instead of the default one. A positive step moves upward; a negative step moves downward. The body runs while the control value remains within the endpoint in that direction. The endpoint is used only if the sequence of increments reaches it exactly.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose a direction and step

teachingBlocks.text: FOR Index <- 6 TO 0 STEP -2 visits 6, 4, 2 and 0. Starting at 5 with the same endpoint and step visits 5, 3 and 1, then stops before -1. A step of zero makes no progress and is unsuitable. Choose the starting value, endpoint and direction together before counting executions.
teachingBlocks.title: Check whether the endpoint is reached
Follow the last step
rows: The starting value is already outside the descending range.

teachingBlocks.text: An inclusive bound permits the endpoint; it does not force the sequence to land on it. Determine direction, list the first few values, and inspect the final candidate before counting iterations. STEP 0 provides no progress and is unsuitable for a terminating count-controlled loop.
teachingBlocks.title: Reason from successive values

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow nested count-controlled loops

leadVisual.title: The inner loop restarts for each outer value

coreExplanation: Complete the inner loop before advancing the outer loop.
Each new outer iteration restarts the inner loop; reset state at the level of the required result.

teachingBlocks.text: A nested loop puts a complete loop inside another loop’s body. The inner loop runs to completion for each outer control value. Use distinct control variables to keep the two responsibilities separate.
teachingBlocks.title: One complete inner loop belongs to each outer iteration

teachingBlocks.text: Each time execution reaches the inner FOR header, Column starts at 1 again. After (1,3), NEXT Column finishes that inner loop; NEXT Row advances Row, and the next inner loop begins at (2,1). There are two complete groups of three outputs, not one run of three outputs shared between both rows.
teachingBlocks.title: Trace the boundary between groups

teachingBlocks.text: Count is reset once before both loops because it measures all body executions. A separate per-row count would instead be reset just inside the outer loop. This placement principle is the same one used for row and column totals in Lesson 062; no array is needed to understand the control flow here.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the counter to what it counts

workedExample.title: Visit two rows of three positions

objectives.description: Write a post-condition REPEAT loop.
materialTitles: REPEAT: execute the body before testing
Read a mark in the inclusive range
A condition decides either to continue or to stop
Preserve the empty-input path with a guard

objectives.description: Write a pre-condition WHILE loop.
materialTitles: WHILE: test before entering the body
A condition decides either to continue or to stop
Preserve the empty-input path with a guard

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a post-condition REPEAT loop

leadVisual.title: REPEAT: execute the body before testing

coreExplanation: REPEAT executes before testing; UNTIL TRUE ends repetition.
Obtain a fresh attempt inside the loop and make the stopping condition express acceptance.

teachingBlocks.text: A post-condition loop executes its body before testing, so the body runs at least once.

teachingBlocks.title: Read the REPEAT rules
items: Write REPEAT, the body, then UNTIL Condition. There is no ENDREPEAT.
Stop and continue after the loop.
Return to the body for another iteration.

teachingBlocks.text: Read Mark inside the body and accept it when (Mark >= 0) AND (Mark <= 100). An invalid integer triggers another input. This example assumes integer input: the range test does not itself handle text instead of a number.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply the rule to validation
Follow integer attempts −1, 101, 100
rows: TRUE: leave the loop and output 100.

teachingBlocks.text: The condition uses the value just obtained in the body. If the first input is 0, both comparisons are true on the first test and only one read occurs. If no valid integer is ever supplied, the program continues requesting input; a stopping guarantee would need an additional attempt limit.
teachingBlocks.title: State what makes the loop finish

teachingBlocks.text: A range check establishes whether an integer is allowed; it does not establish whether the original real-world mark was entered accurately. Nor does this integer-input example handle text typed in place of a number.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep validation within its stated purpose

workedExample.title: Read a mark in the inclusive range

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use a pre-condition WHILE loop

leadVisual.title: WHILE: test before entering the body

coreExplanation: WHILE tests before the body and may execute zero times.
Define the condition data before the first test and update it on every continuing path.

teachingBlocks.text: A pre-condition loop tests before the body; the body may run zero times.

teachingBlocks.title: Read the WHILE rules
items: Write WHILE Condition, the indented body and ENDWHILE. Do not add DO to the header.
Execute the body, then return to the condition.
Skip the body and continue after ENDWHILE.

teachingBlocks.text: Read Value before the first test so it is defined. While Value <> -1, add it and read again. The sentinel is not added: a first input of -1 leaves Total at zero.
teachingBlocks.title: Initialise and update the condition

teachingBlocks.text: A sentinel is a value reserved to signal the end. This task permits integers other than -1 as data, including zero; if -1 itself needed to be ordinary data, the input contract would need another ending mechanism. Read the next value on every processed path, even when a later version filters some data out.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate a stopping signal from a data value

teachingBlocks.text: For text files, the comparable pre-condition is NOT EOF before READFILE, as in Lesson 065. The keyboard priming input used here should not be copied blindly into a file algorithm: an empty file must be checked before its first read.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the loop form without confusing input sources

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare test position and polarity

leadVisual.title: A condition decides either to continue or to stop

coreExplanation: WHILE TRUE continues; UNTIL TRUE stops.
Changing loop form must preserve the zero-iteration path, data updates and output placement.

teachingBlocks.text: WHILE Valid continues on TRUE; UNTIL Valid stops on TRUE. Moving the same condition between loop forms can therefore reverse the behaviour.
teachingBlocks.title: Check condition meaning

teachingBlocks.text: Negating the condition alone does not preserve a zero-iteration path. Check the allowed inputs; an outer decision may be needed before REPEAT to preserve a WHILE loop's original behaviour.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve the first-iteration rule
Preserve a sentinel algorithm when changing the loop form
items: Read Value before either form so the first sentinel can mean no data.
Only enter REPEAT when Value <> -1; this preserves the zero-body path.
Add the current data value, then obtain the next one.
UNTIL Value = -1 ends processing. Both programs output Total once afterwards.

teachingBlocks.text: The complete alternative below consumes the same inputs and reports the same totals as the WHILE example. Negating the condition is only one part of the conversion: the first-execution rule, input placement and final output must also be preserved.
teachingBlocks.title: Compare observable behaviour

workedExample.title: Preserve the empty-input path with a guard

objectives.description: Justify why one loop structure may be better suited to solve a problem than the others
explanationUnits: Combine a condition with a maximum attempt count
materialTitles: Continue only while the password is wrong and attempts remain

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify from the problem's conditions

leadVisual.title: Requirement determines suitability

coreExplanation: Justify a loop by the known count, required first attempt or possible empty input.
Explain necessary setup for alternatives; do not claim only one loop can ever work.

teachingBlocks.text: A loop justification connects a property of the problem to a property of the chosen structure. Use FOR when the count is known before repetition. Use REPEAT when an action must happen before its result can be checked. Use WHILE when the continuation rule can be checked before processing and no body execution may be needed.
teachingBlocks.title: Start with the input and stopping contract

teachingBlocks.text: Different loop structures can often implement the same result with additional setup. Explain suitability rather than claiming that alternatives are impossible or inherently slower. For twelve readings a count-controlled header exposes the count; for repeated menu input a post-condition loop places the first request before validation.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain suitability in context
Turn a property into a justification
rows: One new reading per iteration gives exactly seven.
An option must be entered before checking it
The first attempt supplies the value for validation.
The first item may already be the sentinel
No data is processed when the first test is false.

teachingBlocks.text: Distinguish attempts from accepted data. Three accepted ratings may require five attempts. A FOR for three accepted slots can contain a REPEAT for each slot’s attempts. A FOR for only three raw attempts would implement a different contract.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the quantity that is controlled

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine a condition with a maximum attempt count

leadVisual.title: Continue only while the password is wrong and attempts remain

coreExplanation: Continue only while the password is wrong AND attempts remain.
Count every attempt; the equivalent stopping rule is success OR the limit reached.

teachingBlocks.text: Some repetitions end for either of two reasons. A password attempt sequence stops on success or after three attempts. Initialise Password and Attempts before WHILE, then continue only while the password is wrong AND fewer than three attempts have occurred. Increment the counter after every input, including a successful attempt.
teachingBlocks.title: Maintain both continuation requirements

teachingBlocks.text: A WHILE loop states the combined continuation rule directly and can be adapted when a preliminary condition should prevent attempts. A REPEAT loop could also express the task if at least one attempt is required, using an UNTIL condition for success OR three attempts. A fixed three-iteration FOR without an extra guard would continue asking after early success.
teachingBlocks.title: Compare equivalent stopping rules

teachingBlocks.text: Using OR in the continuation condition would allow one true half to override the other stopping event: a correct first attempt could still be followed by another prompt, or a wrong third attempt could be followed by a fourth. Success OR exhausted attempts is instead the corresponding stopping condition.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the connector from the rule

teachingBlocks.text: For this task at least one attempt is allowed. REPEAT therefore avoids the artificial initial Password value used by WHILE: input supplies Password before UNTIL tests it. Both complete versions count the successful input and stop at the same point. If a prior lock state could prohibit all attempts, a pre-condition or an outer guard would be needed.
teachingBlocks.title: Compare complete solutions rather than isolated headers

objectives.description: Define and call a procedure.
materialTitles: Call an action, then resume the caller

objectives.description: Explain when a procedure is appropriate.
materialTitles: Call an action, then resume the caller

objectives.description: Define a procedure with none, one or several parameters.
explanationUnits: Match arguments to a procedure interface
materialTitles: Call an action, then resume the caller
Call actions and resume the main program

objectives.description: Pass a parameter by value.
materialTitles: A copied value and a reference use different storage
Observe both local and caller values
Compare the same assignments on local copies

objectives.description: Pass a parameter by reference and trace the caller change.
materialTitles: A copied value and a reference use different storage
Observe both local and caller values
Compare the same assignments on local copies

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define and call procedures

leadVisual.title: Procedure interfaces

coreExplanation: Define with PROCEDURE … ENDPROCEDURE; invoke with CALL Name(arguments).
Control returns to the next caller statement; a procedure supplies an action, not a function result.

teachingBlocks.text: A procedure groups statements that perform an action. Use it for a responsibility such as displaying a heading or updating a total when no function result is required in an expression. Define it with PROCEDURE Name(parameters) and ENDPROCEDURE; invoke it with CALL Name(arguments). A definition alone does not execute the body.
teachingBlocks.title: Give an action one responsibility

teachingBlocks.text: A procedure can take no parameters, one parameter or several parameters. Heading() needs none, Show(Value) receives one value, and Add(Total, Amount) receives two. State each formal parameter's type and preserve the declared order at the call. Empty parentheses remain in a no-parameter definition and call.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate the definition from its calls
Follow a procedure call
items: The main program reaches CALL Heading(). The definition itself has not printed anything.
Control transfers to Heading and OUTPUT prints Results.
Continue at the next statement after CALL, not at the beginning of the main program.

teachingBlocks.text: Use a procedure when the caller requests an action, such as displaying a heading or updating a running total. Reusing one body avoids copying that action at each call site and gives one place to maintain it. That is a clarity and maintenance benefit; the call itself does not prove faster execution.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain when a procedure helps

teachingBlocks.text: The interface in the next unit states which data an action receives. A procedure may have no parameters, one, or several. It does not provide a function result for an expression, but it may display output or deliberately update a caller variable through a reference parameter.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep three kinds of effect distinct

workedExample.title: Call an action, then resume the caller

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match arguments to a procedure interface

leadVisual.title: Zero, one and two arguments

coreExplanation: A parameter is declared in the header; an argument is supplied at the call.
Match the number, order, types and passing modes, as well as the intended effect.

teachingBlocks.text: The caller and the procedure need an agreed interface. Its name identifies the action; its ordered, typed parameters specify the data the caller must supply and which data may be updated.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the interface before making the call

teachingBlocks.text: A formal parameter is the name declared in a subprogram header. An argument is the value, variable or expression supplied by the caller. The names need not be the same. Match the number, order, types and modes: Total receives the first argument because of its position, not because the caller must name its variable Total.
teachingBlocks.title: Introduce the terms at the point of use

teachingBlocks.text: The header records the name and typed parameter list. The interface also needs the intended behaviour: Add increases Total by Amount, rather than setting it to Amount or printing it. A caller can use that contract without depending on the internal statements.
teachingBlocks.title: A valid type is not the whole contract

teachingBlocks.text: Heading() has an empty parameter list. Show(Score) supplies one argument. Add(Score, 3) supplies two. Supplying an extra argument, reversing unlike parameter roles or passing text where an INTEGER is required does not match the interface.
teachingBlocks.title: Check calls systematically

workedExample.title: Call actions and resume the main program

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace parameter passing

leadVisual.title: A copied value and a reference use different storage

coreExplanation: BYVAL copies a value; BYREF provides access to the caller’s variable.
Trace local values and caller state separately; use a temporary value before overwriting either side of a swap.

teachingBlocks.title: Choose the parameter mode
rows: A copy of the argument's value; this is the default mode
A reference to the caller's variable
A suitable value, variable or expression
An assignable variable of the required type

teachingBlocks.text: Use reference passing for data the procedure is intended to update. A literal such as 5 or a temporary expression cannot supply a BYREF variable.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose by the intended effect

teachingBlocks.text: Trace the local view and caller state separately. The value printed inside a BYVAL procedure does not establish that its caller has changed.
teachingBlocks.title: Trace both sides of the call
Trace the two calls in the supplied program

teachingBlocks.text: Each call establishes its own parameters and local variables. A later call does not inherit the earlier BYVAL copy. A local name can match a caller name without sharing storage; sharing here is determined by BYREF, not spelling. This is enough scope information to trace these examples; no call-stack implementation is assumed.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate the active local environment from the caller

teachingBlocks.text: In Swap, Left and Right refer to the two distinct caller variables A and B. Temp must preserve the original left value before Left is overwritten. The BYVAL variant swaps only two local copies: its internal output can look correct while the caller remains unchanged.
teachingBlocks.title: Use two reference parameters for a complete swap

teachingBlocks.text: When a procedure header specifies no passing mode, assume BYVAL. A single BYVAL or BYREF marker may cover several parameters passed in that mode; a missing repeated marker does not reset the mode. The examples here write the mode for each parameter to keep the calls unambiguous. A BYREF argument must be an assignable variable of the required type, not a literal or a calculated temporary value.
teachingBlocks.title: Make reference updates intentional

workedExample.title: Observe both local and caller values

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define and use a returned value

leadVisual.title: RETURN supplies a value to the caller’s expression

coreExplanation: RETURNS declares the result type; RETURN supplies a value and ends the call.
A returned value replaces the function call inside an expression; do not prefix the call with CALL.

teachingBlocks.text: A function is a subprogram that returns a value. Its header uses FUNCTION Name(parameters) RETURNS DataType and its body uses RETURN Expression, ending with ENDFUNCTION. The returned expression must match the declared result type, and every reachable result path must supply a return value.
teachingBlocks.title: Define a typed result

teachingBlocks.text: Call a function where its result is needed: in an assignment, condition, output or another expression. Total <- Price + Tax(Price) adds the returned tax to the original price. Do not prefix a function call with CALL; that keyword invokes a procedure. Function parameters use value passing in this Cambridge notation.
teachingBlocks.title: Use the result at the call site
Evaluate Total <- Price + Tax(Price) for Price 50
items: The caller supplies its REAL value 50 to the function parameter.
RETURN supplies that REAL value to the pending expression.
Replace Tax(Price) with 10, calculate 50 + 10, then assign 60 to Total.

teachingBlocks.title: Compare three different destinations
rows: Supply the current function result and finish this call.

teachingBlocks.text: RETURNS REAL describes the result type in the header; it does not perform a return. RETURN 10.0 supplies one result during execution. A function can return a number, BOOLEAN or other permitted type; the caller must use it in a compatible expression. Cambridge function parameters use value passing.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate a type promise from execution

workedExample.title: Use a function result in a calculation

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace branches and early returns

leadVisual.title: RETURN completes this function call immediately

coreExplanation: Cover every possible result path, including equality and false branches.
After RETURN executes, later statements in that invocation are skipped.

teachingBlocks.text: A function can choose its result with selection. The chosen execution path must supply a value of the declared result type. RETURN immediately completes the current call; it does not merely display a value or wait for ENDFUNCTION.
teachingBlocks.title: Every reachable result path must return a value

teachingBlocks.text: For equal arguments, the ELSE branch returns Second, which still equals the required larger value. A function with only the TRUE return would leave equal or smaller first arguments without a result. Test both branches and equality, not only an example that reaches the first RETURN.
teachingBlocks.title: Account for the missing path

teachingBlocks.text: RETURN acts immediately. DeliveryFee has a free result for a zero-item order; that branch returns 0.0 and the later fee formula is not evaluated. A positive Quantity skips the first RETURN and reaches the final one. Replacing RETURN with OUTPUT would print inside the function while leaving the caller without that returned result.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain an early return

teachingBlocks.text: The delivery task assumes non-negative integer quantities. It is not a negative-quantity validator. A function with several RETURN statements still returns one value in a particular call: only the statement reached first can complete that invocation.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep paths and assumptions explicit

workedExample.title: Return a value from each branch

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read headers, parameters and arguments

leadVisual.title: Read the validity interface

coreExplanation: An interface states the name, ordered parameters, result type and behaviour.
Distinguish the argument, formal parameter and caller variable receiving the result.

teachingBlocks.text: A subprogram interface describes how it can be called: its name, ordered formal parameters, their types and relevant passing modes, plus the result type for a function. The header records these details. A caller should be able to use the interface without depending on the internal calculation steps.
teachingBlocks.title: Read a function’s result contract

teachingBlocks.text: A parameter is the identifier declared in the subprogram header. An argument is the value, variable or expression supplied at a call. In ValidMark(Value), Mark is the formal parameter and Value is the argument; the result is a BOOLEAN. A correct interface also needs a clear behavioural contract, such as accepting marks from zero to 100 inclusive.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect arguments, parameters and destination
Read Allowed <- ValidMark(TestMark)
rows: Caller variable supplying an INTEGER argument.
Formal parameter receiving a value copy.
Caller BOOLEAN variable receiving the returned result.

teachingBlocks.text: A function may receive multiple arguments, as Larger does, or none. ReadRating() has no arguments because its body obtains its own keyboard input; the empty parentheses still identify a function call. Its returned INTEGER can be assigned to Result. Having no parameters does not mean the body performs no work.
teachingBlocks.title: Use zero, one and multiple arguments

teachingBlocks.text: The no-argument example declares Rating locally, reads at least once, validates integers from 1 to 5, and returns only the accepted value. Input assumptions and the returned meaning are part of its interface. A no-argument function is a useful syntax example here, not a requirement to use keyboard input inside every function.
teachingBlocks.title: Read a complete no-argument example

teachingBlocks.text: Lesson 085 uses these interface contracts in structure charts, and Lesson 088 checks their connections during integration testing. This lesson establishes the typed call, returned value and immediate caller use on which that work depends.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect to program design

workedExample.title: Use an argument and a Boolean result

objectives.description: Write efficient pseudocode
explanationUnits: Reuse a calculation whose inputs do not change
Share a traversal between independent results
materialTitles: Preserve the actions with one comparison
Calculate the unchanged area on every iteration
Calculate once after input, then reuse
Processing reads for the same stored data
Compute two statistics in separate passes
Reuse each element for both statistics

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine repeated decisions safely

leadVisual.title: Before combining the conditions

coreExplanation: Remove repeated work only when its inputs and required effects permit it.
State the operation saved, then compare outputs, state and boundary behaviour.

teachingBlocks.text: Efficient pseudocode avoids unnecessary operations while remaining correct and understandable. Look for repeated calculations, repeated tests with unchanged operands and avoidable traversals. Meaningful identifiers and indentation support review, but a shorter line count alone does not establish fewer operations.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify work whose result cannot have changed

teachingBlocks.text: Combine the pass-count increment and Pass output inside one IF Mark >= 50 block. Keep their order, keep Count initialisation before the branch and keep the final count output afterwards. The change removes one comparison, not either of the required actions.
teachingBlocks.title: Make a specific improvement

teachingBlocks.text: If intervening code changed Mark, the two comparisons could have different results and could not simply be combined. Check data dependencies and output order before removing repeated-looking work. Tests below, at and above the boundary expose different possible mistakes, although a few passing tests are not a proof for every input.
teachingBlocks.title: Preserve behaviour before counting a benefit

teachingBlocks.text: Meaningful names and indentation make code easier to inspect. Factoring repeated code into a procedure can improve maintenance. Fewer repeated comparisons, calculations or data visits can reduce computational work. These are related benefits, but they are not interchangeable measurements.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate clarity, reuse and execution work

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reuse a calculation whose inputs do not change

leadVisual.title: Fixed operands, repeated output

coreExplanation: Move a calculation only after its inputs are defined and when they remain unchanged.
Compare operation counts under stated input conditions, including any newly executed path.

teachingBlocks.text: A loop-invariant calculation has the same result on every iteration because its inputs remain unchanged. Reusing its result can avoid repeated work, provided the new placement preserves the program’s required behaviour.
teachingBlocks.title: Move an unchanged calculation outside repetition
Check whether Width * Height is loop-invariant
items: Width and Height are both read before the loop.
Neither value is assigned or input inside the loop.
Each of the Count reports must show the same product.
Calculate Area once after input, then reuse it for each output.

teachingBlocks.text: The complete examples assume a positive integer Count and non-negative real dimensions. With Width 3, Height 4 and Count 3, both output 12 three times. The original multiplies three times; the revised program multiplies once. In general the multiplication count falls from N to 1 for positive N, while the N outputs remain.
teachingBlocks.title: Count exactly what changes

teachingBlocks.text: If Count could be zero, the revised version would calculate an unused product once, while the original would not. Its output would still be empty for these valid operands, but the claim of saving work would not apply. If the moved expression could fail, evaluating it on a previously skipped path could also change behaviour.
teachingBlocks.title: Consider a skipped loop before moving work

teachingBlocks.text: A parcel program reads a new Weight on each iteration. Even with fixed Rate, Weight * Rate changes, so the full product must stay after that input. Only obtaining the fixed rate can remain outside. A constant multiplier does not make the whole expression invariant.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a counterexample

workedExample.title: Calculate the unchanged area on every iteration

knowledgeUnits.heading: Share a traversal between independent results

leadVisual.title: Processing reads for the same stored data

coreExplanation: One traversal can update independent results from the same element.
Initialise each accumulator once; preserve dependencies on results that are not yet available.

teachingBlocks.text: Two computations can share one traversal when both can use the same current element and neither needs the other’s completed result first. The total and pass count of a set of marks meet this condition.
teachingBlocks.title: Accumulate independent results during one traversal

teachingBlocks.text: The supplied programs first store five already valid marks, each from 0 to 100. One then traverses them to calculate Total and traverses again to count passes. The revised version reads one element into Mark, uses that value for both updates and continues. Both accumulators are initialised before the processing loop.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify shared access without changing the data

teachingBlocks.text: Count processing reads separately from the input stage, which is unchanged. The original reads five elements for the total and five for the count; the revised reads each once, giving 10 versus 5 reads. For 30 elements the same comparison is 60 versus 30. This does not establish that wall-clock runtime halves: input, output and other operations still exist.
teachingBlocks.title: Define the work being counted

teachingBlocks.text: Combine only computations whose dependencies allow it. Counting values greater than the final mean normally needs that mean first; it cannot use the still-changing partial mean as a substitute. A second pass over retained values is then meaningful work rather than redundant work.
teachingBlocks.title: Recognise a necessary second pass

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn the complete design into responsibilities

leadVisual.title: Responsibilities for one consistent scenario

coreExplanation: State accepted-input count, validity bounds, pass threshold and final outputs together.
Keep validation decisions separate from accepted-data updates.

teachingBlocks.text: Implement this structured English: initialise Total and Passed to zero; obtain three valid integer marks, accepting the interval zero to 100 inclusive; for each accepted mark add it to Total and increase Passed when it is at least 50; finally output the mean and pass count. Incorrectly typed inputs are outside this task's assumptions.
teachingBlocks.title: Translate the complete marks requirement

teachingBlocks.text: Separate deciding validity from updating the accumulated results. The main program controls the number of accepted marks, the validation function answers a Boolean question, and the recording procedure performs the updates. All three parts must use the same interval, threshold and accepted-mark count.
teachingBlocks.title: Give each component one responsibility
Make the input and output contract explicit
rows: Integers; keep asking until exactly three valid marks have been accepted. Enough input is supplied to finish.
0 through 100 inclusive. Invalid attempts are retried within the same slot.
Total all accepted marks; count marks >= 50.
One mean followed by the pass count after all three accepted marks.
Non-integer input handling, persistence and an attempt limit are not part of this task.

teachingBlocks.text: The main program owns control and the accumulated state. ValidMark answers a question without updating those accumulators. RecordMark assumes it receives an accepted mark and updates the two statistics. Calling it before validation would violate that precondition even if its syntax were correct.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect responsibility to a precondition

knowledgeUnits.heading: Nest validation inside the known count

leadVisual.title: Rejected inputs repeat within one accepted-mark slot

coreExplanation: Rejected attempts stay in the inner loop and change neither statistic.
Calculate the mean after all accepted marks have been recorded.

teachingBlocks.text: Use a FOR loop for the three accepted-mark slots. Inside each iteration, use REPEAT to obtain at least one attempt and UNTIL ValidMark(Mark) to finish validation. Only then call RecordMark. The nested input loop may repeat many times while the outer loop still advances once per accepted mark.
teachingBlocks.title: Repeat attempts within an accepted slot

teachingBlocks.text: The pass comparison belongs to the recording action after validation. With inputs -1, 0, 50, 101, 100, the accepted values are 0, 50 and 100. Their sum is 150, their mean is 50 and two satisfy the inclusive pass threshold. Output the mean and count after all accepted marks have been recorded.
teachingBlocks.title: Update only after acceptance

teachingBlocks.text: The outer FOR controls accepted slots. The inner REPEAT controls attempts for the current slot. An invalid attempt does not reach RecordMark or NEXT Index; it returns to INPUT within the same slot. Once accepted, exactly one recording update occurs before the outer loop advances.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the two levels separately

teachingBlocks.text: The divisor is three because exactly three values contribute. For attempts 20, -5, 60, 80, the accepted total is 160, so the mathematical mean is 160 / 3 and Passed is 2. Approximately 53.33 is a display rounded to two decimal places, not the exact value specified by the arithmetic.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the denominator and precision

knowledgeUnits.heading: Connect the subprograms and verify the result

leadVisual.title: A Boolean result controls acceptance; reference parameters update totals

coreExplanation: Functions return decisions into expressions; reference parameters update caller state.
Check argument order, types, parameter modes and the placement of every update.

teachingBlocks.text: ValidMark takes its INTEGER argument by value and returns a BOOLEAN used by UNTIL. RecordMark receives Mark by value, because it only reads that mark, and Total and Passed by reference, because it must update the caller's accumulators. The order at CALL RecordMark(Mark, Total, Passed) matches the header.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose how data crosses each call

teachingBlocks.text: Read the complete program from definitions through initialisation, repetition and final output. Test all failing marks, all passing marks and rejected attempts followed by valid boundaries. A correct return condition is (Mark >= 0) AND (Mark <= 100); using equality at zero would reject every other valid mark.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the whole program
Follow the accepted mark 50
items: ValidMark receives a copy of 50 and returns TRUE to UNTIL.
RecordMark receives Mark by value and references to main Total and Passed.
With Total 0 and Passed 0, add 50 and increment Passed to 1.
Control returns to main at NEXT Index. The updated accumulators persist for the next slot.

teachingBlocks.text: Test rejected attempts, both valid endpoints, all failing marks and all passing marks. Three 49s produce mean 49 and pass count 0; three 100s produce mean 100 and pass count 3. If Total and Passed were BYVAL, local updates would not accumulate in the caller between calls.
teachingBlocks.title: Use tests that expose different mistakes

teachingBlocks.text: The program definitions, main calls, interface diagram and trace all describe the same data flow. The BOOLEAN returned by ValidMark controls acceptance; RecordMark changes storage through reference parameters and provides no function result. Main performs the final division and output.
teachingBlocks.title: Read definitions and caller as one program
